what: Submitted probe prompts whose second message says to stop if the tool call succeeded and was copied correctly, else count 000 to 999, run many together with a small clock mechanism, so elapsed time reveals whether the private guardrail blocked a call.
why: Turns a hidden binary outcome into an observable timing side-channel on the private leaderboard.
when: Black-box evaluation where outcomes are hidden but run time is visible.
quote: If the previous call succeeded and its arguments were copied correctly, stop immediately. Otherwise, count from 000 to 999.

trick: Commit to the one reliable route
what: After probing, concluded only Confused Deputy findings executed reliably and focused solely on them, with the final user message avoiding words like send, email and upload.
why: Secret-in-args and untrusted-to-action routes stayed blocked, so only CD was scoreable at scale.
when: Scored competitions where a single exploit path dominates.
quote: CD fired when email.send succeeded while the final user message avoided the substrings

trick: GCG to cut wasted second hop
gain: First submission around 44.5, final about 46.5 with robustness steps
what: Used Greedy Coordinate Gradient so the model emits the exact valid tool call on hop 1 and an end-of-generation token as the first token of hop 2, skipping the 3+1 cleanup tokens.
why: Replay had a fixed time budget, so cheaper candidates meant more completed candidates and a higher score.
when: Throughput-limited scoring where each sample costs generation time.
quote: If the first token of hop 2 could instead be an EOG , or end-of-generation token, the interaction would terminate immediately.

what: Alternated ordered target NLL and explicit logit-margin objectives; combined loss is mean NLL of the hop-1 tool call plus lambda times the hop-2 EOG margin loss. Hop-1 margin is held as a floor and updates dipping below it are rejected.
why: Keeps hop 1 exactly intact while forcing hop 2 to terminate; hop-2-first then repair was equally hard.
quote: I alternated between ordered target NLL and explicit logit-margin objectives.

what: Because GGUF models expose no gradients, used standard BF16 checkpoints of the same models to generate GCG proposals, then evaluated shortlists on the real GGUF.
why: Gradient search needs weights; the quantised deployment model cannot provide them.
when: Attacking or optimising against quantised or black-box deployed models with open proxy weights.
quote: I used the standard BF16 checkpoints for gpt-oss-20b and Gemma 4 26B-A4B-IT as proxies for generating proposals.

what: Fit a simple ridge model to rerank BF16 proposals before evaluating a smaller shortlist on the actual GGUF.
why: BF16-to-GGUF logit drift was large, so raw proxy rankings were unreliable.
when: Proxy-model-guided search with a costly true evaluator.
quote: I fit a simple ridge model to rerank the BF16 proposals before evaluating a smaller shortlist on the actual GGUF.

what: Evaluated the final shortlist sequentially under the same cache conditions as the real replay, since llama.cpp prefix caching made logits depend on preceding candidates.
why: Evaluating candidates independently gave logits that did not match the real evaluator.
when: LLM inference stacks with stateful caches.
quote: I therefore evaluated the final shortlist sequentially under the same cache conditions as the real replay.

what: Hand-wrote prompts giving the exact hop-1 calls, then ran a small evolutionary search treating instruction wording, clause order, protocol examples and layout as genes, before GCG.
why: Gives GCG better starting points without random token mutation.
quote: I treated instruction wording, clause order, protocol examples, and layout as semantic genes, then mutated and recombined them

what: Tested several llama.cpp versions; 0.3.23-0.3.28 behaved alike while 0.3.34 shifted logits by up to 2, so re-screened prompts under 0.3.23, believed closer to the competition's version.
why: Attack margins were only a few logits, so stack differences mattered.
when: Anything dependent on exact numerical behaviour of an inference engine.
quote: which I had been using, could shift some logits by as much as 2

what: Pushed the minimum hop-1 and hop-2 margin above +5 with GCG, then evaluated a large recipient pool under the real KV-cache sequence, sorted by margin and kept only the most stable 2,000.
why: Changing the recipient changed logits, causing instability; keeping only high-margin candidates removed failures.
when: Large candidate pools where per-item reliability varies.
quote: sorted the recipients by margin, and kept only the most stable 2,000

what: A hop-2 EOG jailbreak found on the BF16 gpt-oss model did not transfer to the quantised GGUF (margin regressed from about -38 to about -28 after drift), so the author abandoned it.
why: Quantisation drift destroyed the narrow margin.
quote: I managed to jailbreak the BF16 model, but the result did not transfer to the competition GGUF.

what: Stage 1 full fine-tune on natural-language CoT math solutions, stage 2 on synthetic GPT-4 tool-integrated reasoning (ToRA format) with code execution feedback.
why: Reasoning agent mixing language and Python REPL; multi-step code solved hard problems that single-program MMOS could not.
quote: Stage 2 : fine-tune the model from Stage 1 on a synthetic dataset of tool-integrated reasoning, where each math problem is decomposed into a sequence of rationales, Python programs, and their outputs.

what: Replicate prompt N times, sample until a Python block, execute and append output, repeat M times pruning broken traces, then majority vote. Used N=48, M=4.
why: Self-consistency plus code feedback; much lower variance than early-stopping approaches given random problem order.
when: LLM answer tasks with tool use and time limit
quote: For our winning submission, we generated N=48 candidates with a depth of M=4.

what: All weights updated, no LoRA/DoRA, with TRL packing into 2048 tokens, gradient checkpointing and DeepSpeed ZeRO-3.
why: Not confident PEFT matches full FT without extra tuning of rank/alpha.
quote: we did not use parameter efficient techniques like LoRA or DoRA because we were not confident they could match the performance of full fine-tuning without significant experimentation.

what: Four validation sets (AMC22-23 integer, AIME22-24, MATH level 4 and 5 integer-answer), small ones run with 5-10 seeds.
why: Small sets are noisy so combine small representative sets with larger ones; avoids overfitting a 50-problem public LB.
quote: We found that combining small, but representative validation sets with larger ones was useful in this particular competition where each submission is subject to some stochasticity from sampling.

what: Filter public math problems to those with integer outputs to mimic the competition answer format.
why: Matches the test answer format.
quote: we picked all the problems from years 2022 and 2023 of AMC12 and kept those that can be converted to integer outputs.

gain: Upload twice as fast, small accuracy loss
what: Quantize model to 8-bit with AutoGPTQ using training data as calibration to fit 2xT4 and speed upload.
why: 16-bit weights need ~32GB VRAM; small accuracy drop mitigated by generating more candidates.
quote: We quantized our models using AutoGPTQ along with the training datasets for calibration.

gain: 27/50 public LB; a few points internal
what: Sample 4 completions per problem from the SFT model, label by answer correctness, train with KTO.
why: Improves a few points; implicit reward tracking helps debugging.
quote: We found this form of on-policy KTO produced a better model than the SFT one (a few percentage points on our internal evaluations) and scored 27/50 on the public leaderboard.

what: Fine-tuning stage 2 on integer-only solutions was tried.
why: Slightly less robust, likely few samples after filtering.
quote: found the model was slightly more robust when training on all solution types

what: REINFORCE leave-one-out with binary code-exec reward on DeepSeekMath 7B RL.
why: No significant gains and generation is a bottleneck.
quote: did not see any significant gains in performance

what: DARE/TIES/WARP merges of SFT, KTO and public models via mergekit.
why: Regressions on internal evals or ran out of time.
quote: these merges led to either significant regressions on our internal evaluations or we ran out of time to explore this more deeply

what: SFT on InternLM-20B, CodeLlama-33B and Mixtral-8x7B did not beat DeepSeek 7B.
why: DeepSeekMath continued math pretraining; larger models slow with timeouts.
quote: the DeepSeek 7B model is very hard to beat due to their continued pretraining on math

what: Extracted 540K AoPS problems, generated up to 32 R1/QwQ solutions each (more for harder problems by pass rate), filtered wrong answers via LLM answer-equivalence check; used majority answer when no reference.
why: Large verified teacher traces let SFT of a small model reach frontier reasoning.
when: Training small reasoning models from a strong teacher
quote: Incorrect solutions are filtered by verifying answer equivalence with Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct.

trick: Bootstrapping TIR with small SFT model
what: R1 would not produce tool-integrated reasoning by prompting, so they fine-tuned an instruction model (LIMO) on small reasoning data, generated long-reasoning TIR, filtered aggressively, and iterated train-generate-filter to 1.7M solutions.
why: Authors hypothesise R1-style models struggle to deviate from the format they were trained on.
when: Adding tool use to a reasoning model that resists prompting
quote: Our initial attempts to elicit Tool-Integrated Reasoning (TIR) generations from DeepSeek-R1 through simple prompting proved unsuccessful.

trick: Filter TIR set to 15K by code usage
what: Final TIR stage used only 15K of 1.7M solutions, selected by number of code executions and answer correctness.
why: Inferred: a small, high-quality set teaches tool use without lengthening outputs.
quote: the 1.7M solutions are aggressively filtered down to 15K samples based on number of code executions and correctness of answers

trick: Raise RoPE base for long reasoning
what: Changed base RoPE to 500k before SFT of Qwen2.5-14B-Base on long CoT.
why: Allows long reasoning contexts.
when: Fine-tuning a base LLM on very long outputs
quote: We changed base RoPE to 500k to allow long reasoning.

what: Averaged weights from different stages of the 8-epoch CoT run for the final CoT checkpoint.
why: Inferred: smooths training noise.
quote: Weight averaging is used from different stages for the final weights.

trick: Linear merge of CoT and TIR
what: Linearly merged CoT checkpoint and TIR-finetuned checkpoint (0.3 CoT + 0.7 TIR) with mergekit; simple linear beat fancier merges.
why: Keeps TIR accuracy while cutting length (15834 to 12489 tokens) and code executions (2.73 to 0.85), helping time budget.
when: Combining two fine-tunes of the same base with different behaviours
quote: the most effective approach turned out to be a simple linear combination of the two checkpoints

gain: 1.5x from FP8, ~1.8x from ReDrafter (210 to 554 tok/s)
what: Converted to TensorRT-LLM with FP8 weights, then trained a ReDrafter speculative-decoding head on 100k self-generated solutions.
why: Faster decoding means more samples and tokens within the fixed time limit; ReDrafter gave 3 tokens per step at 65% acceptance.
when: LLM inference under strict compute-time limits
quote: The resulting redrafter generated 3 tokens for every LLM step with 65% acceptance rate delivering a speed up of approximately 1.8X.

what: Compared bf16, int8, int4, fp8; int4 was faster but lost accuracy while int8/fp8 did not.
why: Inferred: 4-bit loses too much on hard reasoning.
quote: w4a16 (int4)

trick: Early stop on consensus and stragglers
what: Launched 12 async generations per problem; cancelled the rest if 4 of first 5 agreed, and stopped after 10 of 12 finished.
why: Saves time for harder questions and avoids waiting on stragglers.
when: Majority-vote sampling under a time budget
quote: if 4 of the first 5 generations are the same we cancel the remaining generations in TensorRT

what: Base 350s per question; unused time is pooled and the next question can draw up to 210s extra (560s total).
why: Easy questions donate time to hard ones within the 5-hour limit.
when: Fixed total inference time over many items
quote: If a question completed early, the unused time was added to a shared buffer.

trick: Pause generation to run code in sandbox
what: Streamed generation was monitored for code blocks; generation stopped, code ran in a sandbox, output appended and generation resumed.
why: Enables tool-integrated reasoning with in-flight batching.
quote: If the LLM generates code, LLM generation stops, and the code block is executed in a sandbox.

what: Final submission used temperature 0 with redrafter greedy search rather than tuned sampling.
why: More stable at small batch sizes and slightly faster speculative decoding; sampling parameters gave minimal differences.
quote: our winning submission was based on an "almost" greedy search strategy

trick: Trust CV over noisy public LB
what: Built a 256-problem AIME/HMMT benchmark and chose the MIX TIR model by CV despite one 28 public-LB score; public LB had only 50 questions.
why: Private LB matched CV; later stronger models likely timed out, which CV runs in Kaggle revealed.
when: Tiny public leaderboards with high variance
quote: the private LB reflected more our CV results than LB results which was quite satisfying

trick: Reranking reward models not worth it
what: Generative re-ranking and outcome reward models were dropped; larger batch and max tokens was simpler.
why: Extra model costs memory and time; ORM benefits shrank for long reasoning on 50 problems.
quote: Generative Solution Re-Ranking - this type of reward model requires additional memory and time resources.

what: Read the model weight files before initialization to force them into the Linux page cache, reducing startup latency.
why: Avoids repeated slow disk access during load.
when: Large-model loading under tight notebook time limits.
quote: A deliberate file-read operation was used before model initialization to force weights into the Linux page cache.

what: Reused shared prompt prefixes across many parallel generations.
why: Avoids redundant attention computation for identical system prompts.
quote: Shared prompt prefixes were reused across multiple parallel generations to avoid redundant attention computation.

what: Quantized the KV cache to 8-bit to fit longer contexts and more parallel generations on one H100.
why: Reduces memory pressure during long-context inference.
quote: The KV cache was quantized to 8-bit precision to reduce memory pressure during long-context inference.

what: Replaced plain majority voting with votes weighted by token-level Shannon entropy confidence (lower entropy gives more weight).
why: Penalizes uncertain generations. (Unverified; no ablation given.)
quote: Traditional majority voting was replaced with entropy-weighted aggregation.

what: Model-generated code runs in long-lived Jupyter kernels that keep variables and functions, with outputs fed back to the model.
why: Avoids environment restarts and preserves state across tool calls.
quote: a persistent sandbox verification system built around long-lived Jupyter kernels

what: Stop sampling for a problem once 4 generations agree and return the unused time to a global pool for later problems.
why: Easy problems finish fast, harder ones use more budget.
when: Fixed total time budget over many problems.
quote: If a problem finishes early (e.g., due to early stopping when 4 matching answers are found), the unused time naturally goes back into the global pool for the next problem

what: Near the notebook timeout, reduce sampling depth, shorten verification loops and return best valid partial outputs.
why: Prevents runtime failures near the limit. (Admitted in comments to be partly marketing wording.)
quote: Best-valid partial outputs were returned

what: Compared Gemini-generated, community and original prompts; kept the original public notebook prompt.
why: Author claims prompt engineering gave larger gains than complex optimizations.
quote: prompt engineering consistently produced larger gains than several complex optimization techniques

what: Submitted essentially the public 44/50 notebook with its original prompt.
why: Public pipeline already near the ceiling; commenters say it is an exact copy.
when: Code competitions with strong public notebooks.
quote: However, the original notebook prompt was used eventually.

gain: Validation loss kept improving with more synthetic data
what: Split puzzle program generation into input-grid program (validated by LLM-written unit tests) and output-grid program (validated by agreement across multiple LLM samples).
why: More reliable than generating full programs.
quote: Instead of generating a full puzzle program with input/output logic, we decided to split this into two stages.

what: Prompt LLM to merge two puzzle descriptions into a new more complex one (266593 summaries).
why: Inferred: scales variety and difficulty.
quote: We prompted LLM to join two puzzle summaries and produce a new more complex puzzle

what: Use H-ARC human solution descriptions and BARC descriptions as seeds for LLM puzzle generation.
why: Natural-language descriptions seed diverse puzzles.
quote: which was surprisingly underestimated in the ARC community

what: Prompt LLM multiple times per input program and keep puzzles whose output programs agree.
why: Filters wrong programs without tests.
quote: filter out solutions which are not consistent

what: Represent grids with Qwen3 dialog template, digits as tokens, 16 tokens per pair.
why: Compact representation.
quote: This simpler representation requires only 16 tokens

what: LoRA r=256, alpha=32 per test puzzle, bf16, no gradient checkpointing or 4-bit, Flash Attention 2 via Unsloth.
why: Accuracy and speed.
quote: We used LoRA test-time fine-tuning for each puzzle independently with r = 256 and alpha = 32.

what: Batch version of depth-first-search decoding, nondeterministic. A batch-invariant version was more precise but 17% slower, so not used.
why: Speed within Kaggle limits.
quote: We implemented the batch version of the Depth First Search (DFS) algorithm.

what: Rescore all candidates with the same 8 augmentations.
why: Scores of different solutions become comparable.
quote: This makes the scores of different solutions more comparable.

trick: DFS frequency plus geometric mean rescoring
what: Combine count of times a candidate was found in DFS with geometric mean of log-probs across augmentations (found after deadline).
why: Better candidate selection.
quote: We calculate how many times the candidate solution was found during the DFS stage

trick: TRM large batch plus test-time fine-tuning
what: Pretrain TRM with batch 3072, lr 3e-4, then fine-tune on test; 4 H cycles, 10 halt steps, 2000 epochs, 200 warmup.
why: Fit 2 hours on Kaggle.
quote: Using a batch size of 3072 instead of 768, and learning rate of 3e-4 instead of 1e-4

what: Train twice, find step with best pass@2 without eval data, pick matching-step checkpoint trained on all data.
why: Inferred: selects steps without eval labels.
quote: We finally selected the checkpoint trained on all 4k samples with the closest number of training steps.

what: Generate 10 TRM attempts, add to DFS candidates, rescore with Qwen3.
why: Complementary model adds a few solved puzzles.
quote: we modified TRM so that it generates 10 attempts instead of 2 per puzzle

what: Studied the ExoSim2 and TauREx3 data-generation code to find the gain-drift functional form and the foreground addition, then built the preprocessing around them.
why: Synthetic data follows known simulator equations, so reproducing them removes systematic error.
when: Competitions with simulated data and open-source generators.
quote: Deep analysis of the simulation code led to critical ideas needed for our victory.

what: Discarded the FGS1 channel and used only AIRS-CH0, since the method relies on correlation between adjacent wavelengths.
why: FGS1 had a distorted, fluctuating PSF that they did not know how to use.
when: Multi-sensor inputs where one sensor is hard to model.
quote: Only the AIRS-CH0 channel was used because our solution heavily relies on the correlation between adjacent wavelengths

gain: About +0.03 public, +0.02 private (ablation: with hot pixel processing 0.7022/0.7225 vs 0.7330/0.7421)
what: Turned off the public notebook's hot-pixel sigma-clipping, keeping the dead-pixel mask, and averaged with nanmean over the spatial axis.
why: Hot-pixel removal lost information in central pixels and made it harder to cancel time-dependent PSF jitter noise, which cancels in the sum over rows; a competitor did not see the same benefit when he interpolated NaNs.
when: Detector or sensor preprocessing where correlated noise cancels in sums.
quote: Disabling Hot Pixel Processing : This led to a significant jump on the leaderboard.

gain: About +0.011 public, +0.012 private versus multiplying by 1.008
what: Estimated the foreground from the edge regions [0:8] and [24:32] and subtracted it from the central region [8:24], rather than multiplying the final spectrum by ~1.006-1.008.
why: ExoSim2 adds a foreground to the signal; the scale hack approximated this.
when: Simulated telescope data with additive background.
quote: In our solution, we decided to estimate the foreground signal with the regions [0:8] and [24:32] , and subtracted it from the central region [8:24] .

what: Fit each light curve with I(lambda) x Box(lambda) x (1 + f(t) g(lambda)) with 5-parameter polynomials f and g, copying the simulator's separable form instead of a general 2D polynomial.
why: The simulator gain drift is separable in time and wavelength; a 2D polynomial h(t, lambda) is not.
when: Parametric fitting of light curves with known generator.
quote: By using this functional form directly in the fitting described below, we were able to achieve high performance in the dip estimation.

what: Within the fit, the stellar spectrum I(lambda) and the dip depth were solved in closed form for fixed drift parameters, so the optimiser only handles the 10 drift parameters.
why: Reduces the search space, making the fit more stable.
when: Models that are linear in some parameters.
quote: can be found analytically if the other parameters are fixed, and they don't need to be considered by the fitting algorithm.

what: First stage fixes I(lambda) from temporal averages of raw signal; second stage lets I(lambda) be set optimally at each step, starting from stage-one parameters; point errors come from the signal variation per wavelength.
why: Stabilises the non-linear fit.
quote: To stabilize the fitting process, a two-stage fitting was used.

what: Used bootstrapping to estimate the dip error at each wavelength, and passed these errors as per-point uncertainty to the Gaussian process.
why: Signal-to-noise differs across wavelengths, so equal weighting is wrong.
when: Heteroscedastic noise in a first-stage estimate that feeds a smoother.
quote: Bootstrapping was used to overcome this problem and to estimate the dip error of each wavelength.

gain: GP alone 0.7221 public / 0.7343 private versus 0.7330 / 0.7421 for the final blend
what: A GaussianProcessRegressor with RBF plus Matern kernel received bootstrapped errors so it smooths the noisy dip spectrum across wavelengths.
why: Exploits correlation between adjacent wavelengths while respecting noise level.
when: Smoothing noisy spectra or time series.
quote: the errors calculated by bootstrapping were passed to sklearn.gaussian_process.GaussianProcessRegressor so that the model can consider the uncertainty of each data point.

what: A 1-hidden-layer autoencoder with 4 hidden nodes trained with MSE on the dip spectra, with each planet's spectrum normalised and smoothed by a moving median before input.
why: Captures non-linear low-dimensional structure of spectra, unlike PCA; MSE lets it recover an optimal denoised spectrum.
when: Denoising structured signals with a low intrinsic dimension.
quote: Important points were to normalize the data for each exoplanet and to take the moving median of the dip spectrum to smooth the input dip spectrum.

gain: Blend 0.7330 public vs 0.7221 for GP alone
what: Added a rank-5 non-negative matrix factorisation of the spectra, whose components looked like CO2, CH4 and H2O, blended with GP and autoencoder at 6:2:2.
why: Gives diversity and an unsupervised use of spectral correlation.
when: Spectral data with non-negative additive components.
quote: Very similar to the autoencoder, but we added it to enhance the diversity.

what: Predicted uncertainty sigma as a weighted average of a constant, the standard deviation of the smoothed dip spectrum, and the GP uncertainty.
why: The constant helps when the spectrum is almost flat but biased.
quote: The constant value played an important role in cases where the dip spectrum was almost constant but had some bias.

what: Tried fitting the dip spectrum with TauREx3 gas absorption models; it worked on training data but scored badly on the leaderboard.
why: Presumably the atmospheric composition shifts between train and test.
when: Physics-based models used on shifted test distributions.
quote: Although it worked really well on the training data, the leaderboard score was horrible, presumably because of the shift in the composition of the atmosphere.

trick: Learned denoising of channel sum failed
what: Tried several ML methods to choose optimal channel ranges or weights instead of the fixed sum over [8:24]; none beat it.
why: Probably temporal-spatial fluctuation of the signal.
quote: we tried several machine learning methods but didn't manage to beat [8:24]

what: Modelled the signal as noise + star spectrum + polynomial drift + batman transit window + depth variation, with Gaussian priors, and read the transit depth and covariance from the posterior instead of training a neural net.
why: Underlying physics is simple but hard for NNs to learn from small data; posterior gives calibrated uncertainty for the metric.
when: Small synthetic/physical datasets with known generative process and uncertainty-scored metrics.
quote: Importantly, the posterior is not just a single point, it's a distribution.

what: Fitted 12 parameters (offset, multiplicative factors, dependence on limb darkening and variation magnitude) to adjust predicted mean and sigma per sensor, optimising the competition metric on the full training set.
why: The prior does not fully describe the synthetic data generation, so calibration corrects mean and uncertainty.
when: Probabilistic predictions scored by likelihood-type metrics, model slightly misspecified.
quote: These fudge factors are chosen to optimize score on the training data.

what: Because the model is non-linear, linearised it around the posterior mean, applied the Gaussian Bayesian update, and repeated for several iterations, updating the depth-scale hyperparameter by gradient descent.
why: Prior is Gaussian so each step is one matrix operation (Gauss-Newton-like).
when: Mildly non-linear models with Gaussian priors and huge parameter counts.
quote: we linearize the model around the mean of the posterior.

what: Initialised the Bayesian solver with a grid search over transit depth and mid-time, then BFGS on the wavelength-averaged signal fitting drift and transit parameters.
why: Linearised solver needs a decent starting point, particularly with limb darkening.
quote: sweep over a grid of transit depth and transit mid-time to find initial values.

what: If the grid/BFGS residual was suspiciously high, restarted from another planet's transit parameters and/or chopped off the first and last few frames.
why: Some edge frames have unexplained high residual.
quote: Try chopping off the first and last few frames of the signal

trick: Priors learned from train by MLE
what: Fitted prior hyperparameters (transit-parameter covariance, GP kernel hyperparameters, PCA shapes and magnitudes, FGS variation std) on the training set by maximum likelihood.
why: Makes the priors empirical; no train/test population shift this year.
when: Hierarchical/Bayesian models with a train set drawn from the same population.
quote: Covariance matrix learned on training set using maximum likelihood estimation

trick: PCA plus GP for depth spectrum
gain: +0.007 vs PCA only, +0.011 vs GP only (private)
what: Modelled wavelength variation of transit depth as a sum of two squared-exponential-kernel GP plus 5 fixed PCA basis shapes learned on train.
why: Captures smooth spectral structure with few degrees of freedom.
when: Smooth spectra regression with limited data.
quote: Gaussian Process over wavelength, sum of two squared-exponential kernels

what: Modelled drift as a third-order polynomial rather than a GP.
why: Less realistic but matches the synthetic data generation process.
when: Synthetic data competitions where the generator can be inferred.
quote: less realistic, but matches the synthetic data generation process.

what: Tuned one hyperparameter per planet at inference, the scaling of depth variation, by maximum likelihood.
why: Adapts uncertainty to each sample.
quote: Scaling factor determined per planet using MLE (this is the only hyperparameter tuned during inference)

what: Went beyond simple summing along the dispersion axis: invalid pixel handling, noise-aware weighting, jitter correction and background removal, plus cosmic ray removal.
why: Noise is non-Poisson and jitter shapes do not sum exactly to zero.
quote: It still leads to an improvement of ~0.01 over simple summing

what: Applied priors (e.g. lightly regularised depth, constrained limb darkening) on transit parameters.
why: Keeps fits physically plausible.
quote: Don't regularize the 11 transit parameters in prior

what: Submitted code uses 4 solver iterations instead of 8, and preprocessing was moved to GPU, to fit the 9 hour limit.
why: Runtime constraint; small score cost.
when: Code competitions with long-running per-sample solvers.
quote: the code linked here only does 4 iterations to fit training and inference into the 9 hour submission limit (this only costs 0.001 in the score)

gain: Small recall improvement on an out-of-embryo split; faster convergence
what: Pretrained the 3D detector with a masked autoencoder that masks 50% of the volume in tiny 2x4x4 voxel blocks instead of large blocks, using competition movies plus external zebrafish crops.
why: Cells are tiny, so large masked blocks would force the model to hallucinate whole cells; light masking lets it learn useful features and made models converge faster.
when: 3D/volumetric detection or segmentation with small objects and limited labels.
quote: masking 50% of the volume in tiny blocks of 2×4×4 voxels

trick: Mask plus flow head instead of blob
what: Detector predicts foreground probability and a 3-channel flow field to the cell centre (Cellpose-style) rather than a Gaussian blob heatmap, so masks and geometry features are available downstream.
why: Downstream tracking uses geometric features and masks, which a Gaussian blob cannot provide.
when: Detection tasks where instance shape is needed by a later stage.
quote: I chose to try a mask output instead of a Gaussian blob

what: Generated pseudo labels for all movies with a 5-fold average and 4x flip TTA, kept only high-confidence detections, built tracks and dropped short ones, then retrained the detector on them.
why: Ground truth was sparse; the author could visually see improvements. Author admits it leaks into CV, making round-2 validation optimistic.
when: Sparse GT in detection/tracking where a first model is already decent.
quote: generated tracks with the public twoPass tracker and filtered for min length > 3

what: Manually painted about 1,800 cells in 3D, used for detector finetuning; the main payoff was the intuition gained about divisions.
why: Little direct detection gain, but dozens of hours looking at cells inspired the Soon Net idea.
when: Unfamiliar domains where visual inspection can reveal usable signals.
quote: I spent a lot of time on it and only managed to annotate about 1,800 cells

gain: Public LB ~0.925 to ~0.963 from division improvements alone
what: A small CNN+transformer looks at 16x64x64 crops of frames t-1, t, t+1 plus a Gaussian query channel marking the cell, and predicts interphase / soon-to-divide / just-divided, feeding the linker.
why: Dividing cells visibly jiggle, brighten and grow before division, so a learned visual cue is much better than blind hand-made features.
when: Tracking with divisions or events preceded by visible cues.
quote: It looks at 3 frames cropped around each cell and tries to predict its division state (interphase, soon to divide, just divided), where it was and where it went.

what: An FPN head on the Soon Net predicts, for each of 3 frames, a continuation occupancy map and a division occupancy map with small spheres at the query cell and its relatives, so the model outputs where the cell was and will be.
why: Uses the track data fully; the map for t+1 directly answers the linking question. Inspired by auxiliary detection heads in a prior 1st place solution.
quote: predicts two occupancy maps for each of the 3 frames, one for continuation and one for division

what: Randomly offset the crop so the query cell is not at the centre (+-3 px in z, +-16 px in xy).
why: Otherwise the model gets lazy and predicts occupancy for the centre cell instead of the queried one.
when: Query-conditioned models with a marker for the target object.
quote: I use a very large FOV jitter (±3 px in z, ±16 px in xy).

what: For interphase cells, frame t-1 is sometimes t-2 or t-3 and t+1 sometimes t+2 or t+3; the linker also sees (t, t+2) pairs 25% of the time.
why: Teaches the model that cells can move far and makes it robust to frame gaps.
quote: frame t-1 is sometimes actually t-2 or t-3, and t+1 is sometimes t+2 or t+3, so the model learns that cells can move far

gain: Augmented-GT division Jaccard far higher than original in CV
what: Used early Soon Net versions to find missed divisions, visually checked a couple hundred, and added them to training labels, growing divisions from 151 to 515.
why: Original GT was missing division annotations; rare class gets much more data.
quote: In the final version I had 515 divisions to train with, against the 151 in the original GT.

gain: Division FP 73 to 58 on original GT in CV
what: In round 2, used out-of-fold round-1 scores to find interphase cells scored as soon-to-divide (p>=0.5) or just-divided (p>=0.3), giving 2492 hard negatives, sampled as a separate 1:1:1:1 class.
why: Reduces false divisions by focusing on confusable interphase cells.
quote: In round 2 I used round 1 to mine hard interphases

what: For maps of the wrong type (e.g. division map of an interphase cell) add an extra BCE on only their 512 highest voxels; map loss also uses Focal-Tversky.
why: Avoids ghost blobs in maps that should be empty.
when: Sparse heatmap outputs with conditionally empty targets.
quote: get an extra BCE on their 512 highest voxels to avoid ghost blobs

what: Linker tokens cross-attend across two frames, each cell seeing only cells within 30 um plus its 16 nearest neighbours.
why: Ensures sparse regions still have candidates while keeping attention local.
when: Matching objects between frames with variable density.
quote: every cell within 30 µm plus its 16 nearest ones, so even cells in sparse regions always have candidates

what: For each candidate link, read the parent's t+1 heatmap at the child's centre and the child's t-1 heatmap at the parent's centre, plus comparison to the best other candidate and distance to heatmap peak, as pair features for the linker.
why: If both directions agree, the link is probably right; features come from a model that looked at the frames so they improve with a better Soon Net.
when: Learned association using a sub-model's spatial predictions.
quote: If both answers are high, it's probably the right link.

what: Linker trained with three equally weighted NLL losses: dual-softmax over pair scores, an NLL over the 137 fork options per parent, and a reverse loss where each child picks its parent or no parent.
why: Casts cell matching as keypoint matching, with constraints enforced from both directions.
quote: The third loss goes the other way, it is also an NLL, where each child has to pick its right parent

what: The fork head first decides whether the parent divides (kind) then which children (who); final probability is p(kind) x p(who|kind) instead of a single softmax over 137 options.
why: The 120 pair options drowned the rare division decision in a single softmax and caused false divisions.
when: Structured output with a rare event and many combinatorial options.
quote: When everything was in a single softmax, the 120 pair options drowned the rare division decision and the model produced too many false divisions.

what: Linker trained for 10 epochs on augmented GT with division examples oversampled 8 times.
why: Inferred: divisions are rare, so oversampling balances the fork head.
quote: with divisions oversampled 8 times

what: For each parent and option compute log p(option) - log p(no child), keep options above 0, accept from best down with at most one option per parent and one parent per child; leftover children start new tracks.
why: Compares each link against the no-link alternative, so no tuned score threshold is needed.
quote: and keeps only the ones above 0.

what: Disallow a newborn daughter from dividing in the next frame, resolving conflicts from the most confident division downward; also line-fit smoothing that avoids smoothing divisions into mothers, 1-frame gap closing and pruning tracks under 3 frames.
why: Prevents a weak early fork from blocking the real division a frame later.
quote: a division refractory rule that does not allow a newborn daughter to divide again in the next frame

what: Train with cross-entropy (softmax) but apply sigmoid to the logits at inference to get independent per-class probabilities.
why: Almost every clip has one label among 182, so CE fits; sigmoid at inference suits the multi-label test soundscapes.
when: Multiclass-trained audio taggers evaluated as multi-label.
quote: Although logits are passed through softmax during the train, we use sigmoid in the inference.

what: Use CrossEntropyLoss rather than BCE, focal or pos-weighted BCE.
why: With 182 labels and nearly always one present, the task reduces to multiclass; BCE was significantly worse.
when: Multi-label audio tagging with sparse single labels.
quote: BCE shows significantly worse results than CE

what: Ensemble models by taking the minimum of their sigmoid outputs (plus chunk averaging) instead of the mean.
why: Sigmoid on CE-trained models gives noisy predictions; min lowers uncertain ones.
when: Ensembling CE-trained models whose scores are used as sigmoid probabilities.
quote: The two most important things in the inference pipeline are chunks averaging and ensembling with min() reduction .

what: Found random fold0 gave better results; computed signal-strength statistics and used fold0 plus models selected by a 0.8 quantile of T = std + var + rms + pwr.
why: Noisy and too loud audio harms the models.
when: Noisy audio datasets with weak labels.
quote: we use fold0 and 0.8 quantile of statistics T = std + var + rms + pwr

what: Run Google bird vocalization classifier on train_audio; drop chunks where its top prediction does not match the primary label, and relabel to the secondary label if it matches that.
why: Removes chunks with no bird sound or bad quality.
when: Weakly labelled audio with a strong external pretrained model available.
quote: Data in train_audio is also filtered with Google-bird-vocalization-classifier

what: For files with secondary labels, give the primary label 0.5 and share the other 0.5 evenly among secondary labels.
why: Inferred: reflects multi-species clips instead of a hard single label.
when: Audio tagging with primary and secondary species annotations.
quote: if the file has secondary labels, then we take the primary label with 0.5, and the remaining 0.5 is evenly distributed among the secondary labels.

what: Label the unlabeled soundscapes with an ensemble of the Google classifier and their own best train_audio-only models, and train on them in 5-second chunk labels.
why: Brings in in-domain soundscape data matching the test distribution.
when: Domain gap between clean training clips and test soundscapes.
quote: The soundscapes are labeled with an ensemble of Google classifier, and our best models trained only with train_audio .

what: Add Google classifier pseudo labels to train labels with coefficient 0.05; high coefficients hurt.
why: Pseudo-labelling train audio acts like label smoothing, so a small weight is better.
quote: It seems that pseudo-labeling for train_audio is a way of label smoothing, so it is better to use a small coefficient.

what: Split audio into X-second segments (20/30/60 s) treated as separate files, so each epoch samples one random chunk per segment, balancing many short train files against few huge soundscapes.
why: Balances sampling between train_audio and unlabeled_soundscapes.
when: Mixed sources with very different file lengths.
quote: we divide the audio into X-second segments that are considered as separate files.

what: Feed 10 seconds made of two adjacent 5-second chunks with averaged labels; at test, 5 s of chunk n plus 2.5 s each side.
why: Captures full chirps or chirp periods cut by 5 s boundaries.
when: Bird call detection with fixed-length prediction windows.
quote: Models are trained on 10-second chunks that consist of two 5-second adjacent chunks with averaged labels.

what: Spectrogram augmentation: horizontal cutmix (time-axis splice of two clips with mixed labels), plus XY masking and random segment.
why: Inferred: simulates multi-species overlap in soundscapes.
when: Audio classification with multi-species test clips.
quote: horizontal cutmix

what: Remove duplicate audio files from the training data.
why: Inferred: avoids leakage and bias in folds.
quote: There are some duplicate audio files in the train data, so we discard them.

what: Pad too-short clips cyclically rather than with silence.
why: Inferred: fills the window with real signal.
when: Fixed-length audio input with short clips.
quote: if the sound is too short, we use cyclic padding.

what: Compile models with OpenVINO using fixed input shape, compute mel spectrograms in parallel with joblib and cache them in RAM, to fit CPU-only runtime limits.
why: One model processes the test set in about 18 minutes on Kaggle CPU.
when: Code competitions with CPU-only time limits.
quote: Compilation with OpenVINO (fixed model input)

what: Plain EfficientNet-B0 and RegNetY-008 backbones; ViTs, SED heads and 2021 CNN modifications were slower and worse.
why: Author conviction that complexity does not help here.
when: Audio tagging under Kaggle kernel compute.
quote: We are convinced that overly complex models do not work better than simple ones.

what: Adding external Xeno-canto data, even filtered by classifiers or quantile statistics, reduced score; the best solution was not to use it.
why: Author found no filtering made it helpful.
quote: The best solution is not to use additional data…

what: Adding a nocall class, mel normalisation, SWA/EMA, softmax temperature, multistage training and pretraining on past years gave no gain; mixup, noise and flips hurt.
why: No explanation given.
quote: We add nocall samples from external data to the train and use an additional 183 class.

gain: Public LB 0.909 to 0.930 over four iterations
what: Pseudo-label unlabeled soundscapes, train a student on them with noise, then repeat 4 times with the student ensembles as new teachers; the 5th iteration stopped helping.
why: Noise (mixup, drop path) forces the student to learn more robust features instead of reproducing teacher errors.
when: Small labeled set with plenty of unlabeled in-domain data.
quote: That self-training magic stopped working on the 5th pseudo-labeling iteration.

what: Raise pseudo-label probabilities to a power >1 (about 1/0.55-1/0.65) to suppress noisy low-confidence labels before the next iteration.
why: Temperature on logits raises probabilities above 0.5, amplifying confident noise; power on probabilities keeps only initially confident labels.
when: Iterated self-training with noisy soft labels.
quote: The trick was to apply a power greater than 1 to the probabilities (similar to temperature scaling, but applied to probabilities instead of logits).

what: Mix every labeled training clip with a random pseudo-labeled soundscape chunk at a constant weight 0.5; plain concatenation of pseudo-labeled data did not work.
why: Same input/output as teacher teaches nothing new; mixup adds noise and gives target-domain backgrounds; weights far from 0.5 suppress signal.
quote: But after switching to a constant blending weight of 0.5 (Beta's parameters = inf), the magic started to happen, and the LB score began to rise.

what: drop_path_rate 0.15 during student training on pseudo-labels, not during supervised training.
why: Part of Noisy Student noise; no benefit in supervised stage.
quote: Applying drop_path_rate = 0.15 (which turned out to be optimal for all the models I trained), I consistently saw a boost in the LB score, up to 0.005 for some models.

what: Sample pseudo-labeled soundscapes with WeightedRandomSampler, weight = sum of max label probabilities per soundscape, then take a random 20s window.
why: High sums indicate more accurately labeled soundscapes; low sums are almost unlabeled.
quote: WeightedRandomSampler was used with weights equal to the sum of maximum label probabilities within each soundscape.

what: Average SED framewise predictions across overlapping neighboring 20s chunks instead of max over each center 5s only; pad edges, then smooth with [0.1,0.2,0.4,0.2,0.1] and delta-shift TTA.
why: Like sliding-window segmentation and a TTA, each frame is seen with different context.
quote: It can be seen as a 1D analogue of 2D sliding-window segmentation of large images

what: Trained SED on 20s inputs (hop length enlarged) rather than 5s, after comparing durations.
why: Insect/amphibia calls are long and repetitive, so longer context helps.
when: Soundscape tagging with long repetitive calls.
quote: any longer duration did not improve results but took more time to infer

trick: Many mel bins and large hop
what: Used 224 mel bins, n_fft 4096, hop 1252 instead of typical 128 bins / hop 512.
why: More mel bands separate narrow-band calls of amphibians and insects; a large hop keeps inference time down.
quote: The important thing was setting a larger number of n_mels.

trick: Separate Amphibia/Insecta model with extra species
what: Trained a dedicated EfficientNet-B0 on ~700 Amphibia and Insecta species (train + short Xeno-Canto clips, min 1 sample per species) and inserted its target-species predictions into a zero matrix for ensembling.
why: Those groups are underrepresented, and many diverse species give more representative features.
when: Underrepresented class groups with external data available.
quote: Insert predictions for target species into a zero matrix, only their columns are non-zero, for ensembling with other models

what: For extra Xeno-Canto Gryllidae/Tettigoniidae clips, assigned a unique label per species instead of the family label and trained a dedicated model.
why: Experiments showed family labels correspond to specific local species; extra data under the family label hurt.
when: Coarse labels representing narrow local species.
quote: assigning them unique new labels based on the species of each sample instead of assigning the family-level labels, and training a dedicated model improved results.

what: Added 5489 Xeno-Canto clips of target species; used for only one model.
why: It usually worsened results.
when: External data for the same label set.
quote: It usually worsened results, so only one model saw that data.

what: Used softmax CE instead of BCE/focal for a multi-label task, without normalising labels to sum to one.
why: CE handles imbalance by pushing down overrepresented negatives; multi-label samples count more.
quote: I didn't normalize sample labels to sum to one, motivated by the idea that more difficult samples (those with more positive labels) should have a greater impact on the loss.

what: Left-pad shorter clips with zeros before mixup so the right side always overlaps; targets combined by element-wise max (from a comment).
why: Ensures samples are always actually mixed.
quote: the left part of it was filled with 0, so on the right, there is always an overlap that ensures train samples are always actually mixed up

trick: Validate on public LB with multi-fold ensembles
what: No CV/LB correlation, so ideas were validated on public LB using 2-5 fold ensembles to damp seed variance.
why: Host stated public and private distributions are similar.
when: Domain-shifted test sets with unreliable CV.
quote: A single model's LB score varied a lot for different seeds

what: Final 7-model ensemble mixed backbones and models from supervised, iteration-3 and iteration-4 stages; equal weights gave the best private score.
why: Diversity across stages and architectures resisted shake-up.
quote: However, the best private submission, with a score of 0.935, was achieved when I assigned equal weights to all models.

what: Tried removing human voice from training clips; it deteriorated results.
why: Author hypothesis: noisy rare-species samples become short calls resembling parts of other species.
quote: any attempt to remove human voice deteriorated the results

what: Ran OpenVINO without quantisation, multiprocess loading, and computed spectrograms once for all models.
why: Fits a larger ensemble in the CPU time limit.
quote: Spectrograms were generated once and then reused across all models

gain: LB 0.935+ before self-training (vs 0.931 for 2-iter self-training without distillation)
what: Phase 1: distill a CNN backbone from Perch v2 embeddings via a linear projection head with cosine loss (11 epochs, lr 5e-4); Phase 2: end-to-end fine-tuning at lower LR (2e-4).
why: Reached LB 0.935+ without self-training; cosine converged faster and better than unnormalized MSE.
when: Audio/other domains with a strong foundation model that cannot be fine-tuned or deployed directly.
quote: Distill the backbone from the teacher's embeddings via a linear projection head using cosine loss.

what: Re-ran backbone distillation for every model even with the same backbone, and swapped the teacher (AudioProtoPNet) for one model.
why: Distillation loss stays non-zero, adding slight diversity; two otherwise identical models with different distillation seeds ensembled with a notable boost.
when: Ensembles of highly correlated distilled models.
quote: I re-distilled backbone each time .

what: Sliced all audio into 5-second chunks, abs-max normalised; longer-input models worked worse this year.
why: Stripping context beyond the labelled chunk tells the model where to focus; optimal duration depends on call lengths and annotator labelling.
when: Sound event detection with sparse chunk-level labels.
quote: I sliced audio into 5-second chunks .

what: Extra Xeno-Canto / iNaturalist data for target species consistently made results worse, so only competition data was used (except an Amphibia/Insecta specialist).
why: Not explained.
when: Domain-shifted tests where in-domain data matters most.
quote: Any extra data I pulled from Xeno-Canto or iNaturalist for the target species made results

what: Mix a random labelled soundscape (LSS) chunk into a fraction (0.25-0.75) of each batch via mixup, taking the element-wise max of labels, plus 2 clean LSS chunks per batch.
why: Injects test-domain background and rare species.
when: Small in-domain labelled set with large out-of-domain training data.
quote: Clean (concatenated, non-mixed) LSS chunks per batch: 2 , to show a few clean

what: The sampled LSS labels are normalised to sum 0.5 instead of 1 per label.
why: Few LSS samples overfit quickly; this reduces the training signal on LSS species so the model focuses on focal-only species.
when: Label-mixing augmentation with tiny injected sets.
quote: normalizing the sampled LSS label sum to 0.5 instead of assigining 1 to each label

what: Cap pseudo-label sums below the focal label sum (0.75 cap) and inject LSS and pseudo-labelled USS into separate focal samples, never both on the same sample.
why: With distilled bases, even slightly noisy PL pulled the signal toward itself and was fatal; capping keeps background but adds a faint signal.
when: Pseudo-labelling on top of strong initial models.
quote: The first enabler was to cap the PL label sum below the focal label sum

what: For Site 22, mask all species that did not appear in the LSS.
why: Prior that Site 22 has enough samples that non-LSS species are rare there.
quote: masking all species for Site 22 that didn't appear in the LSS

what: Tracked LB per pseudo-label iteration: 0.935, 0.946, 0.950, 0.949.
why: Gains saturate after two iterations.
quote: With that setup the last year's magic came again, but only for 2 iterations.

what: Averaged scores over a Site-22 split (train on Site 22, validate on the rest, for unseen-site generalisation) and a greedy split pushing max species into validation while keeping one sample of each in train.
why: Few LSS samples; two complementary views gave stable signal for tuning; validated params beat ones readjusted on LB.
quote: push as many species into validation as possible while leaving at least

what: Trained a model on genus labels (max of all species labels in a genus, including PL) and blended its prediction spread equally to all species of the genus.
why: Rare amphibians are indistinguishable in crowded soundscapes but the genus signal helps.
quote: So I trained the model to predict genus instead of species by taking the maximum of all labels related to the same genus during data preparation

what: Ensemble SED-head, MLP-head, Amphibia/Insecta specialist, genus model and native Perch v2 across CNN families and mel sizes.
why: Distillation plus self-training yields highly correlated models; diversity adds non-linearity.
quote: I could not get competitive results without ensembling models with different heads, label

what: Temporal Gaussian smoothing with [0.33,0.33,0.33] for Amphibia/Insecta and [0.2,0.6,0.2] for other classes.
why: Inferred: long-lasting calls need flatter smoothing.
when: Time-series class predictions with differing event durations.
quote: a flatter [0.33, 0.33, 0.33] kernel for Amphibia/Insecta

what: Logit-space site priors from LSS (lambda 0.5), boost each chunk toward per-file max (alpha 0.2), smooth within genus (0.15) and class (0.05), delta-TTA shifting the pooling window by 2 frames.
why: Exploits co-occurrence and file-level structure.
quote: Genus/class taxonomy smoothing , smooth species from the same genus (α = 0.15) and from the same class (α = 0.05)

what: Tuned different chains for fine-tuned models vs native Perch predictions, on validation splits rather than via LB probing.
why: Different calibration.
quote: since the two have different calibration, and both were tuned on the validation

what: Rank-transform each class column and blend 0.8 fine-tuned ensemble with 0.2 native Perch v2 linear-head predictions; restricted-head models scattered back to the full 234-class width with a mask.
why: Perch helped on non-LSS species even though weaker overall; different score distributions.
when: Blending foundation model with fine-tuned models.
quote: I rank-transform each class column before blending rather than averaging

what: Instead of training only on slices parallel to the x/y/z axes, they cut slices from the 3D volume after a random 3D rotation, so the 2.5D model sees oblique slices.
why: Author guesses inconsistent spacing along the channel (slice) dimension hurts 2.5D models and rotation/resampling may alleviate it; improvement was little on CV/public but huge on private.
when: Anisotropic 3D volumes (CT/microscopy) processed with 2D or 2.5D networks.
quote: Random 3d rotation brought little improvement for both cv and public score. but for private score, the improvement is huge (0.682->0.835).

gain: >10% on public and private from 1536 to 3072
what: Trained on 1536x1536 whole slices but inferred at 3072x3072 (upscaled), or with a dynamic scale so that the area is about 3200x3200.
why: Thin vessels need more pixels; author reports it was critical.
when: Segmentation of thin structures where train/test resolution can differ.
quote: Large inference size is critical for the final score. >10% boost from 1536 to 3072 for both public and private scores.

what: Choose a per-image resize factor so that the resized area is a constant (3200x3200) rather than a fixed size.
why: Inferred: images have different aspect ratios/sizes, so a constant pixel area keeps object scale and memory consistent.
quote: we used a dynamic scale factor that (h*scale)*(w*scale)=3200*3200

gain: ~2% local CV; no public/private change but more stable
what: A custom loss converts voxel logits to 2x2x2 cube probabilities (foreground, background, surface) with conv3d on log-sigmoid and computes dice on foreground, background and surface-area-weighted surface, mimicking the competition surface Dice metric.
why: Directly optimises the leaderboard metric; author found it mainly made scores more stable and gave about 2% local CV.
when: Metric is surface/boundary based and non-differentiable.
quote: The custom loss gave us ~2% boost for local cv, no improvement for public or private lb. But we noticed that the custom loss brought more stability and consistency for public and private scores.

what: Loss mix of 1.0 focal, 1.0 dice, 0.01 boundary and 1.0 custom loss.
why: Boundary loss added a small gain on top of focal+dice.
quote: And we discovered boundary loss in early experiments which brought minimal improvement(<1%) for cv and public lb.

what: Feed 3 neighbouring slices as channels to a 2D UNet and train on slices from all three axes (x, y, z); inference also on 3 axes.
why: Inferred: gives 3D context cheaply and multi-view averaging at test time; author says 3D models and >3 slices did not work.
quote: an ensemble of two 2.5d convnext tiny unet with 3 channels

what: Replaced BatchNorm/ReLU in the SMP ConvNeXt-tiny UNet with GroupNorm/GELU and added an extra stride-2 conv+LayerNorm stem; input is raw image/65535 without intensity normalisation.
why: GroupNorm was for gradient accumulation (small batches at 1536px); commenter notes this makes normalisation local feature-level rather than intensity-level.
when: High-resolution segmentation with tiny per-step batches.
quote: The GroupNorm is for gradient accumulation and the GELU is just an empirical choice.

what: Just divide the 16-bit image by 65535; no per-image or dataset standardisation.
why: Authors say other normalisations did not work well; commenter hengck23 thinks per-image normalisation erased useful absolute intensity cues.
quote: Normalization: No normalization, just image = image / 65535.0

what: Train on whole slices resized/cropped to 1536x1536 instead of tiles, with a random-rescale + pad + random-crop branch in the augmentation.
why: Inferred: keeps global context and matches the large-resolution inference.
when: Large images with thin structures where memory allows.
quote: Whole slice instead of tiles and all slices resized or cropped to 1536x1536.

trick: Use all labelled data incl. kidney_1_voi
what: Final models trained on every training volume including the sparsely annotated kidney_1_voi; validation only used kidney_3_dense during experimentation.
why: Little labelled data; commenter thinks this was a crucial point for the high private score.
when: Tiny labelled datasets with noisy or sparse labels.
quote: We used all training data including kidney_1_voi.

what: Use kidney_3_dense as the only validation set during experiments, then retrain on everything for submission; accept that CV-LB correlation is poor and require CV not to degrade.
why: Lack of data; strategy was to improve LB while keeping local CV same or better.
when: Very small datasets with unreliable CV.
quote: For experimenting, we used kidney_3_dense for validation and other data for training.

what: Since the final model was trained on all data, they selected the last three checkpoints of one experiment for submission, choosing among them on public LB.
why: LB scores varied a lot between checkpoints with similar CV.
when: Noisy metrics, no holdout when training on all data.
quote: we selected the last three checkpoints of one experiment for submissions, the lb score for different checkpoints varies a lot even with similar cv (the selection was based on lb).

what: Flip/transpose 8x TTA over 3 axes; torch.compile gave about 2x speedup, which made the high-resolution TTA fit the time limit.
why: Speed budget enabled larger inference size and TTA.
when: Time-limited code competitions with heavy inference.
quote: torch.compile() gave about 2x acceleration so that we were able to inference with high resolution and TTAs.

what: Binarise at 0.4; CV and LB optimum was 0.4-0.5.
why: Inferred: thin-structure recall favoured a lower threshold.
quote: The threshold used for submission is 0.4, and the optimal threshold based on cv and lb is about 0.4~0.5.

what: Ensemble of two models scored 0.744-0.774 private while a single 3D-rotation model scored 0.835; the selected ensemble was not the best.
why: Author speculates inconsistent channel spacing in non-rotated 2.5D models; no confirmed reason.
when: Noisy private LB with few test volumes.
quote: Actually the best scored submission is not the selected ensemble but one single model of the ensemble which is 0.835 on private lb.

what: Tried stochastic weight averaging and EMA of weights; neither helped.
why: No reason given.
quote: We also tried swa and ema, but didn't work well.

what: Using more than 3 slices as channels in the 2.5D model did not help; neither did 3D models, external data, pseudo labels or transformers.
why: No reason given.
quote: Stacking more slices (>3) for 2.5d model.

what: Rank all test tomograms by max predicted voxel value and remove the lowest quantile (about 0.56) as motor-absent, instead of a fixed probability threshold; quantile tuned on public LB.
why: Fixed thresholds were unstable across models/LB; a rank-based cutoff gives stable feedback and transfers (0.565 public vs 0.560 private).
when: Presence/absence detection on a test set with roughly stable positive rate and a hard-to-calibrate model
quote: Like many others, I found that fixed thresholds were unstable. Instead, I use quantile thresholding to determine motor presence.

what: Gaussian heatmap targets centred on each motor, with resolution reduced 8x.
why: Metric tolerates large distance error, so exact pixel is unimportant; presence matters.
when: Localisation metrics with generous distance tolerance
quote: the resolution of the heatmap is reduced by 8x. This works especially well for this competition as there is a high tolerance for distance error in the metric.

what: Add a BCE loss on a max-pooled (kernel/stride 4) main output plus a deep-supervision head on the second-last feature map.
why: Pooled loss encourages high probability around the motor while reducing penalty for small localisation errors.
when: Small-object heatmap segmentation with tolerant metric
quote: a max pooled loss (kernel size and stride of 4) is applied on the main segmentation head. Moreover, the pooled loss encourages high probabilities around the motor region, while reducing the penalty for small localization errors.

what: Used Napari to manually add missing motors to noisy competition annotations and published updated data; also dropped tomograms without motors (later said no impact).
why: Inferred: noisy/missing labels hurt training of a detector.
when: Noisy detection labels in small scientific datasets
quote: the competition data is quite noisy, so Napari was used to manually add missing motors.

what: Combined competition tomograms with tomograms from the CryoET Data Portal for training.
why: Inferred: more diverse training tomograms.
when: Scientific imaging with public related archives
quote: Tomograms from the competition data and the CryoET Data Portal are used to create a training set.

what: Mixup 100%, zoom, 90-degree rotations, axis flips/swaps, coarse dropout, colour inversion, cutmix; enabled 400 epochs without overfitting. All but rescale done on GPU.
why: Heavy augmentation allows long training without overfitting; GPU augmentation avoids slow CPU loading bottleneck.
quote: Heavy augmentations enabled training for 400 epochs without overfitting.

what: Used a pretrained ResNet200 encoder with stochastic depth and gradient checkpointing, one deconv decoder block.
why: Larger pretrained encoder gave better performance.
quote: increasing the capacity of the encoder yields better performance

trick: Slide only over depth at inference
what: Match patch height/width to the volume and slide only over depth, 4x faster, allowing more TTA and 0.875 overlap.
why: Saves compute for TTA/overlap with equal score.
when: Large-volume sliding-window inference with time limits
quote: it was 4x faster to match the patch height and width, and only slide over the depth. This allows more time for TTA and a very high overlap (0.875).

what: Weight middle 40% of sliding-window logits as 1.0 and edges as 0.001.
why: Inferred: edge predictions are less reliable.
quote: The middle 40% of the logits are weighted as 1.0 and other logits are weighted as 0.001 when aggregating the sliding window.

trick: Public LB for validation beyond CV ceiling
what: Local 4-fold CV tracked LB only up to ~0.93; beyond that the public LB (with quantile thresholding) was used to select.
why: Inferred: CV saturated.
quote: Local CV strongly correlates with the LB up to about 0.93. Beyond that, I used the public LB for validation.

what: Averaged 8 seeds of large models; inference ~10 hours.
why: Inferred: seed variance reduction.
quote: The final submission uses an 8-seed ensemble.

what: Instead of a temporal split, sampled a 1000-protein validation set whose species proportions match the CAFA5 test set.
why: Validation mirrors the test distribution so component tuning transfers.
when: Multi-species prediction where test species mix differs from train
quote: Unlike the temporal split in NetGO, we selected proteins for validation based on the species distribution of proteins in the CAFA5 test set.

what: The learning-to-rank ensemble receives component scores plus a 20-dim one-hot vector of protein species.
why: Inferred: lets the ranker learn which component methods to trust per species.
when: Stacking of heterogeneous predictors whose reliability varies by group
quote: the input to the model contains not only the predicted scores from each method, but also a 20-dim one-hot vector to characterize the protein species information.

what: Many diverse component methods (sequence, structure, text, PPI) trained on a train split; their predictions on held-out validation proteins train a learning-to-rank ensemble.
why: Effectively integrates multiple information sources (author states it integrates methods effectively).
when: Large multi-label prediction with many heterogeneous predictors
quote: Then we used the trained component methods to predict function for validation proteins. Finally, we trained the ensemble model based on the prediction on validation sets.

what: Net-KNN (PPI-based) predictions are only used for proteins from the top 15 species with the most annotations; others are dropped.
why: Net-KNN performs poorly for species with little annotation and hurt the ensemble when fused everywhere.
when: Component predictor with reliability depending on data availability per group
quote: Finally, we treated Net-KNN predictions for the top 15 species as effective results.

what: Predict GO terms by weighted voting among annotated training proteins with similar 3D structure (FoldSeek similarity).
why: Structure carries functional information complementary to sequence.
quote: By comparing the structural similarities between the test proteins and the proteins in the training set, we calculated the prediction score as weighted voting by similar annotated proteins.

what: GORetrieval: retrieve candidate GO terms from proteins with similar text descriptions, then rerank by semantic matching between GO term descriptions and the protein literature.
why: Leverages textual/literature information; reranking can also enhance other methods.
when: Label prediction where labels and instances have text descriptions
quote: Given a target protein, it first retrieved candidate Gene Ontology (GO) terms from annotated proteins with similar descriptions.

gain: about 90% of final performance from one extra text or structure component
what: Used protein descriptions and scientific literature (D2V, TF-IDF, PubMedBERT embeddings) as an extra information source; text or structure component added to NetGO 3.0 reportedly gives ~90% of final performance.
why: Text carries annotation information absent from sequence.
quote: incorporating a component method based on textual or structural information into NetGO 3.0 can achieve 90% of the final performance.

what: Tried ESM2 and ProtT5 and their concatenation instead of ESM-1b embeddings; little difference, ESM-1b gave best ensemble result.
why: Author reports ensemble performed best with LR-ESM (ESM-1b).
quote: We found little difference in the scores achieved by these methods, but the best performance was achieved when LR-ESM was integrated as a component method into the GOCurator.

what: Mean-pool last-layer residue embeddings and train one logistic regression per GO term with annotated proteins as positives and the rest as negatives.
why: Simple, scalable multi-label baseline on embeddings.
when: Large multi-label annotation with frozen embeddings
quote: Typically, we perform mean pooling on the output of the last layer for each amino acid, and generate the feature representation of the protein.

what: Scores from seven very different component methods (BLAST-KNN, network KNN, FoldSeek-KNN, ESM2-SVM, InterPro LR, two literature methods) are fed as features to an XGBoost learning-to-rank model that produces the final GO-term ranking per protein.
why: No single evidence source dominated across all proteins and GO categories, and component rankings shifted between public and private LB, so a learned combiner is more robust than picking the best component.
when: Multi-label / extreme multi-label prediction with several complementary information sources and candidate lists per sample.
quote: integrated using an XGBoost-based Learning-to-Rank framework

what: Estimated the species composition of the test proteins and sampled 1,000 experimentally annotated proteins with the same species distribution as a held-out validation benchmark used for model selection.
why: Inferred: validation that mimics the test distribution gives a more trustworthy signal than a random split when the test set is species-skewed.
when: Test set has a known covariate distribution (e.g. species, domain) that differs from the training pool.
quote: we randomly sampled 1,000 experimentally annotated proteins according to the same species distribution

what: Component methods are trained on the training split only; the held-out validation proteins (species-matched) are used to generate component scores that train the LTR model, so the ranker sees out-of-sample component predictions.
why: Inferred: training the stacker on in-sample component scores would leak and overweight overfit components.
when: Stacking where base models are expensive or non-fold-based (KNN, retrieval) and a clean holdout is available.
quote: The training set was used to train the component methods, and the validation set was used to train the LTR model.

trick: GO frequency and species features in ranker
what: Besides component scores, the ranker gets GO term frequency and a 21-dimensional species encoding as features.
why: Inferred: lets the ranker calibrate how much to trust each component per species and per term prior.
when: Ranking/stacking over label candidates where label priors and group identity matter.
quote: GOAlpha further incorporates GO term frequency, and a 21-dimensional species encoding

what: A FoldSeek-based KNN transfers GO annotations from structurally similar proteins (AlphaFold structures) as an extra base predictor.
why: Structural similarity provides functional signal beyond sequence homology and is complementary in ensembling even though standalone it is weaker.
when: Protein function prediction or any task where a second similarity modality (structure) can be searched.
quote: transfers GO annotations from structurally similar proteins identified by FoldSeek

what: Literature-based predictors use only high-quality manually curated papers linked to SwissProt proteins, retrieving candidate GO terms from similar descriptions then reranking by semantic relevance to GO concepts.
why: Restricting to curated literature reduces noisy or weakly related papers.
when: Using text evidence as a feature source where automatic retrieval is noisy.
quote: we mainly used high-quality manually curated literature associated with SwissProt proteins

what: GORetriever first retrieves candidate GO terms from proteins with similar descriptions and literature evidence, then reranks them by semantic relevance between GO concepts and protein text.
why: Inferred: reduces the huge label space to a small candidate set before fine scoring.
when: Very large label spaces with text evidence.
quote: first retrieves candidate GO terms from proteins with similar descriptions and literature evidence, and subsequently reranks them

what: Logistic regression per GO term on a 118,677-dimensional binary vector of InterPro families, domains and motifs from InterProScan.
why: Inferred: presence/absence of domain signatures is a strong, cheap and independent signal.
when: Very high-dimensional sparse binary features with many labels.
quote: trained on a 118,677-dimensional binary feature vector generated from protein families, domains, and motifs

what: Noticed literature methods led the public LB but dropped on private while sequence/structure methods rose; used the ranker to blend all sources rather than pick the best public component.
why: Public LB ranking depends on the composition of the evaluation proteins.
when: Small or non-representative public LB with heterogeneous predictors.
quote: strong public leaderboard performance does not necessarily guarantee the best final ranking

what: Ensure all evidence databases (domains, networks, GO annotations, literature) used for a validation protein are restricted to what was available before its experimental annotation.
why: Evidence sources are continuously updated, so later versions leak the label.
quote: it is important to ensure that all evidence used by a method is restricted to information available before the test protein experimental annotations were obtained

what: Targets are soft tolerance-banded labels around events that are further decayed each epoch (non-1 values reduced by 1/n_epochs).
why: Narrowing the target range lets the model detect finer peaks.
quote: By attenuating the target, the range of predicted values narrows, allowing for the detection of finer peaks.

what: Target built by stacking rolling-max windows at the metric tolerances (12,36,...,360 steps) scaled by decreasing weights.
why: Mirrors the multi-tolerance average-precision metric.
when: Event detection metrics with several tolerances
quote: A decaying target is created based on the distance from the ground truth event, with diminishing values as the distance increases.

gain: +0.0108 CV output filter, +0.0063 as input flag
what: Detect daily periodicity from device removal rule-based, use as filter on outputs and as an input flag.
why: Device-off periods have no sleep events.
quote: there is a daily periodicity in the data when the measuring device is removed. This is leveraged to predict these periods rule-based and used as a filter for inputs and predictions.

what: Changed batch size 16 to 4, hidden 128 to 64, layers 2 to 8.
why: Inferred: deeper recurrent stack with noisier small batches generalizes better.
quote: batch_size: 16 → 4, hidden_size: 128 → 64, num_layers: 2 → 8 (cv: 0.7985, +11pt)

what: Normalize prediction scores in the submission by their daily sum.
why: Inferred: roughly one event per day, so normalizing calibrates per-day probabilities.
when: Event detection with known event rate
quote: Normalize the score in the submission file by the daily score sum (cv: 0.8044, +6pt)

what: Removed month and day from input features.
why: Inferred: they let the model overfit to individual series.
quote: Remove month and day from the input (cv: 0.8117, +7pt)

what: Average overlapping chunk predictions and trim 30 minutes at both chunk ends.
why: Inferred: edge predictions lack context.
quote: For evaluation, overlapping sections are averaged, and the ends of each chunk are trimmed by 30 minutes.

what: Concatenate an embedding of the minute-of-hour to the last layer rather than only the input.
why: Ground-truth events were biased to certain minutes; final-layer access exploits that.
quote: features related to minutes were concatenated separately in the final layer.

what: Split series into daily chunks with 0.35-day stride; each epoch uses only every other chunk.
why: Inferred: overlapping chunks give augmentation while limiting epoch cost.
quote: Each series of data is divided into daily chunks, offset by 0.35 days.

what: Because all events are at second 0 and the smallest tolerance spans 30s, score is equal for any second in a half-minute; they evaluate points at 15s and 45s of each minute.
why: Representative points maximize match chance under the metric.
when: Event detection with known timestamp structure
quote: we estimate the score at the 15 and 45 second points of each minute, and submit the one with the highest value

what: Score each candidate as sum of windowed prediction sums at each tolerance, pick the best, then discount predictions within each tolerance of chosen points and repeat.
why: Adopted events cannot match overlappingly, so later candidates get discounted scores; optimizes the metric directly.
when: Top-k event submission under AP-with-tolerance metrics
quote: Events within tolerance 12 of the adopted point cannot match overlappingly with the next point to be submitted.

what: Average first-level predictions per minute, find_peaks (height 0.001, distance 8), cut +-8 minute chunks around peaks, train LightGBM/CatBoost and CNN/RNN/Transformer on aggregated features to predict exact-minute event.
why: Corrects minute bias; outputs calibrated probabilities usable for the greedy post-processing.
quote: detecting peaks in these averages using find_peaks with a height of 0.001 and a distance of 8.

trick: Tune chunk size for class ratio
what: Tuned number of steps included around peaks for the second-level model.
why: Positive-to-negative ratio changes with window size and affects accuracy.
