quote: This step_size was crucial because the ratio of positive to negative examples changes depending on how many steps are included

trick: BCE over KL for soft targets
what: Used BCEWithLogitsLoss rather than KLDivLoss for the soft target.
why: Author reports it worked better.
quote: In my case, using BCEWithLogitsLoss worked better.

what: Trains regressors on the raw PCIAT-PCIAT_Total score instead of the sii class label and converts predictions to sii labels afterwards.
why: Inferred: finer-grained target keeps information lost by binning to 4 classes.
when: Ordinal targets derived by binning a continuous score that is available in train.
quote: Instead of using the provided sii labels, I used the 'PCIAT-PCIAT_Total' score and converted the predictions to sii labels.

what: Sample weights defined by equidistant bins of the target, to counter the excess zeros; also explored Tweedie objective.
why: Did not improve optimised scores directly but brought unoptimised scores closer to the optimised ones.
quote: Weighting did not improve the optimized scores directly but it brought the unoptimized scores closer to the optimized scores.

what: 10-fold stratified KFold stratified by the target bins, seeds changed frequently, and multiple-seed submissions used to gauge public LB variance; LB itself mostly ignored.
why: Stability on a noisy small dataset; avoids overfitting to the LB.
when: Small noisy datasets with continuous target.
quote: Seeds were frequently changed to ensure stability. Submissions with different seeds were used to get further feedback from the public Leaderboard on the variance.

what: Hyperparameter tuning with Repeated Stratified KFold, 10 to 20 repeats.
why: Regular CV tuning gave unstable outcomes on this noisy data.
when: Small noisy datasets where single-split CV noise exceeds tuning gains.
quote: Repeated Stratified KFold was employed during parameter tuning. With 10 to 20 repeats.

what: Values such as body fat over 60% or negative bone mineral content were set to NaN.
why: Removes measurement errors.
quote: Implausible values, such as body fat percentages over 60% or negative bone mineral content, were removed and replaced with NaN.

what: Descriptive actigraphy statistics computed with separate day and night masks; PCA on actigraph data keeping 15 components.
why: Inferred: compresses high-dimensional time-series summaries and captures sleep vs activity behaviour.
when: Wearable time-series summarised into tabular features.
quote: Various descriptive actigraph features were created, with separate masks for day and night.

what: Normalises features (e.g. PU, CU) by the mean of their age group, and drops the originals.
why: PU and CU were strongly correlated with age, which strongly relates to the outcome; normalising reduces the age effect even though the normalised features correlate less with the target.
when: Features confounded by a strong covariate such as age.
quote: By normalizing PU and CU based on the mean of the age groups, the age effect in these features was reduced.

what: Quantile binning applied to a good chunk of the features.
why: Deals with feature noise; author calls the result surprisingly good.
when: Noisy, subjective tabular features with GBDT.
quote: Quantile binning was applied to a good chunk of the features to deal with the noise. Which worked surprisingly well.

what: For each target column, train a Lasso on features with under 40% missing, impute missing values from it; fall back to mean imputation if no valid features or too few samples.
why: Moderately high dimensionality and noise make Lasso a robust imputer.
when: Tabular data with heavy missingness and noise.
quote: For each target column, a model was trained using features with fewer than 40% missing values, and missing values in these features were imputed based on the trained model.

what: Feature selection done manually from feature importance, reducing to 39 features.
why: Inferred: less noise and overfitting on a small noisy dataset.
quote: Feature selection was done manually based on feature importance, reducing the dataset to 39 features

what: Voting ensemble of LGBM, two XGBoost, CatBoost and ExtraTrees regressors.
why: Inferred: diversity improves robustness on noisy data.
quote: The final solution was a voted ensemble consisting of:

what: Ignored the public LB score to avoid overfitting, focused on robustness, and credits luck in picking the best final notebook.
why: Public LB was noisy relative to private.
when: Small test sets with big public/private shakeup.
quote: The LB-score itself was mostly ignored to minimize overfitting to the leaderboard.

what: Trained large ensembles separately for IMU-only samples and for samples with all sensors, combined as a weighted sum of logits.
why: Inferred: roughly half of test samples have only IMU data, so each regime gets models trained for it.
when: Test data with partly missing sensor modalities.
quote: Large ensembles for IMU-only and all-features samples, assembled as weighted sum of logits

gain: Sub-ensembles 0.873-0.874 public at merge time were improved significantly further (per author comment)
what: Post-processing that exploits limited number of samples per class and per orientation per subject, found by optimisation heuristics (details in a separately linked post, not fetched).
why: Inferred: each subject performs a fixed set of gestures/orientations, so predictions can be reassigned to satisfy these counts.
when: Test data with known structure in label counts per group.
quote: Post-processing to take into account limited number of samples with each class and with each orientation per subject (already described here)

what: Trained additional models to predict subject orientation, used in post-processing.
why: Inferred: orientation predictions feed the per-orientation structure constraints.
when: Tasks with a latent group attribute usable in post-processing.
quote: Additional models for orientation prediction

trick: Remove wrongly-worn subjects and bad sequences
what: Dropped subjects who wore the device incorrectly from both train and validation, a sequence without gesture, sequences with gesture/total ratio below 0.2, and sequences with TOF fully missing (for TOF models).
why: Inferred: removes label-noise/outlier sequences that hurt training and make validation unreliable.
quote: remove sequences with gesture/total ratio < 0.2 (this subset includes almost all shortest sequences)

what: Transform left-handed subjects to look right-handed: flip acc_x, convert rotation to xyz Euler angles and flip sign of y and z; same for THM/TOF.
why: Inferred: removes handedness as a nuisance variable and doubles effective data per gesture.
when: Wearable sensor data with a left/right symmetry.
quote: preprocess left handed to match right handed for IMU and THM/TOF. Flip acc_x, convert rot to xyz euler and flip sign for y and z

what: Replaced the 8x8 time-of-flight grid by means over nine 2x2 squares, after turning -1 into null.
why: Inferred: cuts dimensionality and noise of sparse TOF input.
quote: For TOF subsample by taking nine 2x2 squares and calculating mean for each (turn -1 to null first)

what: Replaced TOF value -1 with 500 instead of leaving it as a sentinel.
why: -1 encodes a large distance, so a large number keeps the scale meaningful.
when: Sensors using sentinel codes for out-of-range.
quote: replace -1 TOF values with 500 because -1 encodes large distance

what: Computed a second copy of 35 IMU features (acc, jerk, correlations, magnitudes) on accelerations transformed by remove_gravity_from_acc(), alongside the raw-based copy.
why: Inferred: linear acceleration without gravity gives orientation-independent motion cues.
when: Accelerometer data on a rotating device.
quote: acc_x2 and other ***2 features are important part of the solution.

what: Trained without any scaler; the author reports it gave the largest improvement early on. A teammate adds dividing by 10 is enough since provided scales are already good.
why: Inferred: raw physical scale information is useful and scaling statistics can distort it.
when: NN on sensor data with sensible native scales.
quote: no scalers - it gave the largest improvement at early stage

what: First layers process feature groups (IMU, THM, TOF) in independent branches before merging.
why: Inferred: modalities have different statistics and shapes, so separate stems avoid mixing them too early.
quote: key part - independent processing groups of features at first layers

trick: Mixup plus time shift and stretch
what: Mixup with alpha 0.4 combined with TimeShift (p 0.35, up to 25%) and TimeStretch (p 0.35, rate 0.5-1.5) augmentations; teammate also found data masking helps.
why: Inferred: regularises small, noisy subject-grouped data.
quote: It was hard to pick up right augmetations with right probability & strength and apply it in the correct order.

gain: no CV gain; ensemble diversity only
what: Increase sequence length by 5 at inference time.
why: Does not improve CV but decorrelates ensemble members.
quote: increase sequence length by 5 on inference (it doesn't improve CV score but effectively decorrelates models)

trick: Best of three runs per fold
what: For each fold, train 3 runs and keep the best one.
why: Inferred: reduces seed variance, at the risk of optimistic fold scores.
quote: pick best result for each fold among 3 runs

what: Pad or crop sequences to the 94th percentile of length per fold (~120 steps).
why: Inferred: saves compute and avoids long-tail padding.
quote: pad/crop by 94 percentile in each fold (~120 max seq length)

what: Trained a 3D CNN on TOF data only; it scores about 0.83 alone but improves the blend.
why: Inferred: it captures a different modality than IMU models.
when: Weak but diverse single-modality models in a blend.
quote: 3D CNN for TOF data scores about 0.83 but blends well

what: 5-fold CV grouped by subject.
why: Prevents the same subject leaking across folds.
quote: CV5 with group by subject K-fold, 5 models are used on inference

what: Besides 5 regression heads, add 5 classification heads predicting which of 7 target intervals the biomass falls in (cross-entropy, weight 0.3), borrowing the count-interval partition from crowd counting (UEPNet).
why: Task resembles crowd counting without density maps; interval classification adds a robust signal.
when: Regression from images with skewed targets.
quote: we add an additional classification head for each species to predict the interval where the biomass lies, which resulted in an improvement of approximately 0.03 in both LB and PB.

what: Choose class borders with the UEP partition: binary search a per-interval error budget so each interval has similar accumulated (value gap x count) error, giving uneven borders per species.
why: Inferred: uniform intervals would be dominated by the skewed target distribution.
quote: we use the training set to divide seven intervals for each species

gain: best single-model private (0.66) but lower public; not in final
what: L1 loss with dead zone epsilon = 1 for targets <=20, else 0.1*target clamped at 5, so large values tolerate larger errors.
why: Biomass distribution is uneven; large values have large errors and small values small errors.
when: Regression with heteroscedastic error scaling with target.
quote: we hope that "large values have large errors and small values have small errors"

what: Split the wide image into left and right halves, pass both through the same DINOv3 backbone, fuse concatenated features with one multi-head self-attention layer then MLP.
why: Enhances consistency.
quote: we use a single multi-head self-attention layer to interact with the concatenated features of the left and right sub-images

what: With p=0.2, resize image by 0.85-1.0 and paste at random position on a black canvas.
why: Simulates focal length and viewing angle differences between cameras.
quote: we apply a small size scaling to the images randomly and then complement them with black pixels to simulate the focal length and viewing angle differences of different cameras.

what: Stage 1 freezes DINO and trains fusion layers and heads; stage 2 fine-tunes everything.
why: Chosen empirically as most effective of strategies tried.
when: Fine-tuning large ViT backbones on small data.
quote: Stage 1: Freeze DINO, then train the fusion layers and MLP heads.

what: DINO-Large and Huge performed similarly, so spent compute on 1024 px input per view with Large.
why: Limited compute; input size gave more benefit.
quote: With limited computational resources, the benefit of increasing the input size was better than increasing the model size.

what: Pseudo-label test set with 4 good models, train two DINO-Large on train+test (no CV, SWA of last epochs) then a few epochs on train only; repeat second round to train two DINO-Base; blend 0.4/0.6.
why: Self-distillation on the test distribution; final train-only epochs prevent overfitting to pseudo labels.
when: Small labelled set, test set available at inference.
quote: Online training during testing brought us a gain of >0.02.

what: Scale clover by 0.8, dead by 1.1 if >20 and 0.9 if <10, average GDM with green+clover, and total = 0.5*head + 0.5*(green+clover+dead).
why: Derived partly from open notebooks and partly from CV/LB.
quote: out_gdm = 0.5*out_gdm+ 0.5*(out_green+out_clover)

what: Three folds grouped jointly by state and sampling date, then train only a single fold model because results vary greatly between folds.
why: Fold variance is large.
quote: Divide into three folds, determined jointly by the state and sampling date , and then train a single-fold model.

what: Ranking loss using random crops (crop biomass less than full) plus label-based pairs improved CV but hurt LB.
why: Likely overfitting.
quote: This scheme performed well on the CV, once surpassing our previous best model, but got a poor LB, which might be due to overfitting again~

what: Removing dropout hurt; dropout significantly outperformed no dropout despite expected train/inference variance mismatch.
why: Empirical.
quote: dropout performed excellently in our experiments, significantly outperforming its removal.

trick: Failed: physical constraints and per-species models
what: Hard physical constraints (derive remaining biomass) and one model per species did not help; independent heads without constraints used.
why: Authors believe constraints increase dependence on the training set.
quote: No physical constraints are imposed on them during training, which we believe reduces the model's dependence on the training set.

gain: single model about 0.766 vs about 0.74 for the earlier gaussian-ball UNet (per author comments)
what: Instead of a full UNet decoder to full resolution, computes the pixel-wise loss on the penultimate feature map (a 'partly UNet'): 96^3 input patches, loss on the 48^3 output, with single-pixel targets rather than gaussian heatmaps.
why: They found the penultimate map more accurate than the last one, and box regression gains negligible since particles of one type have similar size; coarse output is enough and faster.
when: 3D/2D particle or keypoint localisation where the metric tolerates small localisation error.
quote: the penultimate feature map has a higher accuracy than the last one, which is surprising at first

what: Drops gaussian-ball heatmap targets; uses single pixels as targets with weighted cross-entropy where positive pixels get weight 256 and background weight 1.
why: Suppressing background with a low class weight removes the need for gaussian heatmaps and handles the very low number of positive pixels.
quote: To account for low number of positive pixels, positive pixels are weighted by 256 and background has weight 1.

trick: Keep unscored class as extra label
what: Trains with 7 classes including background and keeps beta-amylase as a class even though it is not scored.
why: The model learns to differentiate beta-galactosidase from the confusable unscored class.
when: Multi-class problems where an unscored class is a hard confuser of a scored one.
quote: Notably keeping beta-amylase as a class although it is not scored is quite helpful as model learns to differentiate beta-galactosidase from it.

what: Grid-searches per-class thresholds each epoch on the validation experiment; after all folds, refits each fold's threshold on the OOF predictions of the other 6 folds, averages the resulting f4-curves and picks the best threshold.
why: Gives more stable thresholds than a single-fold optimum for the F4-style metric.
when: Metrics depending on a detection threshold, e.g. F-beta on detections.
quote: After all 7 folds were trained we could re-calibrate thresholds, by taking OOF predictions. And fitting the threshold for one fold on the predictions of the other 6.

what: 7-fold CV formed by splitting by experiment (one tomogram per fold); mean f4-score over folds tracked the LB.
why: Experiments are the natural group; folds mimic unseen test experiments.
when: Data with natural groups (experiments, patients, sessions).
quote: 7 folds were used, simply by splitting by experiment. Using mean of f4-score of all 7 folds had some good correlation with LB.

gain: segmentation combined 0.778 vs about 0.766 single models (segmentation ensemble only)
what: To combine two model families whose output feature maps have different distributions, for each class sort all pixel values of A and B and replace B's values with A's values of the same rank (quantile/histogram matching), then blend the feature maps before running detection post-processing.
why: Gives both predictions the same distribution so they can be blended directly at feature-map level.
when: Blending models with different architectures/losses whose raw outputs are not on a common scale.
quote: for each class sort all pixel values for A and B and replace values of B with the corresponding values of A of same rank.

what: Own GPU MixUp implementation inside the model forward: Beta-distributed coefficient per sample, mixes both inputs and targets (not losses), works for 1D/2D/3D, applied with probability mixup_p.
why: Models trained from scratch overfit; mixup allowed much longer training (more than doubles epochs).
when: Small datasets, training from scratch, including dense 3D targets.
quote: Additionally I used my own implementation of MixUp which was highly effective to train longer and prevent overfitting.

what: Uses relatively small FlexibleUnet models (resnet34, efficientnet-b3) trained from scratch; six checkpoints each about 2h on an A100 with bf16.
why: Author found loss design the most important aspect and small models work well.
when: Small 3D data with few training volumes.
quote: In general, we observed that relatively small models work really and the design of loss is the most important aspect.

what: Exports models via jit or TensorRT to speed up inference, enabling a slightly larger ensemble within the runtime limit.
why: Compute budget in code competitions limits ensemble size.
when: Code competitions with inference time limits.
quote: exported models via jit or TensorRT, which gave 200% speedup increase and enabled us to have a slightly larger ensemble.

what: Tried supplemental external or simulated data; it did not help, and the final solution used none.
why: No reason given.
when: Cryo-ET style tasks with simulated data available.
quote: We did not use any external or simulated data!

what: Tried Tversky and Dice losses instead of weighted cross-entropy; they did not work.
why: No reason given.
quote: Other losses (Tversky, Dice)

trick: Discard train.csv, rebuild data via OCR
what: Ignored the official train.csv entirely and rebuilt the training set by extracting transliteration-translation pairs from scholarly book PDFs with an LLM.
why: The official training data came only from one book series and had quality problems; their own pipeline gave cleaner and more data.
when: Low-resource tasks where the true source material is available in unstructured form.
quote: We extracted training data from PDFs provided by the hosts and collected by ourselves (we completely discarded train.csv ).

what: Used GLM-OCR layout analysis plus regex on chapter names to build a chapter dictionary (tablet name -> page range) per book, then extracted per tablet rather than per page.
why: Tablets span pages, so a per-tablet unit preserves complete texts.
when: OCR extraction from books where logical units cross page boundaries.
quote: Using the tablet rather than the page as the basic unit preserves information more completely.

what: Sent the prompt, tablet name and page images to Gemini 3.0 pro to extract sentence-level transliteration-translation pairs, also asking for English translations when the source was German or Turkish; poorly structured sources were handled through a vibe-coded screenshot-paste frontend with preset prompts.
why: Handles layouts and multi-language translations that rule-based OCR cannot; manual screenshot regions cut tokens and cost (about $100-200 total).
when: Building parallel corpora from scanned books.
quote: we sent the prompt, tablet name, and page images of the tablet to Gemini to extract sentence-level transliteration-translation pairs.

what: Prompted the LLM to first understand whole English sentences and then find their start and end in the transliteration (never line-by-line), using numbers, logograms and names as anchors and accounting for SOV vs SVO order and obverse/reverse continuations.
why: Transliteration follows physical line breaks while scholarly translations have the logical sentence structure.
when: Aligning parallel texts where one side is laid out by physical lines.
quote: Use English translation as an anchor: English translations by modern scholars have already sorted out the logical syntax and added modern punctuation.

what: Took untranslated transliterations from the OARE database (excluding tablets already OCR'd) and had Gemini generate translations using dictionary lookups and similar example pairs as context.
why: Adds large amounts of in-domain pseudo-parallel data; used alone it scored 35.0 public / 37.1 private.
when: Low-resource MT with plentiful monolingual source text and a dictionary.
quote: Combining dictionary lookups and similar transliteration-translation example queries, we called Gemini to generate translations.

what: Found dictionary words absent from the training set, then prompted an LLM with 100 example sentences plus 5 such words to write 5-10 new fictional pairs containing them (excluding names and untranslated words); a second synthetic set used 100 random sentences to produce 3-7 pairs.
why: Fills vocabulary coverage gaps with targeted examples.
when: Low-resource MT with vocabulary coverage holes.
quote: conducted a coverage gap analysis between the dictionary and the training set to filter out words truly missing from the training set.

what: Trained 4-fold models, had each fold predict on its own training fold, flagged samples with cross-fold average geo-metric below 20 as hard/error samples, then re-extracted those 740 tablets with the LLM and checked manually.
why: A well-fitted model should reproduce its training targets, so large disagreement signals bad labels.
when: Noisy, LLM- or OCR-generated labels where a fitted model can flag errors.
quote: if the inferred translation was far from the training translation, the sample was considered an error/hard sample.

what: Flagged tablets with a character-length difference over 100 between transliteration and translation, or transliterations over 500 characters, and re-extracted the 131 flagged tablets.
why: Misaligned or overlong segments confuse the model.
quote: Filtering by a character length difference > 100 and transliteration character length > 500

what: Chose the 3-epoch checkpoint by validation eval_loss, not eval_bleu/chrF, which kept improving after 3 epochs.
why: Local validation differs in style and distribution from the hidden test set, so later BLEU gains reflect over-memorizing formats.
when: Seq2seq fine-tuning with a train/test distribution gap.
quote: we selected the 3-epoch checkpoints based on the validation set's eval_loss rather than eval_bleu / chrf

trick: Scale to ByT5-XL once data is clean
what: Moved from byt5-base to large to xl in the last 10 days, trained on 8 H20 GPUs.
why: Larger models gave a significant LB gain, provided there is enough clean data to avoid overfitting.
when: Fine-tuning pretrained seq2seq models when data quality is high.
quote: However, the prerequisite for this conclusion might be: Having sufficient and clean training data, so that larger models do not fall into overfitting.

gain: ensemble private 43.0 -> 43.2, public 41.4 -> 41.6 with this model included
what: Overrode compute_loss to average token loss per sample, multiply by a data-quality weight (1.3-1.4 for best OCR books, 1.0 other English OCR, 0.8 German/Turkish, 0.5-0.7 LLM labeled/synthetic, 0.45 low-quality OCR), then average over the batch.
why: Trusts clean data more; single-model scores did not improve, but the differently biased model added diversity to the ensemble.
quote: we first calculated the average token loss for each individual sample, multiplied it by a predefined sample weight, and then computed the final weighted average across the batch.

gain: best ensemble 41.5 public / 43.2 private; single models about 40-42 private
what: Trained 11 ByT5-XL models on different combinations of the datasets (OCR v1/v2/v3, LLM-labeled, synthetic), some on all data and some on a 9:1 split, and ensembled them.
why: Models trained on different data mixes make different errors; each single model was already near the top.
quote: These 11 byt5 models were trained on different combinations of datasets.

what: Each model generated 10 candidates (4 from beam search with beam 8, 2 each from sampling at temperatures 0.60, 0.80, 1.05); after normalisation, a weighted MBR picks the candidate most consistent with the others using chrF++, BLEU, Jaccard and length reward.
why: Minimum Bayes Risk picks the consensus translation, which matches the competition metric better than a single beam output.
when: Generation tasks scored by overlap metrics, with inference budget for many samples.
quote: beam search ( beam_size=8 ) selected 4 candidates, and sampling at three temperatures [0.60, 0.80, 1.05] yielded 2 candidates each.

what: Pre-compiled the ByT5-XL models to CTranslate2 int8_float32 and ran data-parallel inference on 2 T4 GPUs, using almost the full 9-hour limit; pre-compiling saved about 30 minutes.
why: Quantisation lets many more models and candidates fit the time limit, and more quantised models beat fewer full-precision ones.
when: Code competitions with a hard inference time limit.
quote: More quantized models are better than fewer full-precision models.

what: Sorted the test set by descending character length and ran MBR on all 4 CPU cores in parallel.
why: Inferred: batches of similar length waste less padding, and parallel MBR cuts wall time.
quote: Sorted test_df in descending order by char_length .

what: Standardised the data format carefully in training and avoided output post-processing; a repeated n-gram cleaning (n=2-7) variant scored public 41.6 / private 42.8 versus 41.5 / 43.2 without it.
why: LB-driven post-processing risks overfitting and shake-up, while uniform training formats are under your control.
when: Public LB tuned on a small test subset.
quote: Pre-process the training data as carefully as possible, and post-process the model output as little as possible.

what: Tried training with prefixes to distinguish Akkadian to English, German or Turkish in one model; abandoned along with decoder-only models, continual pre-training, context, TTA and spelling standardisation.
why: No reason given.
quote: Multilingual training, distinguishing akka->en/de/tr using prefixes.

what: Generate 64 images with SSD-1B at 384x384, quantise to 6 colours, extract contours with OpenCV into polygons, pack paths by size/centrality/simplicity until 6000 bytes.
why: Diffusion image plus vectorisation beats directly drawing SVG.
quote: We rank each extracted path by its size, centrality and simplicity and then continuously add them to the SVG until the 6000-byte size limit is reached.

what: Re-implemented the metric image processor efficiently and picked the SVG with highest aesthetic score among 64.
why: Selecting by proxy metric directly optimises the score.
quote: We then calculate the aesthetic score for each of the images and simply return the SVG that got the highest score.

what: Embed prompt text hidden under a low-opacity coloured-pixel repeating pattern so OCR on partially processed image sees nothing but VQA on fully processed image reads it.
why: OCR penalty avoided while VQA benefits from text.
when: Metric with differing preprocessing per component
quote: The fully processed image, which is used to calculate aesthetic and VQA scores, reveals the hidden text

what: Embed visible three-letter string "ZOK" found by search over three-letter combos to maximise aesthetic score without hurting VQA.
why: Avoids OCR hallucinations.
quote: Running a search across three-letter combinations of characters revealed that "ZOK" produced the highest average aesthetic scores without impacting VQA scores.

what: Add colored square patches and short texts (KUZ, 3Q3, SSQ, FRANCE XK ARTS) found by genetic algorithm or hill-climb to raise aesthetic score.
why: Exploits the aesthetic predictor.
quote: Each of these artifacts was found using either a genetic algorithm, a hill climb search, or occasionally a manual guess and check approach.

what: Tiny AutoEncoder VAE, DPM-Solver 12 steps, DeepCache, split across two T4s; stopword removal and path-compressed text.
why: Fit 64 images in ~30s.
quote: Enable DeepCache with cache_interval=2 and cache_branch_id=0

what: Pre-generate 128 images per training prompt, convert to SVG once, and test new aesthetic features by appending paths.
why: Fast iteration.
quote: Whenever we wanted to test a new aesthetic feature we could just append new paths, etc. to the SVGs we'd previously generated.

what: For old metric, differentiable optimisation of 237 small squares plus small text.
why: Gradient optimisation of the scorer.
quote: we used a differentiable approach to find a set of 237 small squares that produced the highest aesthetic score

what: Including CLIP/VQA scores in selection did not help; nor averaging over multiple processing applications.
why: No improvement.
quote: Incorporating CLIP scores, VQA scores, etc. into the equation we used to select the final SVG for submission.

gain: Synthetic data (10k) credited with improving raw performance and generalisation to unseen misconceptions; no isolated number
what: Clustered closely related misconceptions using co-occurrence statistics in retriever/ranker predictions on validation data, then asked Claude 3.5 Sonnet to write 5 new MCQs per cluster, giving the cluster's misconceptions plus 4-5 reference MCQs in the prompt.
why: A single-misconception prompt left the generator unaware of near-duplicate misconceptions and gave no style/difficulty reference, so wrong answers did not map precisely to one misconception.
when: Retrieval/ranking tasks over a fine-grained label pool where labelled data is small and labels are easily confused with neighbours.
quote: I first created clusters of closely related misconceptions leveraging co-occurrence statistics of misconceptions in retriever/ranker predictions on validation data.

what: Prompted GPT-4o with a scratchpad-then-score rubric (0-10) to rate how well each wrong answer follows from its stated misconception, and filtered low-scoring synthetic MCQs. Judge chosen by a vibe test against Claude.
why: Generated MCQs often violated diagnostic power and resolution; curation removes noisy examples.
when: Any LLM-synthesised training data where quality can be checked by reasoning.
quote: I used LLM-as-a-judge to filter out low quality synthetic MCQs. I prompted GPT-4o to rate the quality of the synthetic MCQs as below:

what: Kept the 4k+ new misconceptions the generator invented (extending the label pool to 4791), after removing ones that matched existing labels by string normalisation, by gte-base similarity above 0.995, or that were ambiguously close (0.95-0.995).
why: Extra labels improve generalisation to unseen misconceptions, but naive merging adds conflicts since many are rephrasings of existing ones.
when: Retrieval tasks with an open or long-tail label set where test labels may be unseen.
quote: Remove new misconceptions that have fairly high similarity (between 0.95 and 0.995) with any of the existing misconceptions

trick: Distilled CoT reasoner without labels in input
what: Had Claude write the likely student thought process given the problem, correct answer, wrong answer, true misconception and related misconceptions; then fine-tuned Qwen 7B/14B/32B reasoners on that text with the misconception information removed from the input, so at inference they produce a CoT from the question alone. The prompt forced an order (correct calc, incorrect calc, flaw) to stop the CoT naming the misconception.
why: LLMs are weak at counterfactual reasoning about wrong answers; distilling a stronger teacher's reasoning gives rankers extra signal at test time when the label is unknown.
when: Tasks where a teacher LLM can explain the label given the answer, but the answer is unavailable at test time.
quote: Notably, I omitted the true and related misconceptions from the input for fine-tuning.

what: Added generated CoTs to the reranker input for 50% of training examples and left them out for the other 50%; at inference CoTs are supplied.
why: Encourages the model to use external reasoning when available and fall back on internal reasoning otherwise.
when: Cross-encoder/LLM rerankers with optional side information.
quote: 50% of training data used CoTs and 50% did not.

what: Tried folds by QuestionId (too optimistic), GroupKFold on SubjectId (too pessimistic), and settled on GroupKFold on ConstructId; synthetic data was marked fold 99 and always added to training only.
why: Granularity of the group controls how well the validation mimics unseen test items; ConstructId gave a narrow validation/LB gap.
when: Test set contains unseen groups with hierarchical metadata.
quote: I finally settled on GroupKFold with ConstructId , which yielded a narrow Validation/LB gap and good correlation up to ~0.62 public LB score range.

what: Tracked map@25 and recall@32 and picked retrievers by recall@32, choosing a high-recall Qwen2.5-14B encoder over the best-map@25 encoder; final retrieval averaged similarity scores from several retrievers.
why: Rerankers can only fix what the retriever surfaces, so recall at the rerank cutoff matters more than final-metric quality.
quote: I chose the high-recall Qwen/Qwen2.5-14B encoder (Model 3) instead of the best map@25 encoder (Model 4).

what: Kept the top 32 retrieved candidates plus up to 32 more whose similarity exceeded (top score minus a constant).
why: Inferred: gives more candidates to the reranker when the retriever is uncertain and fewer when confident, keeping recall high within compute.
quote: The dynamic threshold is computed as the top candidate similarity score - constant .

what: Fine-tuned LLM-based retrievers with contrastive temperature 0.01 instead of the usual 0.02.
why: Not explained; reported as a key factor for recall.
when: Contrastive fine-tuning of LLM embedding models.
quote: Setting temperature to 0.01, instead of the typically used value of 0.02 in LLM-based encoders

trick: One positive per label per batch
what: Built contrastive batches so each misconception appears as a positive only once, avoiding queries sharing the same label in a batch.
why: With many-to-one query-label mapping, in-batch negatives that share the label are false negatives and add noise.
when: In-batch-negative contrastive training with duplicated targets.
quote: Ensuring only one demonstration per misconception appeared in each training batch, as multiple demonstrations would introduce label noise through in-batch negatives

trick: Pretrain retriever on uncurated synthetic data
what: Pretrained the 14B encoder on all available synthetic data before the quality-curation step, then fine-tuned on the curated mix.
why: Inferred: large noisy data gives broad coverage; curated data refines.
when: Large synthetic corpus of mixed quality.
quote: Pretraining the Qwen/Qwen2.5-14B encoder with all available synthetic data (before the curation step in section 4.1.1).

trick: Different LRs for LoRA A and B
what: Used LoRA+ style asymmetric learning rates (A 1e-5, B 5e-5) with r=64, alpha=128 on all linear layers.
why: From LoRA+ paper: same LR for A and B is suboptimal for wide models; separate rates give faster convergence and 1-2% better performance.
quote: Retrievers were fine-tuned using LoRA with: r=64, alpha=128, learning_rate_lora_a=1e-5, learning_rate_lora_b=5e-5

what: Randomly included 0 to 2 reference misconception examples in the reranker context during training, and 1-2 from the training set at inference.
why: Retains and leverages the LLM's in-context learning while still letting it rely on internal reasoning when no examples are shown.
when: LLM-based rerankers fine-tuned with small labelled data.
quote: I optionally included a few reference misconception examples (0 to 2) in the model input context

trick: Pseudo-label synthetic data with big teacher
what: Fine-tuned two 72B pointwise rankers on competition data only, used them to produce pseudo labels for the curated synthetic examples, then trained the 14B reranker on competition plus pseudo-labelled data.
why: Synthetic misconceptions are noisier than competition labels, so teacher scores give cleaner supervision.
when: Synthetic or unlabeled data plus a large teacher model.
quote: These models were then used to generate pseudo labels for the synthetic examples.

what: Reranker scores each (question, misconception) with the Yes-minus-No token logit at the last position, with each batch holding 1 positive and many negatives for one query and softmax cross entropy over the group; lm_head frozen. Moved from a classification head to Yes/No tokens to use vLLM prefix caching.
why: Group-wise CE trains ranking directly; Yes/No logits fit vLLM inference with prefix caching and scored similar to a classifier head.
quote: The label was set to the index of the positive misconception and cross entropy loss was used for training.

gain: +0.021 private LB (0.575 to 0.596, together with 2x synthetic data)
what: Raised negatives per positive from 16 to 24 for the reranker while also doubling the synthetic data.
why: Showing rankers many negatives improved performance.
quote: For each positive, I next increased the number of negatives to 24 from earlier 16.

what: 14B pointwise ranker narrows ~64 candidates to 8, 32B to 5, then a listwise 72B orders the top 5; final 25 list stitched from the stages (72B top 5, 32B ranks 6-8, 14B ranks 9-25).
why: Spends the most expensive compute on the few candidates that matter.
when: Reranking under tight inference time limits.
quote: Use a fine-tuned Qwen/Qwen2.5-32B ranker to process top 8 candidates and narrow them down to top 5.

what: Final 72B ranker sees all 5 candidates, 3 CoTs (from 7B, 14B, 32B reasoners) and up to 5 reference examples, one per candidate.
why: More information in context lets it compare candidates directly; position bias was a known risk (TTA with shuffling was not run for lack of time).
when: Final-stage ranking of a short candidate list.
quote: It sees 3 Chains of Thought (CoT) during inference - one each from the 7B, 14B, and 32B reasoners

what: Quantised fine-tuned rankers with AutoAWQ using a subset of the reranker training set as calibration data for each model.
why: Reduces quantisation degradation compared with generic calibration data.
when: Quantising fine-tuned LLMs for fixed-hardware inference.
quote: I used task specific calibration datasets for each model to mitigate performance degradation.

trick: Hard negatives did not help recall
what: Hard negatives and reranker-score distillation improved map@25 but not recall@32; iterative hard negative mining, cross-device negatives, subject-based batching and bidirectional LLM encoders also failed.
why: Not explained beyond the numbers; hard negatives did not help long-tail recall.
quote: Incorporating hard negatives into training batches and distilling re-ranker scores consistently improved map@25 performance, but did not positively impact recall@32 .

what: Ran experiments on the 7B model with about 50% of a training run to read signals, then copied best settings to 14B and 32B; used torch.compile, flash-attention, LoRA not QLoRA, and padding to multiples of 8.
why: Compute-limited iteration; early signal from partial runs is enough.
when: LLM fine-tuning competitions with GPU limits.
quote: (a) ~50% of training was giving good indications on the experiment, (b) I primarily experimented with the 7B models.

what: Train a classifier for P(efs=0) and a regressor for rank of efs_time separately, then combine with a parametric function res=(1-y_fun)*x_fun+y_fun with a,b,c tuned by Optuna, then rank-transform.
why: The C-index rewards giving high scores to likely-censored patients and ordering event patients by time; the regressor only needs to rank efs==1 cases.
quote: when a patient has a high probability of efs == 0 , we should give them a high score. Otherwise, we should give them a relatively lower score and pay more attention to the rank of efs_time .

what: Regression target is efs_time rank normalized to 0-1 separately within efs==1 and within efs==0 groups.
why: Inferred: censored times are not comparable with event times; rank within group gives a uniform ranking target.
quote: efs_time_norm[efs = = 1 ] = efs_time[efs = = 1 ].rank() / sum(efs = = 1 )

trick: Event flag as feature, set to 1
gain: Significant improvement on efs==1 c-index (no number)
what: Train regressor on all rows (efs 0 and 1) with efs as an input feature, sample weights 0.6:0.4, then set efs=1 at inference.
why: Censored rows carry similar patterns, improving efs==1 ranking; the flag prevents the model confusing the two populations.
when: Censored data where one subgroup matters for the metric
quote: by adding samples where efs==0 , the regressor's performance on efs==1 improved significantly!

gain: final CV stratified c-index ~0.6965 vs ~0.692-0.695 single pairs
what: Build all 9 classifier x 3 regressor pairs, fit merge-function constants per pair with 5-fold, then weighted-average the 27 merged predictions with Optuna.
why: Inferred: diversity from cross-type pairings, each pair with its own tuned merge.
quote: Create combinations between classifiers and regressors, then find the best (a, b, c) for the merge function by with 5-folds and then get the merged predictions.

what: Optuna search range for ensemble weights limited to 0.1-1 rather than 0-1.
why: Acts as regularization against overfitting with 27 combinations.
when: Large ensembles tuned on limited CV
quote: I set the Optuna search range for weights to be between 0.1 and 1, rather than 0 and 1. I think this is a form of regularization.

what: Tune (a,b,c) with Optuna on the training part of each of 5 folds, apply to held-out OOF and LB, then compute OOF C-index over 5 loops.
why: Inferred: avoids leakage from fitting merge constants on the data being scored.
quote: use optuna to find the best (a,b,c) to maximize C-index of train_set, then get oof result and LB result with best (a,b,c), do this by 5 loops, then calucate the oof C-index

what: Use identical 10-fold stratified splits with the same seed for every classifier and regressor, and no early stopping.
why: CV was unstable across splits; shared splits make models comparable; no early stopping reduces overfitting risk with many folds.
quote: The CV is very unstable with different splits Strategy. To make the results comparable, I used 10-fold splits with same seeds for all classifier and regressor model training.

what: StratifiedKFold on the concatenation of efs and race_group.
why: Inferred: keeps event rate and group balance in each fold, matching the race-stratified metric.
quote: y_combine = data[ 'efs' ].astype( 'str' )+ '|' +data[ 'X' ][ 'race_group' ].astype( 'str' )

what: Best max depth for LightGBM and XGBoost was 2 (CatBoost 6).
why: Author: little valuable feature interaction; task easy to fit, which may be why NN-like models also work.
when: Small tabular data with weak interactions
quote: The best max depth for LGB and XGB is 2 (for CatBoost, it's 6, and I still don't know why).

what: One-hot encode all categoricals while keeping the originals, and copy continuous features as categorical features.
why: Inferred: lets models treat discretised numeric values as categories.
quote: Copy continuous features as categorical features

trick: KNN graph GNN on tabular rows
what: Build a graph linking each row to its 25 nearest Euclidean neighbours and fit GraphSAGE to the targets.
why: Inferred: a diverse model type exploiting neighbour similarity; AUC 0.7591.
when: Small tabular data, for ensemble diversity
quote: I use KNN to find nearest 25 nodes and create edges(use Euclidean Distance),then use graphsage to fit the targets.

trick: Align fold shifts for rank-loss models
what: When training NN/GNN with pairwise rank loss, fix the per-fold prediction shift so mean/median prediction is the same across fold models.
why: Rank loss is shift-insensitive, so predictions drift per fold and hurt CV on the pooled OOF set.
when: Rank-loss models with pooled OOF metric
quote: the predition would shift over different fold because rank loss is not sensitive to shift, which may cause lower CV when calculate metric in the entire set.

what: Adding noise to some race groups raised CV significantly but did not help public or private LB.
why: CV gain did not transfer.
quote: Adding noise to some race groups significantly improved cross-validation performance, but it didn't work on either the public or private LB.

what: 5th place commenter: adding the rest of the train data with sample weight 0 helped LGB and CatBoost when predicting a subset.
why: Unclear per commenter.
quote: adding rest of train data with sample weight 0 was a big help to my model.

what: Replaced Cfish hand-crafted eval with a simple NNUE (768 inputs, dual perspective, king mirroring, single hidden layer of 64) trained with bullet.
why: With good data even a simple net beats HCE by +100 Elo.
quote: With good data, a simple network can be much stronger (+100 elo) than HCE even without implementing the easily-updatable (UE) part of nnue.

trick: Distill from small Lc0 nets data
what: Used training data from smaller Lc0 ResNets T77 and T79 RL runs.
why: Data from larger networks performed worse.
quote: the smaller ResNet T77 and T79 networks led to the best nnue data, while data generated from larger networks performed worse

what: Stage 1: 10B Stockfish positions on score; Stage 2: resume on 12B Lc0 positions with score plus WDL mix; AdamW linear decay each.
why: Training on weaker data first beats strongest data from scratch.
quote: First, training on weaker data from scratch, then training with the strongest data later leads to stronger networks than directly training on the strongest data from scratch.

trick: Rerun training and keep best seed
what: Re-ran training from scratch several times and chose the strongest network.
why: Variance between runs with identical parameters.
quote: re-running the training from scratch multiple times would lead to stronger networks

what: Stochastic skipping in the dataloader to flatten the piece-count histogram; ported to the Primer filter.
why: Uneven opening-heavy distribution; previously improved Stockfish nets.
quote: targeting a uniform distribution of pieces in training batches using stochastic skipping

trick: Filter data by WDL and sacrifices
what: Skipped positions where outcome disagreed with score, first 28 plies, and kept positions where best move is a sacrifice (skip SEE>=0).
why: Inferred: focuses on informative, tactical positions.
quote: Keeping positions where a piece sacrifice is the best move (skip SEE >= 0)

what: Plotted feature transformer weights as images; zeroed unused pawn weights and mirrored king, transposed weights for compressibility.
why: Correlated sequential bytes compress better; zeros compress well.
quote: transposing these weights reduces binary size by improving compressibility

what: Where a piece group has <=256 unique 16-bit weights, stored 8-bit indices with a lookup table; merged near-duplicates of low-frequency values.
why: Lossless 8-bit storage without quantization Elo loss.
when: Model compression to a size cap
quote: This way, 16-bit feature transformers can be compressed to 8-bit without elo regression.

what: Chose QA=101 and QB=160 instead of default 255/64, largest QA fitting the size cap.
why: Less quantization retains strength.
quote: I ended up at QA = 101 and QB = 160 as that was the largest QA I could fit in the size constraints.

what: Compressed engine with 7z (available in container), decompressed in main.py, and used zopfli for the outer tar.gz.
why: Best compression ratio under 64KB.
quote: I compressed the engine binary with 7z, and decompressed it at runtime in main.py while using zopfli for the outer .tar.gz compression.

what: Ran own fishtest server adapted for Cfish for SPRT, plus fastchess fixed-node checks; used head-to-head win rates against rivals since LB noisy.
why: Elo measurement is crucial; LB scores noisy.
quote: Elo measurements are crucial to measuring progress on engine strength.

trick: Max hash size near RAM limit
what: Measured that error losses grow gradually with RAM and picked an 896kb hash to maximise Elo; environment later changed raising error losses.
why: More hash raises Elo; 3-4% error rate judged acceptable.
quote: took a risky approach of using an 896kb hash size to maximize elo from RAM usage

what: Optimised for sudden death with SPSA at 20s instead of 10s, and scaled optimumTime by 1/3 and 2/5 over default 1/4.
why: Accounts for random delay and pondering time.
quote: I scaled up Time.optimumTime by +1/3x and +2/5x in timeman.c

what: Double grid each iteration and stop by slicing: p=lambda g:F(g[70:]or p(g*2)).
why: Eliminates extra arguments.
quote: there's a "slice recursion" technique

what: str(g), re.sub, eval back; fixed width makes offsets constant.
why: Short edits.
quote: Our final submission used regex in a total of 46 solutions.

what: Reuse p for 2D/1D/0D inputs with a g*0!=0 check.
why: Shared code for row and column ops.
quote: re-use the function p for different shapes of input

what: Enumerate candidate parameters until verification passes; use CRT moduli to enumerate regions.
why: Verification easier than search.
quote: it is more efficient to simply keep guessing the object until the correct one is found

what: Compress solutions over about 200 bytes with zlib+exec using zopfli/libdeflate and a DP re-encoder.
why: Repetition becomes almost free.
quote: Compression would make code repetition almost free

what: Search for shortest expressions for lookup tables and iterated formulas.
why: Brute-force search.
quote: We used the utility pysearch extensively to find the shortest expressions

what: Hardcode one-bit answers using hash of grid and a bytestring, brute-forcing extra bytes.
why: Cheaper than logic.
quote: Both of these tasks need only 1 bit to resolve

what: Exploit judge weaknesses, e.g. least-frequent color on a sliced grid.
why: Tests are limited.
quote: exploit weaknesses in the judge

what: Walrus state variables and list.pop() for lookahead or reverse.
why: Short code.
quote: list.pop() can also implicitly reverse a list

what: Top 3 agreed not to use shell (perl).
why: Legality was clarified late.
quote: we did not use this technique as per mutual agreement among the teams in the top 3

what: 5-fold GroupKFold; labels summed per eeg_id; middle 10,000 frames; CV only on one sample per eeg_id with at least 10 votes.
why: High-vote labels are reliable and match test distribution.
quote: One data from each eeg_id with more than 10 votes was used for CV calculations.

what: Two-stage training: stage 1 on lower-vote data, stage 2 on high-vote data only (10 votes or more), excluding unreliable 1-vote labels.
why: 1-vote labels are unreliable.
when: Noisy crowd labels with vote counts.
quote: Stage2: 15 epochs (10 votes or more)

what: Stack 18 bipolar montage signals cropped at 2000, 5000 and 10000 samples, resized and concatenated into one image for a 2D CNN.
why: Simple but strong: CV about 0.24.
when: Raw time series where CNNs on images work.
quote: 18 signals of bipolar montage were cropped at three different intervals (2000, 5000 and 10000 samples), resized and concatenated into a single image.

what: Used entmax with alpha about 1.03 for outputs of all single models.
why: Labels contain zero-probability classes; slightly crisper outputs.
when: KL-divergence on soft labels with sparse targets.
quote: we decided to use entmax with a small alpha parameter (~1.03) for all our single models, which improved both public and private LB score around 0.004.

what: Per target class, fit non-negative linear regression on models' predictions of that class.
why: CV-LB correlation held even when more overfit to training data.
quote: I used non-negative linear regression for ensemble.

what: 1D temporal convolution with kernel size equal to sampling rate (200) producing feature maps stacked into images for timm models.
why: Learn rhythmic temporal filters per symptom (EEGNet/G2Net idea).
quote: The kernel size was set to the same value as the sampling rate (200).

what: Used superlet time-frequency transform (0.5-20 Hz) instead of STFT, resized to 256x256.
why: STFT lost resolution in time or frequency.
quote: Then, I use superlets as a better representation method.

what: Add offset 0.02 to each vote count before normalising into target distribution.
why: Stronger regularisation for low-vote labels.
quote: Add offset of 0.02 to each vote before normalization.

what: Ensemble many small timm backbones (swinv2, caformer, convnextv2_atto, etc.).
why: KL divergence punishes extreme errors; diversity helps.
quote: Diverse ensemble was effective because the KL divergence is sensitive to errors for extreme predictions.

what: CWT (width 7, 40 scales, stride 16) on each of 18 channels, stacked vertically and resized to 512x512 for MaxViT.
why: STFT, Kaggle spec and CQT did not work; 0.5-40 Hz beat 0.5-20 Hz.
quote: Configured for 0.5-40Hz, which outperformed the 0.5-20Hz setting.

what: Cropped middle 10,000 frames (50 s) of EEG.
why: Performed better than 25 s or 10 s.
quote: Crop 50 seconds (10,000 frames) performed better than 25 seconds or 10 seconds.

what: Used Paul wavelet instead of Morlet in the CWT and varied input length and m parameter across models.
why: Increase variation in input data for ensembling.
quote: To increase the variation in input data, I used Paul as the mother wavelet instead of Morlet.

what: Each epoch randomly pick one eeg_sub_id per eeg_id and use its offset window and labels.
why: Inferred: acts as augmentation across sub-samples.
quote: During training, one eeg_sub_id was randomly selected from eeg_id for each epoch.

what: Tried DOG wavelet instead of Paul.
why: Not explained.
quote: Using DOG (Derivative of Gaussian) instead of Paul.

what: Reverse the data to find date_decision minus min_refreshdate_3813885D correlates ~0.9+ with WEEK_NUM, allowing week estimation on test.
why: Test lacks a usable week column; this feature enables the metric hack.
when: Stability metrics that penalise score decay over time.
quote: I tried Data Reversing and found that the difference between date_decision and min_refreshdate_3813885D had a high correlation (about 0.9 or more) with WEEK_NUM.

what: Subtract REDUCE from scores for the earlier DEVIDE fraction of weeks (clip at 0) to exploit the stability metric penalising downward score trend.
why: The metric rewards a rising trend of Gini across weeks; shifting early weeks lowers the slope penalty.
when: Metrics with a time-trend stability penalty.
quote: The optimal public LB value of REDUCE is 0.03 (at least in my model), and the optimal value in private is probably distributed around 0.02 to 0.04.

what: Chose DEVIDE=1/2 and REDUCE=0.03, the median of the expected private-optimal range, since public/private split spans all weeks.
why: Hedges when the optimum is uncertain and others bet low or high.
when: Tuning a parameter whose private optimum cannot be seen.
quote: Here, I trusted my model and chose neutral, and chose DEVIDE=1/2, REDUCE=0.03, which is the median of the expected distribution.

what: Selected the best-CV no-hack model and the same model with the hack applied as the two final submissions.
why: Hedge against the hack not working.
when: Two final submission slots with uncertain exploit.
quote: The first selected submission is the No Hack model with CV Best Score created in Phase 1, and the second selected submission is the application of Metric Hack to it.

what: StratifiedGroupKFold (shuffled and not); CV differences of 0.001-0.005 were treated as noise, only above 0.01 reliable; FE gains transferred to LB better than parameter tuning gains.
why: Observed correlation with LB.
when: Time-shifted tabular data with a stability metric.
quote: differences in CV of around 0.001 to 0.005 had a low correlation with LB, while differences above 0.01 had a high correlation with LB.

what: Spend effort on feature engineering rather than hyperparameter tuning, since FE-driven CV gains tracked LB.
why: Parameter-tuning CV gains correlated poorly with LB.
when: Tabular competitions with a shifting test set.
quote: CV improvement through model parameter adjustment had a relatively low correlation with LB, and CV improvement through FE had a relatively high correlation with LB.

what: Aggregate each table column per case with Max, Min, Avg, Var, First, Last and max-min difference.
why: Standard for multi-table credit data.
when: Relational tabular data with one-to-many tables.
quote: Max, Min, Avg, Var, First, Last and Max-Min Difference of each item were utilized.

what: Excluded many categorical features (and much of bureau A and person data) from LGBM because they degraded stability and overfit.
why: Test-time behaviour of these sources differed; removal helped.
when: Stability metrics with shifted test data.
quote: some items (mainly categorical types) were excluded because they caused performance degradation and overfitting in LGBM

what: Used LightAutoML Denselight MLP as a model; no transformer model beat it.
why: Simple model resists overfitting on this data.
when: Tabular ensembles needing a neural component.
quote: Surprisingly, I haven't created or found a model that beats Denselight performance.

what: CatBoost was the best single model, using about 117 categorical features natively; LGBM weaker but useful in the blend.
why: Author guesses CatBoost handles many categoricals well.
quote: Catboost was the model that performed best in this competition and I guess it performed well on a large number of categorical features (about 117).

what: Blend weights from linear regression and weighted testing on OOF predictions; OOF-optimal weights matched LB-optimal.
why: Trust OOF-derived weights.
quote: My approach is linear regression and weighted testing in OOF.

what: TabNet, TabTransformer, FT-Transformer, income/expense period statistics and K-means features did not work.
why: No explanation given.
quote: Transformer type models such as Tabnet, TabTransformer, FT-Transformer, etc.

what: For the transparent category where SfM fails, skip reconstruction: order the images and place cameras evenly on a circle around the object looking inward (e.g. 10 degrees apart for 36 images).
why: Transparent objects have little texture; given the low metric thresholds the cameras must be near the object and shot from all sides.
when: Pose estimation on turntable-like captures where feature matching fails.
quote: So, we simply throw the cameras on a circle around the object, that looks towards the object as in this image.

what: Order images by building a pairwise distance matrix (optical flow std, pixel diff, 1-SSIM, 1/num_matches) and solving a Travelling Salesman Problem; final ensemble was SSIM plus matching-based flow.
why: The weight reflects how close two views are, so the shortest tour recovers rotation order.
when: Recovering capture order of unordered views of one object.
quote: We built a distance matrix based on these pair weights and solved the final ordering problem through TSP.

what: Skip image retrieval; keep pairs by raw match counts from ALIKED+LightGlue (30 per detector, 100 across the ensemble).
why: Retrieval CNN quality scores did not reflect on LB.
when: Pair selection for SfM in small scenes.
quote: we decided not to use any image retrieval method. Instead, we rely only on the number of matches generated by ALIKED and LightGlue (LG).

what: Rotate one image of each pair by 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees and keep the rotation giving the most matches.
why: Some scenes contain images not in natural orientation.
quote: Rotate one of each image pair by 0 degrees, 90 degrees, 180 degrees, or 270 degrees, and adopt the rotation that results in the most matches.

what: Cluster frequently matched keypoints of each image with DBSCAN to crop representative regions per image rather than per pair, then match crops too.
why: Per-pair cropping risks discarding areas not matched in that pair.
when: Local feature matching with low overlap.
quote: Instead of the method proposed at IMC2022, where crop areas are calculated for each image pair, we have adopted a new cropping technique that calculates crop areas for each image individually.

what: Ensemble matches extracted from original and cropped images at 1280 and 2048 resolutions, with unlimited ALIKED keypoints.
why: Higher resolution gives more accurate matches.
quote: In LB experiments, the best results were obtained with a combination of 1280 and 2048 for both original and cropped images.

what: When COLMAP returns multiple models, align them to the best using Horn alignment and project others in to register more images.
why: Maximises registered images.
quote: we used Horn alignment to estimate the transformation matrix between them, and then we projected other reconstructions to the best one to register as many images as possible.

what: For scenes with few registered images, relax the match-count threshold and rerun, keeping the reconstruction with more registered images.
why: Low registration scenes were being under-matched.
quote: We relax the number of image matches threshold to address scenes with a low number of registered images.

what: Cache ALIKED keypoints and descriptors per image, use mixed precision and both T4 GPUs to run SfM in parallel.
why: Cut runtime within limits (best sub took 4h42m).
quote: Cache keypoints & descriptors , generated by ALIKED for each image.

what: Built a self-made dataset of plastic and glass bottles for validating the transparent module; local CV used selected train/test scenes.
why: Public data had too few transparent scenes to tune on.
when: Rare categories in the test set.
quote: we even generated our own transparent scene dataset with some plastic & glass bottles

what: Run COLMAP with a single thread so validation results are reproducible.
why: Inferred: multithreading adds nondeterminism that confounds CV.
quote: It is important to limit COLMAP by 1 thread.

what: SP/SG, LoFTR, DKM, RoMa, OmniGlue, XFeat, DISK and SIFT, plus NetVLAD/DINO retrieval scored by frustum IOU, did not beat ALIKED+LightGlue on LB.
why: Authors cite low repeatability and noisy matches for dense methods.
quote: Eventually, ALIKED and LightGlue were the best LB choice for us.

what: Evaluated retrieval models using ground truth poses by the average IOU of volumetric frustums of each camera with its candidates; this did not correlate with LB.
why: Offline proxy for pair quality.
quote: we evaluated the the score for these methods using ground truth and intrinsics by calculating the average IOU of volumetric frustums of each camera with its candidates

what: Image de-blurring, DFSFM refinement, NMS, disambiguation (Doppelgangers) and 3D RANSAC cleaning gave no LB gain or timed out.
why: Little improvement or runtime limits.
quote: we experimented with the single image restoration de-blur method but did not get noticeable improvement on LB

trick: MASt3R as dense matcher in COLMAP
what: Use MASt3R semi-dense matches (fast_reciprocal_NNs) as the matcher feeding a standard COLMAP reconstruction, instead of detector+LightGlue.
why: Higher precision (fewer mismatches) so it matches messy scenes where detector-based methods fail; trained on object-centric data too.
when: Structure-from-motion with hard or messy image sets
quote: By simply using the MASt3R model as a semi-dense detector-free matcher and integrating it into a general COLMAP pipeline, I achieved a score of 42-45 on the PublicLB.

what: Candidate pairs formed as union of neighbours from MASt3R-ASMK, MASt3R-SPoC, DINOv2 and ISC retrieval.
why: More pairs raised score; union of diverse retrievers gives coverage faster than a heavier single one.
quote: I generated candidate pairs for matching within a scene by taking the union of neighbors from multiple image retrieval results.

what: Also run ALIKED and SuperPoint keypoints through the MASt3R matcher in addition to dense matches.
why: Adds sparse precise points; small gain.
quote: These additional keypoints might regionally overlap with points subsampled by MASt3R, but this approach improved the score compared to using only MASt3R matches.

trick: Maximise image pairs within time limit
what: Observed more matched pairs raised score from ~45 to ~50 so focused on speed to fit more pairs.
why: More pairs improve reconstruction.
quote: Furthermore, I found that increasing the number of image pairs led to a higher score, reaching approximately 50.

what: Compile CUDA curope, swap attention for scaled_dot_product_attention (flash), fix use_amp, run on T4x2 in parallel over scene subsets.
why: Fit heavy matcher in Kaggle time limit.
when: Running heavy foundation models in notebook-limited competitions
quote: Replace attention implementations used in mast3r/dust3r/croco with torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention .

what: Farthest-point-sampled seeds, 1-vs-all MASt3R matching to assign cluster labels, small clusters as outliers; dropped in final.
why: No significant difference vs multiple COLMAP reconstructions.
quote: It turned out that, since image matching primarily uses MASt3R, there wasn't a significant difference whether I used pre-clustering or multiple reconstructions from COLMAP.

what: VGGT tracking head with pre-extracted keypoints worked locally but hit TimeoutError on submission.
why: Runtime limit.
quote: it resulted in a TimeoutError in submission.

trick: Train image NN on external data first
what: Pull external ISIC data and train the NN on it first; its predictions for competition data are saved and used downstream.
why: Inferred: more lesion images; predictions become stacking features.
when: Medical image classification with public related datasets
quote: Train model on external data via runing few last cells in NN-competition-train.ipynb (also saves model predictions for competition data)

what: Train a Stable Diffusion model with kohya-ss sd-scripts and generate synthetic lesion images, then train the classifier on them.
why: Inferred: augment the rare malignant class.
quote: To train SD model for synthtic data generation simply run sd_train.ipynb

what: Train two image NNs (EVA and EDGENEXT) and then top-level GBDT models on their outputs plus tabular data.
why: Inferred: GBDT combines image-model scores with metadata.
quote: first time with MODEL_NAME = "EVA" and second with MODEL_NAME = "EDGENEXT"

what: Used the positive and negative example comments provided in test.csv (for the unseen rules) as additional LLM finetuning data.
why: Inferred: the test rules are new, so the labelled examples are the only in-distribution signal for them.
when: Test set contains new classes/rules with a few labelled examples shipped in the test file.
quote: The idea is to use positive and negative examples in the test.csv as training data.

gain: described as significant improvement, no number
what: Dropped the subreddit column before deduplicating training rows, so identical texts across subreddits collapse.
why: Including it creates unnecessary duplicates across different subreddits.
when: Text datasets with metadata columns that make near-duplicate rows look distinct.
quote: I excluded the subreddit column before deduplication, since including it can create unnecessary duplicates across different subreddits.

what: Upsampled the test.csv examples once (2x weight) and finetuned for one epoch, i.e. one epoch on train and two on test examples.
why: Gives more weight to the examples that match the test rules.
when: Small in-distribution set mixed with larger out-of-distribution train set.
quote: I upsampled examples from test.csv once to increase their weight, and then finetuned for one epoch.

what: Masked the chat-template tokens before and after the Yes/No answer so only the answer token contributes to the loss.
why: Extra tokens (e.g. newlines in Qwen3 templates) waste training; masking also standardises convergence across models so one hyperparameter set works for all.
when: Finetuning chat LLMs as classifiers via a single answer token.
quote: I manually excluded these tokens from the loss computation

what: Switched from vanilla transformers/pytorch to Unsloth to finetune 14B models on limited GPU memory.
why: Much better memory efficiency, enabling larger and better models.
when: Kaggle notebooks with 16GB GPUs and LLM finetuning.
quote: it can easily fit a 14B model within 16GB of GPU memory

what: Collected candidate first tokens for yes (Yes, YES, Y, yes, True, plus space-prefixed forms) and no, found from the top-K predicted tokens, and scored as sigmoid of log-odds between the two sets.
why: After finetuning, probability mass can still be scattered over other tokens in a full-vocab output layer.
quote: So I constructed a candidate set of first tokens for many variants:

what: Sorted test data by length and used a single forward() pass to read last-token logits instead of generate().
why: Avoids generation overhead and padding waste, allowing six LLMs within the 12h limit.
when: LLM inference with time-limited code competitions.
quote: Sort test data by length

what: For each model, computed rankings within each rule, normalised to [0,1], then ensembled the normalised values.
why: Metric is computed per rule-grouped data so ranks should be comparable within rule; (a commenter notes ranking without grouping by rule is a mistake).
when: Metrics/data with distinct groups (e.g. rules) where score scales differ per group.
quote: computed per-rule rankings, normalized the scores to the range [0, 1]

what: Skipped local validation and finetuned models online, validating on the public LB.
why: Only two rules in train; the public LB is a random ~30% split and so an unbiased, low-variance estimator of private.
when: Train/test distribution shift (new rules) where realistic local validation is hard, and the LB split is random and large.
quote: Therefore, all models were finetuned online and validated using the public LB.

gain: +0.005 public LB over best single model
what: Weighted average of six models: Qwen3-14b, Qwen2.5-14b, Qwen3-8b, Qwen3-4b-instruct, llama3.1-8b and a small encoder (Ettin-400M).
why: Ensemble improved over the best single model (0.9344 vs 0.9297 public); even the weaker encoder was used to enrich the ensemble.
when: LLM classification with several comparable backbones.
quote: The final ensemble is a weighted average of these six models.

gain: Valid patch count 'increased a LOT' (no number)
what: Had the LLM emit SEARCH/REPLACE edit blocks (file path, search chunk, replace chunk) and converted them to a git diff afterwards, instead of asking for a unified diff directly.
why: Models mess up line counting and other details when writing diffs directly, so many patches are invalid; the edit format sharply increases valid patches.
when: LLM code-repair / patch generation, especially with smaller local models.
quote: After using a SEARCH/REPLACE scheme (similar to what VsCode does), I noticed the the amount of valid patches increased a LOT.

trick: LLM-generated issue-reproduction tests as patch filter
what: Generate 5 candidate fail-to-pass (F2P) reproduction scripts per issue, run them, and keep only those that reproduce the issue. Later use them to accept or reject candidate patches.
why: Gives a verifier for candidate patches without ground truth, which raises precision under a penalty for wrong answers.
when: Code-repair tasks with a penalty for wrong answers, where abstention is allowed.
quote: Then, I would run all the tests and keep only those that actually reproduced the issue and nothing else.

what: Tests were required to print the 'reproduced' verdict and nothing else; a test printing both the reproduced and the other-issues markers was discarded.
why: Inferred: ambiguous output signals a broken or unreliable test.
when: LLM-generated test scripts used as verifiers.
quote: I would remove the tests as it looks suspicious.

what: If none of 5 tests reproduced the issue, generate 5 more at higher temperature; if still none, skip the sample entirely (no submission for it).
why: Without a reproducing test there is no way to validate patches, and wrong answers are penalised, so abstaining is better.
when: Scoring with negative marks for wrong answers and allowed skips.
quote: If none of the 10 tests reproduced the issue, I simply skip the sample as there is no way to assess my candidate repair patches.

what: Two-stage retrieval: the model picks relevant existing test files, is shown skeletons of their functions and classes, and chooses which to inspect; imports from those files are also supplied in the test-generation prompt.
why: A 32B model has the right idea for the test but fails on imports and class usage; context fixes these silly mistakes, unlike big models that memorise APIs.
when: Using small local LLMs for repo-level code generation.
quote: first ask the model to find relevant unit tests files that were important to the problem and, then, providing the model with the skeleton of all functions and classes in those files

what: Of the 5 test generations, one gets full context (imports plus relevant classes/functions), one only imports, and three no context; one is greedy and the rest sampled.
why: The optimal amount of context varies a lot per sample, so mixing context levels makes it likely at least one good test exists.
when: LLM generation pipelines with uncertain prompt-context sensitivity.
quote: I noticed that the optimal amount of context would vary a lot from sample to sample, so this layered approach helped quite a bit in making sure I had good F2P tests.

what: Besides F2P tests, run the existing unit tests the model selected during localization and compare against the unpatched baseline results; accept a patch only if results are similar or better.
why: Rejects patches that break existing behaviour; the author credits it with precision.
when: Patch acceptance under a penalty for wrong answers.
quote: and compare that with the reference (unit tests result when no repair patch is applied).

what: Submit a patch only if it passes both F2P and P2P checks, accepting very few samples (9 correct, 2 wrong, 109 skipped on private).
why: Precision matters because wrong answers are penalised heavily.
when: Metrics that penalise wrong predictions more than skipped ones.
quote: I was quite strict on accepting the patch for submission, so this helped with precision

what: For each of 2 sampled edit locations generate 4 repairs (first greedy, others temperature sampled), giving 8 candidates to filter by tests.
why: Diversity plus a greedy anchor gives a higher chance one candidate is right; the verifier picks.
quote: For each edit location, I generated 4 repair samples (first with greedy decoding, the others with temperature).

trick: Greedy or low temp at every step
what: Used greedy or very low temperature sampling at essentially every pipeline stage, with higher-temperature samples added only for diversity.
why: Author credits it for making scores consistent across seeds (0.056 to 0.098 LB).
when: Multi-stage LLM pipelines where robustness across reruns matters.
quote: Always making sure to have greedy sampling (or very low temp) at pretty much every step in the pipeline (along with other higher temps generations for diversity)

what: Validate each candidate patch with a git apply dry run before running any tests.
why: Inferred: cheaply discards malformed patches before spending test time.
quote: I started by validating them with a dry-run of git apply to make sure they were valid.

gain: Best runs took 5-7 hours (3 to 10 min per sample)
what: Ran F2P and P2P tests in parallel with timeouts, and installed packages concurrently with test execution, via subprocess with a waiting thread.
why: Cuts runtime so more samples and candidates fit into the limit.
when: Code-execution inference under notebook runtime limits.
quote: All tests (F2P and P2P) had timeout and ran in parallel to save time.

what: Refactored Agentless to build the repo structure dictionary once at the start instead of at every step.
why: The original regenerated it each step, costing 5-20 s each time.
quote: I refactored the code to only generate the repo structure

what: Two time protections: skip everything remaining if global runtime exceeds 20 hours, and skip a sample if it takes over 12 minutes.
why: Prevents a hidden-test rerun from timing out the whole notebook.
when: Code competitions with hard notebook runtime limits on unseen test data.
quote: one to skip everything remaining if the global runtime was above 20 hours and another to skip the sample if we were more than 12 minutes on that sample.

what: Tried reasoning LLMs instead of Qwen2.5 Coder 32B.
why: They were slow, produced long thinking, and did not beat the coder model.
quote: All the reasoning LLMs I tried were super slow and wouldn't improve much on the Qwen Coder 32B generations.

what: Tried generating a test, running it and feeding the error back to the model to fix it.
why: Not working in the time available; the author thinks it could work with more time.
when: LLM test generation with execution feedback.
quote: Agent mode, i.e., generating a test, running and then providing the error back to the model to fix (I only tried this very late so I still think it could work with more time)

what: Trained with MAE even though the metric is R-squared.
why: Author: converges faster, better at convergence and more stable than MSE.
quote: It performs better than MSE in every way- it converges faster, is better at convergent, and is more stable.

what: Added outputs predicting the loss of each target, trained with MAE.
why: Surprisingly effective as an auxiliary task; also gives sample confidence.
quote: The idea is simple- I also predict the loss of each target. I also used MAE for the confidence loss.
