quote: around 40k samples was still unstable, and around 80k samples the model started to use candidate counts / candidate rows much more reliably.

what: For unseen query operators, infer the prompt's mode and used rule groups from the other operators, then pick among remaining rules by operator priors and train frequency.
why: Narrows to few rules with no direct example.
quote: we inferred the prompt-level mode and already-used rule groups from the other operators.

what: Submitted checkpoints periodically as a noisy external signal (averaging repeated submissions) with local validation as a check; final two submissions were the extra-trained adapters.
why: Limited GPU for local eval; temp=0 vLLM still non-deterministic and Private fluctuated across nearby checkpoints.
when: Noisy-eval competitions with scarce local compute.
quote: generation with temperature=0.0 was still not fully deterministic, so scores varied across repeated submissions.

what: Measured per-category how often the trace solvers produce correct answers within the 7680-token budget versus the SFT model, noting leakage since the solver was designed on full train.
why: Shows the model reaches near solver ceiling; remaining gap is solver coverage.
quote: This is not an unbiased evaluation.

what: Embed small-molecule SMILES with ChemBERTa to enrich the (cell_type, sm_name) keyword input.
why: Gives chemical structure information for tiny categorical inputs.
when: Few categorical inputs with large outputs where entities have structure
quote: I immediately decided to use ChemBERTa embeddings of SMILES encodings and observed a significant improvement

trick: Target statistics per entity as features
what: Added mean, std and 25/50/75 percentiles of training targets per cell type and per small molecule as input features.
why: Encodes how each entity typically behaves.
quote: the mean, standard deviation, and (25%, 50%, 75%) percentiles of differential expressions per cell type and small molecule in the training data.

what: Tried BioWordVec embeddings and Wikipedia definitions of cell types and molecules; noisy text embeddings did not help and fine-tuning fell short.
why: Author: natural language descriptions came with noise.
quote: While this is interesting from the biological point of view, it did not improve the leaderboard score.

what: Reshaped flat feature vectors into 2D sequences and used LSTM, GRU and 1D-CNN, which beat GBMs, MLP and 2D CNN.
why: Author reports they performed better on validation.
quote: I finally selected LSTM, GRU, and 1-d CNN architectures as they performed better on the validation sets.

what: Optimized weighted MSE, MAE, LogCosh and BCE (on sigmoid of predictions and targets) simultaneously.
why: BCE on sigmoids gives larger loss near zero where most targets lie, while MSE says no mistake.
when: Regression with targets concentrated near zero
quote: I simultaneously optimized 4 loss functions via weighted averaging: MSE, MAE, LogCosh, and BCE.

what: Apply BCE to sigmoid(output) vs sigmoid(target) for regression.
why: Sends stronger gradient signal when values close to zero.
quote: the BCE loss applied on the sigmoid of predictions and targets returns a higher loss (i.e., sends a better signal to the optimizer) when the values involved are close to zero

what: Create extra training samples by zeroing 30% of random input features and keeping the true target.
why: Noise robustness; partial molecule information should still predict response.
when: Small data with dense embedding inputs
quote: I randomly replace 30% of the input features’ entries with zeros, and add the resulting input feature together with the correct target as a new training datapoint.

trick: Fold difficulty analysis by cell type
what: Analyzed per-fold cell-type composition to explain very different fold scores, finding CD8+ T and myeloid cells hardest.
why: Fold scores varied (1.15-1.19 vs 0.86-0.90) due to cell-type mix.
quote: The differences in the validation MRRMSE in the above figure motivated me to take a closer look into the validation sets, where I found different distributions of cell types.

what: Blend LSTM, 1D-CNN and GRU predictions, e.g. 0.25 LSTM + 0.65 CNN.
why: Different architectures complement each other.
quote: With 0.25xLSTM + 0.65xCNN the Private LB is 0.725

what: ChemBERTa run with random LM head (600-d) and no padding gave the best private score.
why: Author found removing padding improved results.
when: Using pretrained encoders as feature extractors
quote: Run ChemBERTa Model with random LM head (600-d) and no padding to obtain 0.719 on Private LB

what: Trained on first 400 days and validated on the last 81 days.
why: CV aligned with leaderboard so no shake-up expected.
quote: train on first 400 days and choose last 81 days as my holdout validation set

what: Split seconds_in_bucket into 3 groups and compute per date/group/stock first-value and rolling-mean ratios of base features.
why: Inferred: captures within-auction-phase dynamics.
quote: agg features based on seconds_in_bucket_group

what: Per date and seconds_in_bucket, ratio of cross-sectional mean and normalised rank of each base feature.
why: Inferred: captures a stock's position relative to the market at that moment.
quote: rank features grouped by seconds_in_bucket

what: Kept top 300 features by CatBoost importance to fit memory and allow more online-training rounds.
why: Memory limits and runtime.
when: Large feature sets under memory/time limits.
quote: I just choose top 300 features by CatBoost model's feature importance.

what: Unidirectional GRU over 55 time steps per stock-day predicting targets at each step, state zero-initialised each day.
why: Not bidirectional to avoid label leak; learns sequence info.
quote: Yes, it's seq2seq model but not bidirection for avoiding label leak.

what: Transformer encoder over the 200 stocks at one timestamp predicting all targets, with output minus its mean.
why: Targets are market-neutral so zero-mean outputs match them.
quote: A small trick that turns output into zero mean is helpful.

what: Retrain models every 12 days on received new data during inference, 5 times (CatBoost from scratch, NNs fine-tuned).
why: Adapts to recent data as history targets arrive.
when: Forecasting API competitions revealing targets over time.
quote: I retrain my model every 12 days, 5 times in total.

what: Store features one file per day and load day-by-day into a preallocated float32 array to avoid doubling memory when concatenating.
why: Allows more features in online training.
quote: For achieving this, you should save training data one file per day and also loading day by day.

what: Skip online training if total inference time reaches a threshold, to stay inside the runtime limit.
why: Avoid overtime.
quote: I just skip online training if total inference time meets certain value.

what: Subtract the stock-weight-weighted mean of predictions at each timestamp rather than the plain mean.
why: Metric defines targets via weighted index.
when: Targets defined relative to a weighted index.
quote: Subtract weighted-mean is better than average-mean since metric already told.

what: CatBoost, GRU, Transformer weighted 0.5/0.3/0.2 from validation, no stacking.
why: Second-level model is time-consuming and does not help much.
quote: It's very time-consuming to train a second-level model and doesn't help much in fact. So i just use weighted sum.

what: Instead of having the policy output a raw launch angle, the action is a (source, target planet) pair; Rust env code converts it to the angle, avoiding the sun and other planets.
why: Raw angles gave only a semi-reasonable policy far from competitive; target selection removed the hardest geometric part of the action space.
when: RL for games with continuous geometric actions where a discrete target set exists.
quote: I modified the action space such that the model only had to select a target planet instead of a raw angle.

trick: Single forward pass for all players
what: Actions for all players are computed in one transformer forward pass, with per-player summary/plan/value tokens, instead of one observation per player; joint probability over all eligible sources is used in the PPO loss.
why: Saves 2-4x compute versus per-player observations.
when: Self-play multi-agent RL with symmetric observations.
quote: With this architecture, I could compute the actions for all players in a single forward pass, saving me 2-4x the compute over a standard one-observation-per-player approach.

trick: Scale model with raw entity inputs
what: Used a 200M-parameter, 38-block transformer over unaggregated entity tokens (planets, fleets, comets) with minimal feature engineering, after validating at 1-5M parameters.
why: Author's bet on the bitter lesson: scaling beat domain-specific engineering; each parameter increase gave large gains.
when: Simulation/RL competitions with abundant compute and a simulator.
quote: Each time I increased the number of parameters, the performance increased dramatically, so I continued scaling

what: Added learned extra tokens (4 actor plan, 4 value, 4 scratch, plus summary tokens) to the entity sequence.
why: Scratch tokens act as shared global workspace for attention.
when: Set/entity transformers needing global state or per-head readout tokens.
quote: Scratch tokens had no explicit purpose except to serve as a shared global workspace for the attention operation.

what: Fleet size is sampled from a truncated discretized logistic mixture with 8 components, conditioned on the chosen target's value vector added to the source stream.
why: Inferred: gives a continuous-like, multimodal distribution over integer sizes without hard bins; author found discrete bins unnecessary.
when: Integer-valued actions with wide range in RL.
quote: truncated discretized logistic mixture model with 8 mixture components to select the fleet size

what: Value tokens go through an MLP then softmax over remaining players, estimating each player's win probability; reward is +1 winner, -1 losers, gamma 1.0.
why: Keeps value head well-defined in four-player games.
quote: softmax operation over all remaining players to estimate their win probability

what: Rewrote the Python environment in Rust with parity tests against replays, multithreaded env stepping, observation-to-tensor conversion inside Rust, and preallocated pinned buffers.
why: Python env too slow for RL throughput.
when: Simulation competitions where env speed limits RL.
quote: The included Python environment was too slow for RL, so I rewrote it in Rust.

what: Verified the rewritten simulator against actual replays with extensive parity tests.
why: Ensures policy trained in the fast sim transfers to the real environment.
when: Whenever a re-implemented simulator is used for training.
quote: I used extensive parity tests against actual replays to verify that the simulation matched.

what: Self-play opponent checkpoint is replaced only when the current model wins >70% of head-to-head evals; policy KL and value cross-entropy terms against the previous best checkpoint stabilise training.
why: Stabilises self-play training.
quote: Once the model won >70% of its evaluation games, it replaced the previous best checkpoint.

what: Trained without an action mask for obviously bad moves (launching into the sun), re-introduced it only for late fine-tuning and test time.
why: Author hypothesises that no mask forced the model to internalise more physics.
when: RL where invalid/bad actions can be masked.
quote: I tried training with an action mask that prevented the model from doing obviously silly things like launching its ships into the sun, but, much to my surprise, this made the trained model worse.

what: Fit 200M parameters into a 100MiB file with 4-bit NormalFloat codebook quantization (group 128, fp16 scale per group); int8 for linear layers at runtime.
why: Submission file size cap; 4-bit lost little (~40% win vs the unquantized model head-to-head), 3-bit lost too much.
when: Submissions with strict model size caps.
quote: To fit the 200M-parameter model into 100MiB, I used 4-bit NormalFloat codebook quantization with group size 128 and one fp16 scale for each group.

what: Cap visible fleets (largest prioritised); if overage time runs low on slow CPUs, switch to a 5M model to finish the game.
why: About 8% of 4p games would exceed time; by then the critic said games were mostly decided and the small model converted 100% of winning positions.
when: Agent competitions with per-turn time limits and variable hardware.
quote: I would switch over to using a much faster 5M model to play out the rest of the game.

what: Wrote no code manually; used Codex and reviewed only generated docs; discards greenfield code freely.
why: Greatly accelerated implementation; ideas still came from the human.
when: Greenfield competition code with low stakes.
quote: I didn't allow myself to write any code and tried to manually review as little code as possible.

what: Undiscounted returns made the agent gain a ship lead then stall, wasting training compute on decided games; author would add early truncation or surrender.
why: No incentive to win sooner.
when: RL with win/loss reward and gamma=1.
quote: so it would just acquire a ship lead and then stall for the rest of the game.

what: Pure self-play with 90% two-player games in late training; matchmaking flipped to mostly four-player after deadline, author would balance modes and add league play against past checkpoints.
why: League play prevents strategic cycles and self-overfitting.
when: Games with changing matchmaking or multi-player modes.
quote: I mistakenly assumed that this was the intended behavior to better differentiate the top of the leaderboard

trick: Direct signal regression from rectified image
what: Rectify images (homography + grid remap), then regress all lead values directly (no signal mask), with backbone features split into 4 row groups and widened to 4x image width.
why: Standardised format removes spatial distortion; direct regression beats mask or pixel-coordinate approaches (those were not competitive).
quote: Transforming various image styles into a standardized format minimizes inconsistencies from different perspectives.

what: Do the rectification remap from the original high-resolution image (either via homography at 3200x2400 or direct remap of rescaled grid points).
why: Preserves features.
quote: Input images are generated using two different approaches to maximize feature preservation

what: Resample model outputs to target length with scipy.signal.resample instead of linear interpolation.
why: Better suited for ECG signals.
quote: Instead of linear interpolation, resampling is performed in the Fourier domain using scipy.signal.resample.

what: Grayscale image concatenated with coordinate-based feature channels.
why: Gives both intensity and spatial context.
quote: images are converted to grayscale and concatenated with coordinate-based features as model inputs

what: If |II-I-III| mean <0.01 blend leads I, II, III toward II=I+III, and if |aVR+aVL+aVF| mean <0.01 blend toward sum zero; also mix long II with II.
why: Physical lead relations denoise predictions.
quote: Apply 'II = I + III' if np.abs(II-I-III).mean()<0.01

what: TTA with gamma 1.0/0.9/1.1 and with crop/resize of Stage 1 inputs (1560x1248 centre crop 1440x1152; 1600x1280).
why: Inferred: averages out sensitivity to brightness and scale.
quote: The implementation of TTA improved overall performance by 0.07

what: Generate synthetic blank ECG images, perturb ground truth, and add Moire, flares and overlaid non-rectified images.
why: Prevents anomalous outputs under occlusion or noise.
quote: Synthetic blank ECG images were generated to prevent the model from predicting anomalous values when encountering occlusions or noise.

what: Ensemble 10 different backbones (ConvNeXtV2, EfficientNetV2, HGNetV2, MambaOut, CAFormer, InceptionNeXt), prediction strategies and output lengths with weights.
why: Inferred: diversity.
quote: A total of ten models were ensembled.

what: Used first ten training samples (later 30 images from 10 ids) as validation; batch size 1 with SmoothL1, AdamW, lr 1e-4 cosine.
why: Not explained.
quote: To validate the model, the first ten training samples were used as a validation set.

what: Compute grid points as weighted average over the feature map for sub-pixel precision, and fit a surface to remove outliers with gaps filled by interpolation.
why: Smoother edges and better structure of rectified images.
quote: Surface fitting is utilized to identify and remove outliers, with the resulting gaps filled through interpolation or the regression function itself.

what: Trained on LLM-generated PII essays from public datasets (nbroad's Mistral dataset was the most useful) plus a self-made 2k-sample dataset.
why: Inferred: synthetic essays add many more PII examples than the small labelled train set.
when: Token classification with scarce positive labels where an LLM can synthesise realistic data.
quote: @nbroad https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/nbroad/pii-dd-mistral-generated (by far the most useful!)

what: Created an additional 2k-sample synthetic dataset following a public notebook and used it in some training runs.
why: Inferred: more diverse data for ensemble members.
quote: we also created our own dataset of 2k samples and used it for some training runs

what: Kept all essays including those with no PII and down-weighted the O class in cross entropy to 0.05 instead of downsampling negatives.
why: Inferred: keeps negative-context diversity while handling class imbalance through loss weight.
quote: o_weight = 0.05

what: 4 folds by document id modulo 4, then one or two full-fit runs added to the ensemble.
why: Inferred: full-fit models use all data while fold models give OOF for tuning.
when: Small labelled sets with ensemble weights tuned on OOF.
quote: Each experiment was trained on 4 folds (document % 4) then 1 or 2 times full-fit.

what: Custom DeBERTa head with multi-sample dropout, used as one ensemble architecture.
why: Smoother training curve with fewer loss spikes.
quote: Multi-Sample Dropout Custom Model: Helped to train with a better-fitted train curve and less of spikes

what: Inserted a BiLSTM layer before the token classifier for diversity; fixed NaN losses by initializing the layer and saving with save_safetensors=False.
why: Adds architectural diversity and smoother training correlated with LB and CV.
quote: Bilstm we did have issues when training with Nan loss. So initializing the layer and also saving with save_safetensors=False, helped there.

what: Used models trained on different datasets as teachers for a student trained on other datasets with the same validation folds, with CE plus temperature KL distillation loss.
why: Teacher transfers knowledge from data the student does not see directly.
when: Several models trained on disjoint or different datasets.
quote: This worked great and and improved CV and LB by about 0.005-0.01.

what: For some essays, swap first and last names before training; one ensemble run used this.
why: Inferred: breaks dependence on name position/order.
quote: For some essays, swap the first and last names before training the model

what: Tuned a separate probability threshold for each of the 13 PII labels.
why: Inferred: labels differ in precision/recall trade-off under a recall-weighted metric.
when: Multi-label token classification with recall-weighted metric.
quote: Using different thresholds for each PII label, rather than using the same threshold for all 13 PII labels

what: If a token is predicted NAME_STUDENT anywhere in a document, relabel all identical tokens in that document; also drop name predictions not title-cased or containing digits/underscore.
why: Patterns observed from OOF mistakes.
when: Entity recognition where entities repeat in a document.
quote: If a token X in a document is predicted as NAME_STUDENT, all tokens X in the same document will be turned into NAME_STUDENT.

what: Rules from OOF error analysis: long phone numbers become ID_NUM, drop ID_NUM by length, URL_PERSONAL under 10 chars, EMAIL without @, repair spans, add regex predictions.
why: Models make systematic format errors that simple rules fix.
quote: Removing EMAIL predictions which don't have @

what: Weighted voting over 7 groups / 10 models with group weights and voting threshold tuned by Optuna on OOF.
why: Inferred: directly optimises the metric on OOF.
quote: The weights of different groups and the voting threshold are tuned via Optuna on the out-of-fold cross validation

what: Of 3 final submissions, two used full postprocessing and one a more conservative version.
why: Guard against postprocessing overfitting the OOF.
when: Heavy rule-based postprocessing tuned on limited data.
quote: We selected 2 submissions with the full postprocessing and 1 submission with more conservative postprocessing, in the case if the postprocessing overfits

what: Trained with max length 1600-2048 for 3-4 epochs at LR 1e-5 so whole essays fit.
why: Inferred: avoids stride/chunk artifacts; strided inference was listed as not working.
quote: The models are trained on a max length of between 1600-2048 for 3-4 epochs.

trick: CatBoost with model predictions as baseline
what: For each of LightGBM, XGBoost, CatBoost and NN, trained a new CatBoost model using that model's OOF predictions (as raw logits) as the baseline, i.e. the starting value that boosting corrects.
why: Author does not know why it helps; CatBoost corrected even CatBoost's own predictions.
when: Tabular classification where a final-stage learner can add on top of OOF predictions.
quote: What I think might have been my secret sauce was that for each of these model predictions, I trained a CatBoost model using the initial model predictions as a baseline.

what: Used OOF predictions as the baseline and converted predicted probabilities to logits since the tree libraries do not return logits natively.
why: A CatBoost baseline is added to the raw model output, so it needs raw values.
when: Using the baseline option with binary classification.
quote: The baseline needs to consist of 'raw values', which in the context of binary classification means the logits.

what: Treated numeric features as categorical too, keeping both the numeric column and a categorical copy.
why: Not explained; community tip found most effective.
when: Synthetic tabular data with discrete-valued numerics.
quote: What I found most effective was to maintain both the numeric feature and a categorical copy of it.

what: For each of XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost, used Optuna to find 10 sets of hyperparameters and averaged the predictions of all 10; also used large max_bin values.
why: Inferred: averaging near-optimal configs reduces variance relative to a single best config.
quote: I used Optuna to find 10 different sets of 'optimal hyperparameters' and averaged their predictions to get an overall prediction for each.

what: Used large max_bin settings in the GBDT models, taken from a community tip.
why: Inferred: finer binning of numeric features preserves detail.
when: GBDTs on numeric data with many unique values.
quote: Shoutout to @omidbaghchehsaraei 's post here for the tip to use large max_bin values.

what: Final level was a neural network stacking the four CatBoost-corrected predictions.
why: It squeezed out the last bit of performance (author's words).
when: Stacking a small set of strong OOF predictions.
quote: The final step was a Neural Network to stack these 4 predictions together.

trick: CV size argument vs public LB
what: Based every decision on CV, noting that CV covers 60% of data while the public LB covers 8%.
why: Larger evaluation sample means a more reliable signal than the public LB.
quote: That means that a CV score measures your performance on 60% of the entire dataset, whereas the public leaderboard measures your performance on only 8%

what: Did no feature engineering beyond numeric-as-categorical copies, but did include the original dataset.
why: Past playground experience that feature engineering is of little use.
quote: I didn't do any other feature engineering, as my experience from past playground competitions has usually been that feature engineering is of little use.

what: Chose as a final submission an early solution with higher CV (0.94173) but lower public LB (0.94284) than his heavily tuned one, because he found no code errors; it won.
why: CV covers far more data than the public LB slice.
when: Playground and other competitions with small public LB.
quote: Despite this, I couldn’t find any errors in my code, so I decided to trust the CV score and use this solution as one of my submissions.

gain: Hill climbing, Ridge and LR ensembles scored clearly lower CV (no number)
what: Fed the OOF files of all base models into AutoGluon to build the ensemble, defining the CV folds himself to avoid leakage, instead of hill climbing, Ridge or logistic regression stackers.
why: Not explained beyond CV scores: other ensemblers did not come close.
when: Stacking many OOF prediction sets on tabular data.
quote: After training all the models and collecting their OOF files, I let AutoGluon handle the ensembling, ensuring to define the CV strategy myself to avoid leakage.

what: Trained two AutoGluon models, one with and one without the original dataset, which had the highest CV and were the most important in the ensemble.
why: Inferred: AutoGluon's internal stacking provides strong diverse base models.
when: Tabular playground competitions with an original source dataset.
quote: Additionally, I trained two AutoGluon models, one with and one without the original dataset.

what: Trained XGBoost and three LightGBM variants on four different data pipelines, two of which included the original dataset; no feature engineering, and the Name column was kept.
why: Diversity across data pipelines; synthetic data inconsistencies are best left as they are.
when: Playground competitions generated from a real dataset.
quote: with the original dataset being included in two of the pipelines.

what: Did no feature engineering, dropped no features and kept the Name column despite temptation to remove it.
why: Author says that for synthetic datasets it is usually best to leave inconsistencies as they are.
quote: I didn't do any feature engineering and did not drop any features, despite the temptation to remove the Name column.

what: Of 69 trained models, the winning blend used 24 with a simple AutoGluon ensemble, and it beat his more elaborate ensembling attempts.
why: Not explained; CV was higher.
when: When many ensembles tried over-fit the public LB.
quote: fewer models and a simpler ensembling approach worked better this time around.

what: For each categorical column give the GBDT the original label encoding plus target-encoded mean, median, min, max, nunique and count encoding (7 representations total).
why: Gives GBDT multiple ways to understand the categorical column.
when: Tabular GBDT with categorical columns and a large dataset.
quote: We give the model the original column plus 6 different representations of the original.

what: Create new categorical columns by concatenating 2 to 6 existing columns (e.g. Occupation + '_' + Gender), then apply the full TE/CE encodings to them; the published code uses 20 such columns.
why: Encoding combinations captures interactions and improved CV and LB.
when: Tabular data with several categorical / low-cardinality columns.
quote: we can create more categorical columns by combining existing categorical columns. Then we can engineer more encodings from the new columns and improve CV score and LB score even more.

what: Treat numeric columns as categorical and apply TE mean/median/min/max/nunique and CE; also combine numeric with numeric/categorical columns and encode the result.
why: Lets the model capture non-monotonic per-value effects.
when: Large tabular data with discrete-ish numeric features.
quote: Another technique that often works is to treat numerical columns as if they are categorical.

what: With 23 base columns (after date decomposition), random combinations of 2-6 columns (about 145,000 possible) were evaluated in a for-loop with cuDF-pandas: build column, nested-fold TE and CE, train XGBoost; keep combos that improve CV. Ran for days and found 170 good combinations.
why: GPU allows 10x-100x more combinations than CPU; the 1.2M rows make chance CV gains unlikely.
when: Large tabular datasets where categorical interactions matter and GPU is available.
quote: Whenever feature engineering a combination with TE and CE improves CV score, the code saves it to a list. After running for multiple days, the code found 170 powerful combinations.

what: Final submission is one XGBoost with 611 features, learning_rate 0.001 and 20,000 estimators, target_encode kfold=10; full version CV 1.016 versus simple version (229 features, lr 0.01, 2,000 trees, kfold=5) CV 1.019.
why: In this competition feature engineering improved CV and LB, so a single strong model beat spending time on diverse ensembles.
when: Playground tabular tasks where FE gains are real.
quote: My final submission is a single XGBoost model with 611 features!

trick: Fill NaN with global train mean in TE
what: In the in-fold target encoder, unseen/NaN categories are filled with the mean computed on the whole train set rather than the in-fold df_tmp, accepting slight leakage.
why: Author: all NaN map to the same value rather than five different per-fold values, so GBDT handles them consistently; improved CV and LB.
quote: Using train and accepting a little leakage improved CV and LB score, so I went with that.

what: Uses GPU RAPIDS (cuDF, cuML) for dataframe ops and models so 10x-100x more experiments fit in the same time.
why: Accuracy comes from the number of experiments run.
when: Any tabular competition with a GPU.
quote: Using GPU let's us perform 10x to 100x more experiments in the same amount of time as CPU.

what: Trained 4 multiclass XGBoosts on the 8 original classes plus a random-noise 9th class.
why: Inferred: noise samples act as contrastive negatives regularising class boundaries.
when: Tabular multilabel with correlated defect classes.
quote: Build 4 noise contrastive xgbs: original 8 classes and 1 noise as 9th class, run multiclass

what: Built 8 one-vs-rest binary XGBs alongside the multiclass models.
why: Inferred: complementary views of each label.
quote: Build 8 binary xgbs;

what: Stacked 12 models, using only the 8 real-class outputs of the noise-contrastive models.
why: Inferred: noise column carries no target information.
quote: When stacking, only use results of 8 classes.

what: Generate features with OpenFE (192 from 8 columns), drop highly correlated ones, then sequential feature selection of ~20 features separately for LGBM, XGB and CatBoost.
why: Model-specific feature sets add quality and diversity.
quote: Selecting ca. 20 features (in addition to the original columns) using Sequential Feature Selection, individually for LGBM, XGB, Catboost.

what: Add complete original Abalone dataset to training in every fold, never to validation.
why: Commenter: LB resembles the synthetic distribution, so original rows are poor validation but useful training.
quote: Use complete original Abalone dataset for training in each fold, never for validation.

what: Optimise 49-model blend weights on OOF using Nelder-Mead; weights with negatives summing to 0.997 beat clipped and normalised ones.
why: Consistently outperformed constrained weights.
quote: The best results included negative coefficients and summed up to 0.997. That seemed cheesy to me but consistently outperformed coefficients that were clipped at min=0.0 and scaled to sum up to 1.0.

what: Custom MSLE loss in LightGBM, reg:squaredlogerror in XGB, log1p/expm1 for other models.
why: Match loss to metric.
quote: LGBM: custom MSLE loss

gain: Individual CV 0.14680 but adds ensemble diversity
what: XGB multi:softprob classifier with a softmax-based regression head over discrete target values, used as an ensemble member.
why: Author does not know why; maybe the synthetic dataset and discrete target. Got weight despite worse CV (0.14680).
quote: I still don't know why it works (maybe due to the synthetical nature of the dataset and the discrete regression target)

what: Run Bayesian sweeps by copying the notebook up to 5 times with the same Sweep ID.
why: Easy parallelization compared to Optuna.
quote: Just copy your notebook up to 5 times, use same Sweep ID, and run it.

what: Include AutoGluon (indirectly adding NNs) with OOF predictions in the blend.
why: Diversity; individual CV best at 0.14592.
quote: AutoGluon indirectly adds some ANN to the ensemble, though.

what: Without OOFs, a public ANN submission was blended with a weight (17%) found against public LB.
why: Adds a diverse model; own submission without it would also have won.
quote: In the absence of OOFs I used some submissions against public LB to find an optimal weight of 17%

what: SMOTE, augmentation or removing outliers did not close the gap of models predicting max 20 rings (29 in train).
why: Worsened CV.
quote: Any approach to tackle that gap (SMOTE, augmentation) worsened CV significantly.

what: Wrap trainer for CV and prediction in a custom Python package deployed via Kaggle API.
why: Comparable results across experiments.
quote: Wrap often-used code (e.g. Trainer for CV and prediction) into a custom Python Package to guarantee comparable results when experimenting.

what: Trained separate 5-fold models on subsets defined by Previously_Insured, Vehicle_Damage, and their four combinations, in addition to full-data models, and fed their OOFs to the stacker.
why: Gives the stack specialised, diverse models; the author confirmed they generalise at lower complexity on each subset.
when: Tabular data with strong binary segmenting features.
quote: Component models on previously insured (2 models), vehicle damage (2 models), previously insured + vehicle damage (4 models)

what: Stage 1 and Stage 2 each trained trees and NNs (stage 2 on stage 1 OOFs); a final XGBoost stacker used 78 selected OOF sets.
why: Author found the XGBoost stacker gave the best CV-LB relation.
when: Large tabular data with many diverse models.
quote: XgBoost stacker as the last step was the most effective option for CV-LB relations

what: Stacked tree models on top of neural network OOFs and neural networks on top of tree OOFs.
why: Diversity between families boosted CV and LB together.
when: Stacked ensembles of mixed model families.
quote: We stacked tree models with neural networks and vice-versa

trick: Add supplementary data to every fold
what: Added the full original (supplementary) dataset to each training fold, never to validation folds.
why: Gave the highest CV; keeps validation on synthetic distribution.
when: Synthetic playground data with original dataset available.
quote: Training data from the competition, with the supplementary dataset added to each fold in entirety- this approach boosted our CV to the maximum

what: Found rows duplicated between original and test data and reversed the predicted labels for them, applied in all submissions.
why: Synthetic generation flipped labels for duplicated rows, so this exploits that pattern (details in the linked discussion; not given here).
when: Synthetic data derived from a public original dataset.
quote: We discovered the target reversals discussed here on day 1 and used it in the auto ML submission as well.

what: Collated features into a versioned feature store (12 versions) with standard naming, so any model could use ready-made datasets.
why: Speeds brute-force experiments and keeps CV comparison consistent.
quote: Using such a centralized feature store with tried-and-tested features helped us iterate through our brute-force experiments well and quickly

what: Tested new features only on the competition synthetic data, using one fold and a simple CatBoost with permutation importance.
why: Avoids bias from the supplementary data and keeps screening cheap.
when: Large datasets where full CV per idea is costly.
quote: We resorted to testing the feature importance on a single fold only using a simple catboost model consistently.

what: Added OOF predictions from one public kernel (XGBoost with max_bins) into the stack as a diversity source.
why: Adds diversity not available from the team's own models.
quote: Using the public kernel helped us a bit towards the end of the competition

what: Excluded XGBoost from the base layer because it did not improve final stack CV despite good solo scores.
why: Inferred: redundant with other GBDT learners.
when: Choosing stack members by marginal CV gain.
quote: XgBoost weak learners -they were good in isolation but did not improve the final CV score when we included them in the final model

what: Linear blends, Optuna weights, hill climbing and a CatBoost stacker did not beat the XGBoost stacker.
why: No reason given.
quote: Linear approaches, Optuna, Hill Climb

what: Did not resample or reweight for class imbalance.
why: Author: dataset large enough.
when: Large imbalanced tabular data with AUC-style metric.
quote: We never considered handling it due to the large data size

what: Used A100/A6000/4090-class hardware instead of Kaggle free GPUs to train many NNs.
why: Neural networks and a 78-model stack needed heavy compute.
quote: Committing resources to a competition is necessary when required. Using better resources enabled us to experiment better

what: Use the probability of being poisonous from an exact solution of the original dataset (a public notebook) as a new feature.
why: Author: proxy for the original-data signal still present in the synthetic data; also adds diversity.
when: Synthetic data derived from a known original
quote: I added the probability of being poisonous as a new feature, reasoning that it could be a proxy for the "signal" from the original still present in the current dataset.

trick: Large OOF zoo with Ridge stacker
what: Collected ~80 OOF arrays (72 used) from diverse models and combined them with Ridge, which gave the best speed/LB tradeoff; hill climbing used too but took 2+ hours beyond 60 models.
why: Diversity plus CV-LB consistency.
quote: Gathered a veritable zoo of models, ensembled them, kept an eye on CV & model diversity, & kept ensembling while score increased

what: Fed all 72 OOF arrays into AutoGluon as features and let it ensemble; also first used hill climbing to pick 8 OOFs plus the best AG OOF when run time was limited.
why: Inferred: AG stacks nonlinearly and robustly.
quote: At long last, I decided to throw caution to the winds, and threw all 72 OOFs into AG

what: Running AutoGluon on GPU with long runs boosted score (0.98482 -> 0.98524 reported by another competitor).
why: Inferred: GPU enables the NN/boosted models to fit properly in time.
quote: just using a GPU made the score jump from 0.98482 to 0.98524

gain: same score in about half the time; ~0.0001 variations
what: Excluded XGBoost and CatBoost from AG (weakest there), then kept only GBM and XT; ran individual models alone via AG and ensembled manually.
why: Frees time budget for better models.
quote: giving more time to the better performing models

trick: Random Forest and Extra Trees members
what: Included Random Forests and Extra Trees in the ensemble because they were competitive on this noisy data.
why: Inferred: noise-robust, diverse.
quote: Random Forests and Extra Trees were quite competitive this time around

what: Overwrite own prediction with another model/ensemble prediction when the latter has probability above ~0.99.
why: Inferred: only trusts the other model where very confident.
quote: insert confident disagreements

what: Setting LGBM num_threads to the number of CPU cores sped it up.
why: Faster training.
quote: one can speed up LGBM by setting "num_threads" = number of CPU cores

what: Ran AG on Lightning.ai with 32 CPUs for 3 hours when Kaggle GPU quota was exhausted; matched the 12-hour Kaggle result.
why: Compute workaround.
quote: reasoning that it might just be better than 12 hours with 4 CPUs on Kaggle

what: Blending others public submissions raised public LB but did not generalise; trust CV, keep CV-LB gap consistent.
why: Public LB overfit even with millions of rows.
quote: Moral of the story - trust your CV score, and keep building while keeping CV and LB in good agreement.

trick: Catboost outlier classifier OOF as feature
what: Train a CatBoost classifier (Optuna-tuned) to predict whether price is a high outlier (above Q3+1.5 IQR); use its out-of-fold probability as an extra feature in LGBM and the NN rather than in the ensemble.
why: Inferred: gives the downstream regressor an explicit tail-risk signal for the skewed target.
quote: The hyperparameters were found by optuna. The oof predictions were not used in the ensemble.

what: Add all categoricals as target-encoded columns using the median instead of the mean, recomputed inside each fold.
why: Median is robust to outliers in price; in-fold recomputation avoids leakage.
quote: I did this leakfree, meaning that I recomputed the targetencoded columns in each fold.

gain: CV 72468 vs 72300 for Ridge, yet better on private
what: Second final submission: a robust public NN with four extra numeric features being OOF predictions of SVR, LGBM, CatBoost classifier and XGB; NN stacker beat the Ridge ensemble despite worse CV.
why: Inferred: NN stacker uses OOFs as features and can capture nonlinearity.
quote: The NN ensemble had a crossvalidation score of 72468, but in the end was better than the Ridge ensemble.

trick: Include original data in some models
what: Added the original (non-synthetic) dataset to training for some models, even twice for LGBM.
why: Inferred: adds true-distribution signal; also adds diversity.
quote: I included original data in some of the models (even two times in LGBM)

what: Second LGBM with label-encoded categoricals (rare merged into one category) and max_bin raised to 30000.
why: Inferred: lets high-cardinality numeric/label values split finely.
quote: I used a second LGBM (LGBM5), where I label encoded all categorical data

what: Included an RBF-kernel SVR instead of linear SVR as a diverse OOF member.
why: Inferred: non-tree diversity.
quote: I did compute a SVR with a rbf kernel as suggested by broccoli beef

what: Ran AutoGluon restricted to FASTAI models with nested bagging inside 20 outer folds to keep OOF leak-free.
why: Inferred: cheap NN diversity with no leakage.
quote: I included fastai computations from Autogluon (with a nested cv over 20 folds to be 100% leakfree)

what: Used 20 CV folds for the ensemble members.
why: Inferred: more training data per fold for noisy target.
quote: I used 20 cv folds

trick: Pseudolabel call needed for original data
what: AutoGluon fit() ignores extra data; fit_pseudolabel() must be used to include original data (author discovered his AG preds did not use it).
why: Caveat about tool API.
quote: Autogluon, when using TabularPredictor.fit() , is not using the original data.

what: Submitted a different-style NN stack as second final submission on impulse; it won.
why: Hedge between differently built ensembles.
quote: I needed a second final submission and I decided spontanously on the last day

what: Decomposes sales into separate factors (store, product, trend, holiday, New Year) estimated one after another rather than one joint model; store and product factors use relative sales, holiday and New Year factors are estimated last after removing other effects.
why: Relative sales normalise variations from other factors; holiday effects are hard to isolate from the time trend so are evaluated last.
when: Synthetic/structured sales forecasting with strong multiplicative group effects.
quote: using relative sales to calculate store factor and product factor helps normalize variations caused by other factors.

what: Another competitor (kdmitrie) showed that evaluating the factors simultaneously is better than sequentially, which also removes ordering concerns.
why: Avoids order dependence between factors.
quote: it is better to evaluate the factors simultaneously rather than sequentially.

what: Uses the Python holiday package to build per-country holiday features, treated basically; author notes it misses some holidays that influence sales and suggests pruning ineffective holidays and adding missing ones.
why: Holidays affect sales; the package is incomplete.
quote: A more refined approach would involve identifying and removing holidays that do not significantly impact sales while also adding missing holidays that do.

what: Author's suggested (not implemented) validation: 5 folds training on the first 2,3,4,5,6 years and evaluating on the 3rd to 7th year.
why: Mimics forecasting future years from the past.
quote: I would use a 5-fold scheme where the model is trained on the first 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 years and evaluated on the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 6th, and 7th year, respectively.

what: Add 11 genetic-programming-derived features at ensembling stage rather than to base models.
why: GP features did not help alone or in base models; helped at the ensemble.
quote: adding 11 GP-derived features at the ensembling stage

what: Use a Keras ensemble as CatBoost baseline, then boost on the models plus GP features.
why: Equivalent to boosting residuals.
quote: CatB has the ability to use a strong “baseline” model as a seed before ensembling

what: Prefer NNs and Lasso, then hill climbing; NN ensembling of 40-50 models in 1-2 hours.
why: No tuning needed.
quote: my preference is with NNs and Lasso for regression

what: Inspect Lasso coefficients on one-hot data to recover the generator formula.
why: Interpretable.
quote: Lasso feature coefficients were extremely informative in this competition.

what: Final hill climbing across several first-level ensembles.
why: Robustness.
quote: making a second-level ensemble by hill climbing

what: GP restricted to + - * / reproduced target formula but gave no extra benefit.
why: Too similar to existing models.
quote: Basically, they don’t bring diversity.

what: AE latent features added; did not help.
why: Not stated.
quote: produced features that worked well on their own

what: Extract digits of numerical features and build pair/triple/quadruple interaction features between digits, with TE/CE.
why: Author calls FE the most important part.
quote: Combination of digits between each numerical feature (pairs, triples, quadruples) + TE/CE.

what: Combine base features in pairs and apply target and count encoding.
why: Inferred: captures interactions.
quote: Combination of base features (pairs) + TE/CE

what: Compute TE/CE of base features and digits on the original dataset; also TE using other columns (employment_status, debt_to_income_ratio) as targets.
why: Inferred: adds external signal and auxiliary-target encodings.
when: Synthetic data derived from an original dataset
quote: TE of base features on the original dataset using

what: Add a small group of features at a time and keep it if CV improves.
why: Controls feature selection.
quote: I just add a small group of features at a time and if they improved CV, I kept them

what: Add round features, quantile-binned numericals and categorical version of credit_score.
why: Small CV gains.
quote: Quantile binned numericals

what: Train about 100 diverse models (GBDTs, many NN types, LR, ET) with little tuning.
why: Diversity over tuning.
quote: My strategy for this comp was to train as many diverse models as possible and not spend that much time tuning them.

what: Use ridge and hill climbing as ensemblers.
why: Linear blends are robust.
quote: Ridge and HC were the best ensemblers in this comp

what: Stacking with LGBM/CB/NNs was much worse than linear methods.
why: Not stated.
quote: but they were much worse than linear methods.

trick: Hill climbing over singles and ensembles
what: Greedy hill-climbing selection over a large pool of OOF predictions, where the pool contains both single models and previously built ensembles.
why: Inferred: the pool is diverse, and greedy forward selection picks complementary members without needing explicit diversity metrics.
when: Tabular tasks with many OOF prediction sets and a ranking metric (AUC).
quote: I included in HC both single models and other ensembles. Such a mixed approach worked for me in previous competitions.

trick: Ridge stacking on HC top models
gain: Ridge CV 0.70860 vs HC 0.70886, but better Public and Private LB
what: After HC plateaued, fed the top-36 HC-selected models (rank-transformed predictions) into a Ridge meta-model with alpha=10.
why: Ridge regularisation stabilises weights; the author says stabilisation can matter more than raw CV optimisation.
when: Plateau in single-stage blending where CV gains no longer transfer to LB.
quote: The Ridge Ensemble (based on Top-36 models from HC and alpha = 10) had slightly lower post-cutoff CV than HC (0.70860 vs 0.70886), but performed better on both Public and Private LB.

what: Use hill-climbing purely as a model selector, then fit a regularised linear stacker only on the selected models.
why: Author: two-stage ensembles may improve results when single-stage methods reach a plateau.
when: Ensembles stuck at a CV/LB plateau.
quote: two-stage ensembles may improve final results when single-stage methods reach plateau

what: Experimented with alphas on rank-transformed predictions as Ridge inputs.
why: Inferred: rank transform makes base-model outputs comparable in scale for a linear stacker and fits AUC.
quote: I experimented with different alphas on rank-transformed predictions and different numbers of models.

gain: Private 0.70514 (alpha 5, Top-34) vs 0.70504 for RidgeCV alpha
what: Tuned Ridge alpha manually rather than letting RidgeCV pick on CV; RidgeCV would choose alpha 0.1, missing the better a6-a8 range.
why: CV-optimal alpha was not the best generalising one under distribution shift.
when: Shifted test distribution where CV is only a rough guide.
quote: Automated RidgeCV optimizing on CV in this competition would pick a0.1 (highest CV 0.70875) which gives worse private score (0.70504 vs 0.70514) and the optimal alphas (a6-a8 range) would be missed.

what: Evaluated with a post-cutoff cross-validation scheme (credited to another competitor) instead of plain CV, and tracked the CV vs Public LB gap.
why: Inferred: the test set is shifted from train, so CV restricted to a post-cutoff split mimics it better. Exact scheme is not described in this writeup.
when: Data with a train/test distribution shift.
quote: especially @masayakawamata for the shared post-cutoff cross-validation approach

trick: Use CV-LB gap to stop and pick
what: Stopped adding models when CV and Public LB diverged; accepted a final ensemble because the CV-LB gap (0.00121) looked acceptable.
why: Adding models raised CV while Public LB fell, a sign of distribution shift.
when: Competitions with shift between train and public/private test.
quote: Any addition of new models caused improvement in CV, but Public LB dropped.

what: Added a/(b+1e-8) ratio features for medically meaningful pairs such as LDL/HDL, total cholesterol/HDL, triglycerides/HDL, systolic/diastolic BP.
why: Ratios capture relationships between related variables (e.g. LDL/HDL is a standard risk indicator).
when: Tabular medical/risk data with related numeric measurements.
quote: the ratio of "bad" cholesterol to "good" cholesterol (LDL/HDL) is a standard medical risk indicator

trick: Square and cube of top numerics
what: Added squared and cubed versions of the top 10 numeric columns as an extra feature set.
why: Captures U-shaped and S-shaped relationships; restricted to top columns to avoid feature explosion.
when: Tabular data feeding diverse models into a blend.
quote: Square features (captures U-shaped relationships)

what: Concatenated the original (real) diabetes dataset with the synthetic competition train data, used only for training, with preprocessing and encoding done inside CV folds.
why: More samples and more stable models; keeping the original rows out of validation avoids leakage.
when: Playground-series synthetic data generated from a real dataset.
quote: The combined data was used only for training, with all preprocessing and encoding performed inside cross-validation folds.

what: Built a wide pool of trees and NNs varying depth, learning rate, regularisation, feature sets (ratios, polynomials, target encoding) and seeds, as raw material for HC and Ridge.
why: Author says HC picks complementary models, so diversity comes from exploration rather than correlation filtering.
quote: In the Ridge Ensemble, I focused purely on performance (post-cutoff AUC) rather than correlation-based diversity.

what: Group by a column (Weight Capacity), build an equally spaced histogram of the target within each group (about 7 bins, bin count a hyperparameter), and merge each bucket count back as features. Computed within folds.
why: Gives the model the shape of the within-group target distribution rather than a single statistic.
when: Regression with a high-cardinality numeric or categorical key.
quote: I had fun inventing this technique. I have never seen it being used before.

what: Per group compute target quantiles (5,10,40,45,55,60,90,95) and return them as 8 columns.
why: Richer description of the group target distribution than mean/std.
quote: and return the 8 values to create 8 new columns.

what: When a groupby aggregate uses the target column, compute it with nested folds to prevent leakage.
why: Avoids target leakage into OOF validation.
quote: (If COL2 is a target column, we use nested folds to prevent leakage).

what: Encode the missingness pattern across several columns as one integer by summing isna() times 2**i, then use it for groupbys and combinations.
why: Captures joint missingness as a categorical key.
quote: We can create a new column from all the NANs over multiple columns.

what: Create extra columns from the most important numeric feature by rounding it to 7, 8, 9 decimals, usable as categorical keys.
why: Synthetic float values repeat at different precisions, creating groups.
when: Synthetic data with a dominant float feature.
quote: We can create more powerful columns based on this column by binning this column with rounding!

what: Extract individual decimal digits (positions 1-9) of Weight Capacity as separate int8 columns.
why: Digits of IDs and codes can carry info such as brand or colour; the author compares to product IDs.
when: Floats that might encode identifiers or synthetic generation artefacts.
quote: This technique seems weird but it is often used in real life to extract info from a product ID where individual digits within a product ID convey info about a product such as brand, color, etc.

what: Label-encode each categorical (NaN as -1) and combine all pairs into 28 new categorical columns, then target-encode/group on them.
why: Without combining, a tree needs many splits to isolate a set of category pairs; after combining and encoding, one split suffices.
quote: We can create 28 more categorical columns by combining all combinations of categorical columns.

what: Group the original dataset by Weight Capacity and merge the mean price back as orig_price, treating the original as manufacturer suggested price and the competition as store prices.
why: Gives each row knowledge of the original price for the same key.
when: Playground synthetic data generated from a known original dataset.
quote: We can treat the original dataset that this competition was created from as the manufacture suggested retail.

what: Divide groupby-derived columns by each other (count per nunique, std per count).
why: Inferred: ratios give trees quantities they cannot easily form themselves.
when: After building many groupby aggregate features.
quote: we can can then combine these new columns to make even more new columns!

trick: Add feature groups one idea at a time
what: Add each idea's dozen features to the model together; keep them if CV improves, else discard. After hundreds, consider feature elimination (RFE or XGB importance) and retune hyperparameters, then continue searching.
why: Controlled incremental search over thousands of ideas.
quote: I try each idea one at a time. Each idea will create about a dozen features together.

what: Used RAPIDS cuDF-pandas with XGBoost on GPU to run over 300 models and thousands of feature ideas in a month.
why: Experiment speed is the key to finding creative features.
quote: In one month, I trained over 300 XGBoost models and tried thousands of different feature engineering ideas!

what: Won with one XGBoost on about 500 features; a 138-feature version on a Kaggle T4 also reached first place.
why: Features gave the gain, not blending.
when: Synthetic competitions where FE finds the signal.
quote: My final solution is a single model trained with 500 features using 1xA100 GPU 80GB.

what: 3-level stack with XGB and MLP at level 2 on 73 L1 OOF sets, 50/50 average at level 3.
why: Non-linear level 2 can pick different models per scenario (e.g. Episode_Length missing), which linear blending cannot.
when: Data with strong regime switches / missingness
quote: But a stack (non-linear level 2 model) will use predictions from one model when predicting with ELM and use the predictions from another model when predicting without ELM.

trick: Train models with key feature removed
what: Drop the dominant column Episode_Length_minutes from all rows and train models on the rest for the stack.
why: Gives strong specialists for the missing-feature scenario.
quote: We can remove Episode_Length_minutes from all rows and train a model to predict Listening_Time_minutes from all other columns.

what: Predict target / Episode_Length and multiply back by actual or imputed length.
why: Exploits near-linear relationship.
quote: we can create a new target with train['new_target'] = train.Listening_Time_minutes / train.Episode_Length_minutes .

what: Train models to predict Episode_Length_minutes on train and test together, then impute or replace it.
why: Test rows have all other columns, so more data.
quote: we can use both train.csv and test.csv data to train and predict Episode_Length_minutes .

trick: Pseudo labels from test in stack
what: Add test.csv with pseudo labels to training of all models.
why: Uses information from test columns.
quote: We can add test.csv data with pseudo labels to the training of all our models.

trick: Diversity over score; weak models in stack
what: Include models with CV 13.2 and even 26 RMSE; build 75 models with different features/hyperparameters including max_depth 5 to 20.
why: Diversity matters, not performance.
quote: When building an ensemble it is all about diversity and nothing about performance.

what: Train GBDT on residuals of Lasso, SVR and MLP.
why: Diverse L1 models.
quote: GBDT - Boost over RAPIDS Lasso

what: cuML Lasso and SVR on 6000 engineered features; TabPFN 20x with 10,000-sample subsamples.
why: Adds diverse model families on GPU.
quote: uses 6000 features!

trick: Save every OOF to enable stacking
what: Save OOF and test preds for all experiments; stacking XGB on them moved to first place on LB.
why: Reuse of experiments.
quote: It is good practice to save all OOF and Test PRED to disk for every experiment

trick: Reuse public notebooks as stack members
what: Re-run public XGB/LGBM/AutoGluon notebooks on own folds and make variations.
why: Cheap diversity.
quote: I incorporated all 3 of these public models into my final stack

trick: GPU hill climbing over hundreds of models
what: Feed hundreds of GBDT, NN and cuML models into GPU hill climbing to auto-select ensemble members.
why: Automatic selection from many diverse candidates; GPU speed makes it feasible.
when: Tabular regression with many OOF sets
quote: Hill climbing is great because it automatically selects models for us.

what: Keep XGBoost with cuML target-encoded features (CV 0.0605-0.061) with 25% weight though individually worse.
why: Diversity matters more than single model CV.
quote: This demonstrates that diversity is more important than single model CV score.

what: Train linear regression OOF, set target = y - LR_OOF, train NN on it, add LR prediction back at inference.
why: Linear model captures linear relationships so NN learns the rest better.
quote: I trained my public notebook NN on the residuals from a NVIDIA cuML LinearRegression model. This improved CV 0.0608 => 0.0599 .

trick: GBDT on NN residuals for diversity
what: Train XGB on residuals of NN predictions; no single CV gain but improved ensemble.
why: Creates diverse model for hill climbing.
quote: This did not improve the XGB CV score but it made a new diverse model that improved my hill climbing ensemble CV score.

what: log1p of each feature then all products, divisions, sums, differences between pairs, fed to XGBoost.
why: Inferred: lets trees capture multiplicative relations in synthetic data.
quote: Then i created all products, divisions, sums, and differences between all pairs of features.

what: Bin each numeric (and log1p) feature into 9 equal-width bins, cross all pairs into 81-value categoricals, use as cat_features; 9 bins tuned.
why: CatBoost handles categoricals well; numerics often behave categorically.
quote: CatBoost loves categorical features, so I converted each numerical feature into 9 equal width binned values.

what: Group by 1-3 binned features (e.g. Sex, Weight_bin, Body_Temp) and compute z-score of another feature within group; 26 such features.
why: Compares individual to similar peers.
quote: This means i make groups from Sex, Weight, Body_Temp and compute z-score for Heart_Rate.

what: After finding weights from 5-fold OOF, retrain every model on all train with iterations = avg early-stopping rounds x 1.25 (1/(K-1) more), multiple seeds, weighted average with OOF weights.
why: Models see more data; adjusted iterations compensate.
when: Any GBDT/NN ensemble with fold-based weights
quote: Then we retrain all the models using 100% train data and use fixed number of iterations equal to 25% ( which equals to 1/(K-1) ) more than average number of iterations from 5-Kfold early stopping.

trick: Ratio target tried, did not help
what: Tried target divided by minutes; did not help ensemble CV this month (did in previous).
why: Models learn linearity anyway.
quote: I did try using ratio targets (similar to what I did in last month's competition about podcast listening times) but it didn't help my hill climbing ensemble CV this month.

gain: Ensemble of public notebooks went from CV 0.384 to 0.386
what: Treat the 8 features as categorical, build all pairs (28), triples (56) and quadruples (70), and target encode each of the 162 columns for each of the 7 one-vs-rest targets (1134 columns), plus the same from the original dataset, giving 2268 columns for XGBoost.
why: Combining and encoding lets trees isolate useful category combinations with one split, and lets models reverse-engineer the synthetic data generation process.
when: Playground synthetic data with a few categorical-like features.
quote: First we make all pairs which is 28 new columns. Then we make all triples which is 56 new columns.

what: Instead of appending the original dataset as extra rows, target-encode categorical columns using original-data group means and merge them in as new columns (also keep row-appended variants for ensemble diversity).
why: Lets models reverse-engineer the Kaggle synthetic generation; strongest when the original targets are random, since only the synthetic signal matters.
when: Playground-series competitions built from a public original dataset, especially with weak signal in the original.
quote: Most public notebooks in this competition used the former technique. But no public notebook used the latter.

what: Train stage-1 models (XGBoost, CatBoost, NN, linear) as one-vs-rest binary classifiers for each class and stack their OOF probabilities.
why: Author comment: per-class binary models give more decorrelated predictions, which helps the meta-learner. Inferred as partial.
when: Multiclass tasks scored on ranked probabilities.
quote: We can train individual models to predict single binary classification, Is the target y=0? , Is the target y=1? etc etc.

what: Train a level-2 NN with categorical cross-entropy on stage-1 OOF probabilities to output calibrated multiclass probabilities.
why: MAP@3 likes calibrated probabilities, and the stacker fixes calibration regardless of stage-1 calibration.
quote: We train an NN level 2 stacking model with categorical cross entropy loss and it doesn't matter if stage 1 models are calibrated or not.

what: Also built an XGBoost multi:softprob level-2 stacker and averaged it with the NN stacker.
why: Different stacker families make errors differently.
quote: The average of NN level 2 and GBDT level 2 is better than each stage 2 model individually!

what: Train each model many times with different seeds (NNs 100 times, GBDTs dozens of times on 100% data) and average the probabilities before taking the top 3.
why: MAP@3 is very sensitive to training randomness in predicted probabilities; averaging reduces it.
quote: This metric is very sensitive to the randomness of training (and predicted probabilities).

trick: GPU hill-climbing weights over many runs
what: Final ensemble is 9 diverse models, each trained many times (about 300 prediction sets), with the 9 weights found by GPU hill climbing.
why: Diverse GBDT, NN and cuML models combine better than any one; cuML makes diverse ML models fast.
quote: The effectiveness of hill climbing comes from creating a diverse set of models.

what: Fit a cuML linear regression first, then pass its logits as dtrain.set_base_margin so XGBoost boosts from them (boosting over residuals).
why: Gives trees a linear starting point so they model what the linear model misses.
when: GBDT where a simple model captures global trends.
quote: Then we use XGBoost's dtrain.set_base_margin(LINEAR_REGRESSION_LOGITS) to begin the boosting from the predictions of the linear regression model.

what: In the final days add test rows labeled with the best ensemble's probabilities; NNs take soft targets natively and XGBoost uses a custom multiclass soft-target objective. Also used pseudo-label columns (KNN features).
why: Adds test-distribution data using the ensemble's knowledge.
when: Late-stage competition boost with a strong ensemble.
quote: For XGB, we write a custom objective to train multi-class with soft targets.

what: Retrain key models on all training data, using XGBoost iterations 25% above the early-stopping average and a fixed-step LR schedule for NNs derived from the 5-fold plateau schedule.
why: Uses all the data; more data warrants slightly more rounds.
quote: we use fixed number of iterations equal to 25% more than average fixed during early stopping

trick: Blend diverse model into public notebooks
what: Built one distinct heavy model (the target-encoding monster, about 3000 features, ~50GB VRAM on A100 80GB) and added it to an ensemble of public notebook models.
why: Diversity is the benefit; it lifted the public ensemble.
when: Playground competitions with strong public notebooks.
quote: This diverse monster model boosted an ensemble of public notebooks from CV 0.384 to 0.386.

what: When the dataset is small, use minimal feature engineering and an equal-weight ensemble of a few diverse models, using original data in simple diverse ways.
why: Little room for complex engineering; Inferred: simple averaging avoids overfitting weights.
quote: Minimal to no feature engineering and equal weight ensemble of a few diverse models.

what: Picked the best CV ensemble as the final submission, which was also the best on LB.
why: CV was reliable.
when: Large-data tabular competitions with consistent CV.
quote: I chose my best CV ensemble which was also my best LB score.

what: Used only the mean statistic when target encoding, not std/min/max/skew.
why: Each statistic must be computed for all 7 targets, exploding features, and many are uninformative for binary targets; the few tried did not give enough improvement.
quote: Also note, that many of these stats are un-informative for classification problems.

what: Extract digit features from numeric columns and combine them, with target encoding (mean/std/skew) of feature and digit combinations.
why: Inferred: synthetic data generated from noisy numbers leaks structure in digits.
quote: Certain combinations of digits + TE (mean/std/skew)

what: Add a categorical copy of each numerical base feature (for NNs and GBDTs).
why: Inferred: lets models treat low-cardinality numbers as categories/embeddings.
quote: A categorical copy of each numerical base feature

what: Add sin/cos cyclical features from public notebooks even for non-periodic columns like study hours.
why: Inferred: acts as a nonlinear rescaling; a commenter wonders the same.
quote: Cyclical features from @yekenot 's notebooks

trick: Separate feature sets per model family
what: Used different feature sets for NNs (categorical copies, TE of combinations) and GBDTs (ordinal mapping of categoricals).
why: Each family did best with its own set.
quote: Feature set 1 (this did best with NNs):

what: Focused on making stronger models (RealMLP, TabM, XGBoost etc.) rather than many different models; best single model placed 7th. RealMLP was best.
why: Author: RealMLP completely outperformed other models in this and one other comp.
quote: I focused on making stronger models rather than a lot of different models this time.

what: Ridge regression on OOFs of 190 models; other ensemblers (hill climbing, AutoGluon, CatBoost) were worse.
why: Inferred: author gives no reason.
quote: My final ensemble has a total of 190 models ensembled with Ridge: CV 8.56634, LB 8.53096, PB 8.57273 (with post-process).

trick: Save OOFs of all tuning trials
what: Hyperparameter-tune best models (RealMLP, TabM, GBDTs) with random search (~30 trials in the TabArena search space) and keep OOFs from every trial for the ensemble; sweeps via WandB.
why: Inferred: many differently-parameterised models add diversity.
quote: My boost from around 8.5335 down to 8.5309 was due to hyperparameter tuning all my best models (RealMLP, TabM, GBDTs) and saving all the oofs from all the trials.

what: Applied isotonic regression to OOF predictions before Ridge and after; it helped mid-competition but the final ensemble without it was slightly worse on public LB and much better on private.
why: Inferred: overfit to public LB; no explanation given.
quote: Turns out, my final ensemble without the post-process is only slightly worse on LB and a lot better on PB

what: Generated about 150 OOF prediction sets, then ran 2500 Optuna trials where each trial selects a subset of OOFs to maximise overall OOF AUC; only about one tenth were consistently chosen.
why: Averaging everything hurt; selection matters as much as generation.
when: Large pools of OOF predictions from diverse models.
quote: Simply averaging all of them hurt performance, so I used Optuna to search for effective subsets:

what: Combined the selected OOFs with ridge regression (squared-error with L2) rather than AUC-optimised weights, hill climbing or nonlinear stackers.
why: Ridge shrinks weights, handles correlated predictions, and on actual submissions looked more stable than hill climbing at similar CV.
when: Noisy datasets with highly correlated base models.
quote: In my experiments, nonlinear meta-models tended to overfit, while Ridge produced more consistent improvements.

gain: final private 0.95535 vs 0.95534 for the highest-CV submission
what: Submitted ensembles stopped at different stages to study CV vs LB; above CV about 0.95578 the relation broke down, so the final submission was chosen from CV 0.95578-0.95580 rather than the best CV of 0.955865.
why: Beyond a point, CV gains reflect exploiting fold-specific behaviour (split overfitting) and do not transfer.
when: Large ensemble searches on fixed folds where gains are tiny.
quote: But once the CV started going beyond 0.95578+ , the relation clearly became worse

what: Built several parallel feature sets (binning variants, digits, all-categorical strings, frequency, GP features, original-data stats, DVAE latents) and trained models on different combinations purely to diversify OOFs.
why: Different representations give slightly different split structures and errors that the blender can exploit.
when: Tabular ensemble competitions where model diversity pays.
quote: Rather than searching for one optimal feature set, I created multiple representations of the same base features.

what: Discretised numeric features with qcut, equal-width cut, and simple rounding (Age/5, BP/10), alongside the raw values.
why: Grouped values change tree split structure and add diversity.
quote: Different binning schemes produce slightly different split structures, which helps increase diversity.

what: Extracted integer digit positions (units, tens, hundreds) and the first decimal digits of numeric columns as features.
why: Digits can capture hidden structure from how synthetic or rounded data was generated.
when: Synthetic or rounded tabular data (Playground series).
quote: Integer digit positions (units, tens, hundreds, etc.)

what: Converted all base features to strings and fed them as categorical variables (the ALL_CATS feature set) in the best models.
why: Inferred: lets models learn per-value effects of numeric columns that take few distinct values.
when: Low-cardinality numerics in synthetic tabular data.
quote: I also converted all base features into string format and treated them as categorical variables.

what: Added the frequency of each feature value as an extra feature.
why: Rare values can carry signal and frequency complements target encoding.
when: Boosting models on categorical or discretised features.
quote: Rare values can carry useful signal, and frequency encoding often complements target encoding well in boosting models.

what: Used gplearn to automatically generate nonlinear interaction features and trained models on them.
why: Not meant to dominate individually but to give alternative representations that improve ensemble diversity.
when: Tabular ensembles needing diverse feature views.
quote: Using gplearn , I generated nonlinear interaction features automatically.

what: Computed target mean, smoothed mean, weight of evidence and entropy per feature value from the original (pre-synthetic) dataset and attached them to the synthetic rows.
why: Acts as external target encoding with no leakage from the synthetic training labels.
when: Playground competitions generated from a public original dataset.
quote: This can be viewed as a kind of external target encoding

gain: DVAE+ALL_CATS XGBoost CV 0.955426 (slightly below the best single models)
what: Trained a denoising variational autoencoder on the base features and used its latent codes as features for XGBoost.
why: Provides nonlinear representations that add OOF diversity even if single-model CV is not better.
quote: I trained a Denoising Variational Autoencoder on the base features.

what: Models with lower standalone CV, such as RGF (0.95498) and TabICL on 100k subsamples (0.95497), were frequently selected by the subset search.
why: Ensemble contribution depends on complementary errors, not standalone score.
when: Ensemble selection with structurally different learners.
quote: However, some models with slightly lower standalone CV — such as RGF and TabICL — were still selected frequently during ensemble search.

what: After producing OOF, retrained GBDT and RGF models on the full training set with 20 seeds, n_estimators set to 1.25x the average CV best iteration, and averaged predictions, instead of averaging fold models.
why: Models see more data; found better in the author's experiments.
when: Boosted-tree test predictions when training set is larger than test.
quote: I set n_estimators to 1.25 × the average best iteration obtained during CV

trick: Align folds for OOF and blender
what: Used one fixed StratifiedKFold (shuffle, seed 42) for every base model and the ensemble stage, so the meta-model's CV is not contaminated.
why: OOFs are only truly out-of-fold for the split that produced them; a different split lets the meta-model train on rows that influenced the base predictions.
when: Stacking and ensembling with OOF predictions.
quote: When generating OOF predictions and training an ensemble model, the CV splits should be aligned.

what: Used pytabkit RealMLP with HPO classifier plus Optuna searches (space from TabArena) and n_ens=8 internal ensemble members.
why: Felt especially helpful for prediction stability.
when: Tabular MLPs with noisy small gains.
quote: One setting that felt especially helpful for prediction stability was using n_ens=8

what: Soft and hard pseudo labeling, knowledge distillation, very deep GBDTs, high-order interactions, other autoencoders and nonlinear stacking did not improve CV.
why: Author concludes more complexity does not necessarily generalise better; no specific mechanism given.
quote: Pseudo labeling (both soft and hard)

what: Mapped each synthetic MonthlyCharges/TotalCharges to the nearest value in the original IBM dataset (MC_snap, TC_snap) and kept the difference as a separate feature.
why: The snap recovers the true original value; the diff encodes the generator's perturbation magnitude.
when: Synthetic (GAN/generator-based) datasets built from a public original dataset.
quote: Map each synthetic float to its nearest value in the original IBM dataset:

what: Extracted the digit at each decimal position, the 2-digit fractional integer, mod10/mod100, round-number flags, and fractional residuals from common denominators for the raw and snapped numeric columns.
why: Generator rounding/sampling leaves artefacts in the digits that carry class signal.
when: Synthetic tabular data with continuous columns.
quote: Extract the digit at every decimal position:

what: Within each outer CV fold, ran an inner 5-fold loop to compute target encodings for raw categoricals, bigram/trigram combos, binned numerics and snap/anchor keys.
why: Prevents label leakage from the encoding into the training rows.
when: Target-encoding features inside CV, especially for stacking.
quote: All target encoding (TE) uses a nested inner 5-fold loop within each outer CV fold to prevent label leakage:

what: Target-encoded not only the mean but also std, min, max, median and several quantiles per group.
why: Inferred: richer description of the target distribution within each category.
quote: TE statistics beyond the mean: std, min, max, median, quantiles (5th, 10th, 45th, 55th, 90th, 95th)

what: Computed churn probability per feature value once from the 7,032-row original IBM dataset and added it as a feature.
why: The original data carries no synthetic-training labels, so there is no leakage.
when: Playground tasks generated from a public original dataset.
quote: churn probability per feature value computed once from the 7,032-row original dataset

what: Built TC_deviation = TotalCharges - tenure*MonthlyCharges, the same on snapped values, plus per-month and ratio features.
why: Captures how far actual total charges deviate from what monthly charge and tenure predict.
when: Features with a known arithmetic relation.
quote: TC_deviation is particularly powerful

what: Binned MonthlyCharges into up to 5,000 quantile bins, converted to strings and target-encoded; this essentially recovers the 1,584 original unique values.
