why: Fine binning acts as an identifier of the original customer archetype.
when: Numeric features with few underlying distinct values.
quote: Quantile bins (up to 5,000 bins)

what: Computed frequency encodings of snapped values and ratios of synthetic_count / original_count (or log1p of train_freq/orig_freq) per value.
why: Measures how much the generator over- or under-sampled each original value.
when: Synthetic data derived from an original dataset.
quote: Count ratio features ( synthetic_count / original_count ) measure how much the generator oversampled each value.

what: Built a cKDTree on standardized (MonthlyCharges, TotalCharges, tenure) of original rows; for each synthetic row, attached the nearest original customer's churn label as a feature.
why: Gives a noise-free anchor from the original data with no leakage.
when: Synthetic datasets with an available original.
quote: find the nearest original customer and attach their churn label as a feature.

what: Encoded a (snapped continuous value, categorical code) pair as a single integer, e.g. int(MC_snap*100) + cat_code*100000.
why: A single tree split on the integer equals splitting on both attributes at once.
when: Tree models needing numeric x categorical interactions.
quote: Encodes a (continuous, categorical) pair as a single integer category.

what: Added TF-IDF character n-grams of the string form of numeric columns, Benford's-law leading-digit deviation, and counts of integer-like, quarter-like and half-like values.
why: Generator artefacts show up as repeating decimal patterns and abnormal digit distributions.
quote: the deviation itself is a feature

what: Trained a separate model on the original rows to predict each feature column from all others; its PRED_* outputs on synthetic rows measure consistency with the original distribution.
why: Encodes how typical each synthetic row is relative to the true data.
when: Synthetic tabular data with an original dataset.
quote: Train a separate model on the original 7,032 IBM rows to predict each feature column from all others

trick: Denoising AE fitted on original only
gain: best variant 0.918345 OOF AUC, matching the best single models
what: Trained a denoising autoencoder only on the original rows (Gaussian-noise corrupted), then used its reconstruction errors and latent embeddings on the synthetic rows as XGBoost features.
why: Measures each synthetic row's deviation from the true data manifold.
when: Synthetic data with a clean original dataset.
quote: trained exclusively on the 7,032-row original IBM dataset to reconstruct input features corrupted with Gaussian noise

what: Fit PCA (12 components) and Gaussian random projection (12) on the original data and projected synthetic rows into that space, plus sin/cos tenure features.
why: Gives the model geometric information on how rows relate to the true data manifold.
when: Synthetic data derived from an original dataset.
quote: Fit PCA (12 components) and Gaussian Random Projection (12 components) on the original IBM data

trick: Original rows added to NN folds
what: A residual MLP augmented each training fold with the original IBM rows so the model sees ground-truth archetypes alongside synthetic examples.
why: Inferred: original rows are clean labelled data from the same underlying distribution.
when: Training on synthetic data with an available original.
quote: uniquely augments each training fold with the original IBM rows

what: Used max_bin=16,000 for XGBoost on digit-position features.
why: Allows fine-grained splits on decimal artefacts.
when: Trees on near-continuous features carrying fine-grained signal.
quote: use max_bin=16,000 for fine-grained splits on decimal artifacts

what: Trained an XGBoost model with the rank:pairwise objective instead of binary:logistic and Platt-scaled the output to [0,1].
why: Directly optimises the ordering that ROC AUC measures, also adding diversity.
quote: Uses rank:pairwise instead of binary:logistic , directly optimizing the ordering that ROC AUC measures

what: Pre-computed numeric pair interactions (a_bin * 9 + b_bin) as input for CatBoost and passed raw categoricals natively.
why: Symmetric (oblivious) trees cannot chain splits to approximate interactions, so they must be explicit; native ordered target statistics replace manual TE.
quote: cannot chain splits to approximate interactions

trick: Depth-2 YDF and cuML RF for diversity
what: Added ultra-shallow Yggdrasil forests (max_depth=2) and GPU random forests (bagging) to a boosting-dominated stack.
why: Their prediction surfaces are almost orthogonal to deep boosted trees, which adds ensemble diversity.
when: Large stacks where diversity is the goal.
quote: Its value is purely ensemble diversity.

what: Built a k=8 KNN graph over rows (cuML KNN) and trained a two-layer GraphSAGE so each row's prediction uses its neighbours' features.
why: Structural inductive bias unavailable to MLPs.
when: Tabular tasks where similar rows share outcomes.
quote: a KNN graph (k=8, built via cuML GPU-accelerated KNN)

what: Level 1 produces row-aggregating features (KNN, TE, DAE, PCA); level 2 and 3 are GBDT/NN models trained on 5x5 nested OOF of the previous level; level 4 is a logistic regression on level 2 and 3 OOFs.
why: Stacked models learn from earlier models' OOF predictions, so information from other rows is injected without leakage.
when: Playground tabular competitions with no inference limit.
quote: The second level is many GBDT and NN using 5x5 nested OOF from level 1.

what: Built 850 diverse candidate models (hundreds of FE variants, 4 GBDT libraries, 25 NN architectures) and selected about 150 for the final stack.
why: Diversity plus selection is credited as the secret sauce.
when: Tasks with large compute and no inference cap.
quote: the secret sauce involved creating 850 diverse potential models to select a final 150 models from.

trick: Logistic regression stack over hill climbing
what: Final meta-learner is an L2-penalised GPU logistic regression on logits of all OOFs; the author found Log Reg or Ridge beats hill climbing lately and uses all OOFs, with greedy forward selection only for analysis.
why: L2 prevents any single model dominating and handles correlated models.
quote: Lately I have observed that using Log Reg or Ridge performs better than HC.

trick: LLM agents run EDA and propose features
what: Prompted GPT, Gemini and Claude to do their own multi-round EDA on the relationship between the 600k synthetic rows, 7k original rows and targets, then to write feature and model code from the findings; ideas were circulated between LLMs for improvement.
why: The LLMs discovered patterns the author missed; about half of the ideas came from asking for a model not already in the ensemble.
when: Any new tabular dataset with unknown quirks.
quote: Then they used their discoveries to create many new feature engineering ideas to extract signal.

what: Ported preprocessing, feature engineering and training of every model to GPU (cuDF/cuML) on 4xA100, so most models train in under an hour.
why: Allows hundreds of experiments in a month.
quote: I convert every model's ETL (preprocess and feature engineering) and model training to GPU.

what: TabPFN v2.6 had to subsample to 5k-10k rows per estimator, with 32 estimators at 10k beating 64 at 5k (0.9134 vs 0.9127), staying below full-data models.
why: Context-length limits.
when: TabPFN on datasets with hundreds of thousands of rows.
quote: must subsample to 5k–10k rows per estimator due to context-length limits

what: A denoising autoencoder pre-trained on train+test with swap and Gaussian noise, then fine-tuned with a classification head, could not exceed 0.915.
why: No explanation beyond saturation of the supervised phase.
quote: the supervised fine-tuning phase could not exceed 0.915 despite the pre-training advantage

gain: CV 0.9805 for XGBoost and RealMLP each
what: Replaced a 3-class model with Low-vs-Rest on all data and Medium-vs-High on only Medium/High rows (OOF produced for all rows), combined into class probabilities by multiplication.
why: Models almost never confuse Low and High, so the hierarchy fits the data structure better than a flat multiclass.
when: Ordinal/hierarchical multiclass where extreme classes are well separated.
quote: models almost never confuse Low and High classes

trick: Second stage OOF on all rows
what: Trained the Medium-vs-High classifier only on Medium and High samples, but generated OOF predictions for the whole dataset.
why: Inferred: the combined probability formula needs the second prediction for every row.
quote: Only Medium and High classes were used for training, but OOF predictions were generated for the whole dataset.

what: Compared training the second classifier on true Medium/High labels versus on rows predicted by the first model, and chose the latter.
why: Inferred: training on predicted subset matches inference-time distribution.
quote: I considered two options: train the second binary classifier on true Medium and High labels or on predicted by the first model.

what: P(Low)=p1, P(Medium)=(1-p1)(1-p2), P(High)=(1-p1)p2 to convert two binary outputs to class probabilities.
why: Gives a proper 3-class distribution for ranking/threshold tuning.
quote: Conversion to class probabilities was done by formulas

what: Applied the same two-binary decomposition when blending model probabilities.
why: Inferred: keeps the blending aligned with the structure.
quote: I applied same scheme with 2 binary classifiers for probabilities blending.

what: Blended OOF predictions by logit transform followed by LogisticRegressionCV on 5 folds, with all OOFs on the same 5-fold split.
why: Inferred: logit-space linear stacking is robust.
quote: Blending was made with transform to logits + LogisticRegressionCV on 5 folds.

what: Used two greedy threshold selection algorithms optimizing OOF balanced accuracy for final class decisions.
why: Balanced accuracy needs class-specific cutoffs after ranking.
when: Imbalanced multiclass with balanced accuracy metric.
quote: both are greedy selection based on OOF balanced accuracy

what: Ensembled 61 OOF sets, mostly from public notebooks with different FE, re-running models when a notebook had one model.
why: Diversity from different FE pipelines.
quote: I used OOF predictions from public notebooks with different FE for ensembling.

what: Ensured every OOF used 5-fold CV before stacking.
why: Mixed fold schemes make stacking unreliable.
quote: I also ensured that all OOF predictions were obtained on 5 folds cv.

what: Chose two final submissions with different predicted High-class counts on test.
why: Many submissions had similar CV; the High count was the key difference and hedging worked.
when: Tight leaderboard with imbalanced classes and two selectable submissions.
quote: I chose 2 subs with different High class predictions count on test and one of them worked well on private set.

what: After an adversarial-AUC per-variable check showed Driver differed most between original and competition data, trained some models without Driver (Driver_Dropped) and some without original data.
why: Original and synthetic competition data differed significantly; removing the shifted feature reduces mismatch.
when: Playground/synthetic data augmented with the original dataset where there is distribution shift.
quote: showed the adversarial AUC for each variable

what: Modulated the influence of the original dataset via sample weights; 0.5 to 1 gave about the same score, 0.25 reduced CV and LB.
why: Original data helps but differs from the synthetic data.
when: Mixing original and synthetic training sets.
quote: I also played around with modulating the impact of the original via sample weights

what: Built a pool of 186 OOF prediction sets from diverse models (XGB, LGBM, CatBoost, RealMLP, TabM, FT-Transformer, AutoML libraries, etc.) and fed them to ensemblers.
why: Inferred: with a large diverse pool, individual hyperparameters matter less and the stacker finds complementary signal.
when: Tabular playground competitions with many cheap models.
quote: I couldn't reach my goal of 200 OOFs, ending up with 186

what: Tried many ensemblers (Ridge, LR on logits, GBMs, MLPs, AutoGluon); AutoGluon was best, logistic regression on logits close behind.
why: Inferred: logit-space linear blending is a robust stacker for hundreds of correlated OOFs.
quote: Autogluon was the best overall, followed closely by LR with Logits.

what: Final submission was a 50-50 blend of AutoGluon and LR-logits ensembler outputs.
why: Two strong ensemblers have different errors.
when: Final-stage squeezing at the top of a tight leaderboard.
quote: A blend of two strong ensemblers often does better than both

what: Added 4 level-2 (stacked) OOFs to the pool of level-1 OOFs; kept one submission without them as a leakage hedge.
why: Gain at risk of leakage, so a leak-free alternative was kept.
when: Late-stage stacking when leakage risk is acceptable.

why: Hedge between two final submission slots.

quote: so I decided to keep one submission free of this

what: Deliberately avoided LB probing, suspecting some competitors overfit the public LB.

what: Several notebooks with 200-400 engineered features, plus reuse of others' features.

what: Transplanted features and hyperparameters between well performing models to create new diverse OOFs.

what: Built 30-100+ models across GBDTs, RealMLP, TabM, ET, HGB, RF, YDF, FT-Transformer, TabNet and AutoML libraries (Autogluon, LightAutoML, FLAML, PyTabKit), with Claude Code used to add models quickly.

what: Several notebooks with 200-400 engineered features, plus reused features from others.

what: Did not choose the best-LB submission formed by voting over 3 submissions.
why: Judged it a lucky combination from a few extra rare-class cases.
quote: I decided that it was just a lucky combination

what: A new ensemble member can come from new features, borrowed public hyperparameters, or small tweaks instead of per-model HPO.
why: With a big ensemble HP optimisation matters less.
quote: The bigger your ensemble, the less important it becomes to optimize HP.

gain: 380-model ensemble reached around 10th place on public LB in 4 days
what: A single autorun coding agent read the competition, downloaded data and built a diverse ensemble, recomputing ensemble CV and submitting to the leaderboard itself after each batch of 10-50 models.
why: Big diverse ensembles are a strong playground strategy and an agent can run it unattended.
quote: Every time it added another 10-50 group of models, it would compute new ensemble CV score and submit to Kaggle LB by itself.

gain: Single RealMLP CV 0.97070 / LB 0.97174; single XGB CV 0.97020
what: Two frontier agents from different vendors were each told to build the best single NN and best single XGB; when one lagged, tips from the leader were shared with the trailing agent.
why: Competition plus occasional cross-pollination keeps both improving.
quote: When one was lagging, we would share tips from the leading agent to the trailing agent and soon the trailing agent would take the lead!

trick: Focus on one strong single model
what: Agents studied where the single model made mistakes and added features or tweaks for each failure; a single model beat the 380-model ensemble, and the final ensemble added only about 0.0003.
why: Author argues error-driven single-model improvement and diverse ensembling both address the errors of existing models.
quote: They continually studied the single model and analyzed where it made mistakes

gain: +0.0035 from basic FE, +0.0006 tuning, +0.0006 advanced features (CV)
what: Used stock PyTabKit RealMLP_TD_Classifier, no custom architecture: raw features CV 0.9660, basic feature engineering 0.9695, then tuning and advanced features about +6e-4 each.
why: Author's decomposition of where the gain came from.
when: Tabular classification with a strong NN baseline.
quote: Using raw features RealMLP had CV 0.9660 then some basic feature engineering (similar to previous comps) improved this to CV 0.9695.

what: Had an agent build a tar.gz packet and a prompt, manually uploaded multiple packets in parallel to ChatGPT Pro (each working about 2 hours) and fed the returned ZIP of discoveries back to the agents.
why: Extra parallel reasoning produced new tabular feature engineering ideas that improved best single model CV and LB.
when: When a stronger offline reasoning model can only be used by hand.
quote: we asked Fable to build a tar.gz packet and write a prompt that we (humans) can (manually) upload to ChatGPT Pro

what: Asked the lead agent to assess the data science skill of about six different LLMs from a hub, then assign each multiple jobs to improve ensemble CV and LB.
why: Model diversity of the workers, as in a prior competition where a variety of LLMs worked well.
when: Large agent swarms with many available models.
quote: we asked Fable 5 to interview new LLMs from NVIDIA Inference Hub's roughly 150 potential LLM and then enlist them to help us.

what: Ran agents from scratch, with some clues, and with all public and domain knowledge, plus hybrid starter folders with partial info, and added all resulting models to the ensemble.
why: Like human teams working independently first, uninformed agents give more diverse models.
quote: And let it try from nothing. Then i give it some clues and it tries again.

what: Every agent continually writes markdown logs of what it did and learned; when one plateaued, another agent read its logs and advised what to tell it.
why: Records let a different model diagnose a plateau; the unstuck agent then built a better single model.
quote: Every agent needs to continually write MD files logs of what it is doing and what it did.

what: Train models on (target-target_shift2)/installed_capacity and target/installed_capacity instead of the raw target.
why: Normalization helps large-capacity counties like county 0 which are hard to predict.
when: Panel forecasting with entities of very different scale
quote: Normalized by installed_capacity helps a bit.

what: Gave up chasing public LB with more models; retrained fewer models every month on new data during the forecasting phase.
why: Private LB covers 8 extra months, so adapting to new data matters.
when: Time-series competitions with rolling private test
quote: So I just gave up chasing higher public leaderboard score by ensembling with more models and decided to retrain less models every month.

what: Train on first 500 days, hold out the remaining days; only check final overall score, not single-model scores.
why: Gave good indication of leaderboard score.
quote: train on first 500 days and set the rest days as my holdout validation set which has good indication with leaderboard score.

gain: NN adds about 0.9 to final score
what: GRU over 24 hourly steps with 600 dense features plus embeddings of county, product_type, hour, month, weekday, day, outputting 24 hours; blended with XGBoost.
why: Few teams used NNs; blend gives diversity.
quote: NN models boost my final score by 0.9.

what: fw_new_feature = installed_capacity * forecast solar radiation / (temperature+273.15).
why: Inferred: approximates solar production physics.
quote: fw_new_feature from this discussion help a bit(about 0.1~0.2)

trick: Separate XGB models per target and is_consumption
what: Four XGBoost models for two target definitions and two is_consumption values, sharing 600 features.
why: Inferred: different target definitions complement each other.
quote: My final solution consists of 4 XGBoost models (for two targets and two is_consumption) and 2 GRU models (for two targets).

trick: Failed: splitting by is_business, CNN, transformer
what: Splitting models by is_business, 1D-CNN, transformer, multi-day GRU input and solar features did not help.
why: Author: no strong connection among counties so transformer does not help.
quote: split into more models given is_business equals 0/1.

what: Replaced pairwise similar/non-similar classifiers with embedding models (SupCon, nextvit_small) trained per modality, retrieving candidate pairs via nearest neighbours.
why: Embeddings scale to huge sets and maximize separation between similar and dissimilar samples.
quote: Switching from classification to embedding models for western blots improved the score by +0.017

what: Trained a YOLO lane detector (3,732 hand-annotated images), ran it on about 6M blots (27M boxes), and trained lane-level duplicate embeddings.
why: Each individual lane should be unique, revealing duplications panel-level matching misses.
when: Detecting partial reuse of sub-regions with repeated structure.
quote: each individual lane within a blot should be unique as well

trick: Whole-panel mask if most lanes match
what: If more than 50% of a panel's lanes are matched, use the entire panel bounding box in the mask instead of individual segments.
why: Inferred: ground-truth masks cover whole duplicated panels.
quote: If more than 50% of lanes in a panel are matched, use the entire panel bounding box in the mask

trick: Build own mass dataset from PubMed
what: Downloaded about 2 million PubMed Central archives (~14 TB) with open licenses, extracted figures, detected panels and deduplicated into millions of unlabeled blot/microscopy images for embedding training.
why: Embedding models need large in-domain data with one image per identity.
when: Self-supervised/metric learning where the domain is publicly scraped.
quote: By mid-December, I had collected ~2 million .tar.gz archives (~14 TB)

what: BioFors had mislabeled pairs, so re-annotated all positive pairs and as many negatives as possible.
why: Reliable progress needs clean validation.
quote: without a clean validation set, it was nearly impossible to make reliable progress

what: InfoNCE replaced by SupCon with temperature 0.07-0.09 and the largest batch size that fits; N images plus one augmentation each give N positive pairs.
why: Other metric learning losses consistently underperformed.
quote: using a temperature between 0.07 and 0.09 and the largest batch size permitted by GPU memory

what: Synthetic artifacts (letters, boxes, zoom callouts, arrows, lines) and CoarseDropout to simulate inpainting and copy-paste, plus inversion, CLAHE, grayscale for blots.
why: Reflect real failure cases.
quote: along with CoarseDropout (inspired by real inpainting and cell copy-paste examples that my model struggled to handle correctly)

what: For overlap embeddings, cropped two views sharing at least one lane using lane-detector boxes, restricting crops to gaps between black lanes.
why: Simulates overlap and zoom cases realistically.
quote: The cropping process was then restricted to the green-highlighted regions shown below, corresponding to the gaps between black lanes in the western blot image

what: Clustered microscopy images and manually labeled clusters as suitable or unsuitable for overlap/zoom cropping.
why: Not all images permit valid overlap crops.
quote: I clustered the dataset and manually labeled the clusters into two categories: suitable for cropping and not suitable.

what: When no match is found, fall back to the best public segmentation kernel, constrained by blot/microscopy masks.
why: Covers forgery types the pipeline misses.
quote: If no matches were found, fall back to the best available public Kaggle segmentation kernel, constrained by Blot/Microscopy masks.

what: Focused on western blots and microscopy/macroscopy and deprioritized rarer types based on literature prevalence.
why: Time investment follows expected test composition.
quote: I focused on two categories (western blots and microscopy/macroscopy images) and deprioritized the rest

what: Separate embedding models and augmentations for blots and microscopy.
why: Different visual statistics and duplication patterns.
quote: Training separate models for western blots and microscopy/macroscopy images, with domain-specific augmentations.

what: Reannotated organizer YOLO panel data and added hard failure cases and sampled unlabeled images; YOLO12x trained, plus a multiscale ensemble.
why: Organizer detector had missed detections, false positives and inconsistent labels.
quote: I reannotated the dataset to correct inaccurate bounding boxes and labeling errors

trick: SIFT for microscopy, ALIKED for blots
what: LightGlue with SIFT plus RANSAC for microscopy; ALIKED with MAGSAC (Glue Factory trained) for blots.
why: SIFT beat modern alternatives on microscopy but failed on blots; ALIKED cut inference from ~2.5 h to ~20 min.
quote: this significantly accelerated inference (from ~2.5 hours to ~20 minutes)

what: For blots, every embedding candidate is kept for mask generation even without keypoint matches.
why: Inferred: keypoints are unreliable on blots, embeddings are trusted.
quote: For western blots, all candidates were retained for mask generation, even when no keypoints were matched.

what: Adding a body-imaging class gave a small public LB gain but did worse on private than the submission without it; used in one of two final submissions.
why: Public gain did not generalize.
quote: However, on the private leaderboard, it performed worse than the 0.450 submission that did not include body imaging panels

what: Formulated wellbore TVT prediction as a 2D alignment between horizontal-well positions and typewell positions, trained a U-Net with cross-entropy on a probability map over the alignment grid.
why: Inferred: classification over alignments handles multi-modal ambiguity better than direct regression.
when: Sequence-to-reference alignment or curve matching problems.
quote: I formulate the problem as a 2D alignment task and use cross-entropy loss as the main objective.

what: Target is an exponentially smoothed probability distribution centred on the ground-truth alignment, normalised along the typewell dimension.
why: Inferred: soft targets give graded credit to near misses.
quote: The training target is an exponentially smoothed probability distribution centered around the ground-truth alignment

what: Added Huber loss on the expected TVT path computed from the predicted probability map, and a GR penalty loss mean(probability x grid GR gap).
why: Expected-path loss ties the map to the metric; GR penalty gave a small extra improvement.
when: Probability-map outputs scored on a decoded value.
quote: mean(probability × grid_GR_gap)

what: Replaced LayerNorm with BatchNorm in the pretrained ConvNeXt backbone of the U-Net, training in BF16 to avoid NaN losses.
why: Consistently worked better empirically.
when: Dense prediction on small datasets with pretrained ConvNeXt.
quote: Replacing LayerNorm in ConvNeXt with BatchNorm consistently works better, although BF16 training is required to avoid NaN losses.

what: Used simple average pooling and interpolation for downsampling and upsampling in the U-Net.
why: Performed better than learnable alternatives.
quote: simple average pooling + interpolation performs better than learnable alternatives

what: Calibrated typewell GR with the visible region by aggregating (TVT, GR) into TVT bins, interpolating to the typewell axis and blending with the original GR.
why: Inferred: aligns reference curve with the actual well's tool response.
when: Matching a well log to a reference log.
quote: Typewell GR is calibrated using the visible region by aggregating (TVT, GR) into TVT bins, interpolating back to the typewell axis, and blending with the original GR values.

trick: Particle filter with rare large jumps
gain: PF features cut CV RMSE from 7.7 to 6.7 early on
what: Improved the public particle-filter baseline by allowing low-probability large jumps, calibrated typewell GR, FFBSi smoothing, blending diverse config profiles and updating particles in 64-sample bins; used as input channels.
why: Handles faults and discontinuities; standalone CV about 7.4 RMSE.
quote: Allowing low-probability large jumps

what: When particle-filter channels are present, feed accumulated TVT rather than only TVT differences.
why: PF channels already contain accumulated TVT information.
when: Using filter outputs as CNN features.
quote: using accumulated TVT performs better than using only TVT differences

gain: Local CV improved about 0.3 RMSE, standalone 11.4 RMSE
what: Assuming the geological surface S = TVT + Z + C is locally linear, predict dTVT = a dX + b dY - dZ with (a,b) estimated by weighted least squares from XY-neighbouring wells; fed as channels.
why: Neighbouring wells share the same geological surface.
when: Spatially correlated targets with geometric structure.
quote: ΔTVT = aΔX + bΔY − ΔZ

trick: Trust CV over LB with diagnostics
what: XY-neighbour features improved local CV but hurt public LB; the author checked neighbourhood quality statistics (distances, weight ratios, cosine correlation) and found none explained it, so attributed it to inconsistent labels and trusted local CV. The model won after a private shake-up.
why: Diagnostics found no systematic cause of the LB drop.
when: CV/LB disagreement with a small public set.
quote: Therefore, I attribute the discrepancy to inconsistent labels and chose to trust the local CV

what: For about 10% of wells without reliable XY-neighbour information (detected with neighbourhood quality statistics vs training distribution), use a separate weight set with models lacking XY channels and with z_diff instead.
why: XY-based predictions are unreliable when neighbours are far or poor.
when: Ensembles with features whose reliability varies per sample.
quote: I use models without XY-neighbor channels and include the z_diff channel instead

what: Sample a new TVT path with TVT + Z unchanged using block bootstrap on real TVT differences, regenerate GR by matching the typewell with smoothed-noise TVT, and simulate rare fault jumps.
why: Creates physically consistent new training wells; judged one of the two most important augmentations.
when: Domain-simulatable sequence data with small training set.
quote: Randomly sample a TVT path while keeping TVT + Z unchanged.

what: Apply GR' = a x GR + b to the typewell GR.
why: Forces the model to rely on curve shape more than absolute values.
quote: forcing the model to rely more on shape than absolute values

what: Rotate or shift particle-filter channels during training, along with reverse path, MD stretching, channel masking, tail cropping and sequential masking along the typewell axis.
why: Reduces shortcut learning from the PF input.
when: Stacked models where one input is a strong pre-computed prediction.
quote: PF rotate/shift (corrupt PF channels to reduce shortcut learning)

what: Most code, including the particle filter in an unfamiliar area, was written with Codex using GPT-5.5/5.6.
why: Lets the author implement domain methods quickly.
quote: Most of the code was written with Codex using GPT-5.5/5.6.

what: Transformer-based backbones were tried; CNNs consistently performed better and only ConvNeXt made the final solution.
why: No reason given.
quote: CNN-based backbones consistently performed better

what: Training simulated/augmented and real data jointly beat first pretraining on simulation then fine-tuning.
why: No reason given.
quote: Training with simulated/augmented data and real data jointly worked better for me than a two-stage approach

what: Split localisation into a 3D ConvNeXt predicting the instance (slice) number per level, then a 2D model predicting x,y on the median predicted slice, producing test coordinate labels that the severity stage crops around.
why: Inferred: reduces a 3D localisation problem into two easier sub-problems and gives labelled crops for test data where coordinates are not provided.
when: Medical volumes where test lacks keypoint labels
quote: I separated 1st stage into instance_number prediction and coordinate prediction.

trick: Dual cls+reg heads for slice index
what: Slice-depth model trained with both a classification head (32 logits per level, cross entropy) and a regression head (L1 on normalised z), with x,y regression as auxiliary loss; the two predictions are combined by per-level median.
why: Inferred: the two formulations make different errors; median fuses them.
quote: I ensembled this 2 type of predictions using median for each level

what: Pretrained the coordinate-prediction models on a public coordinate dataset before fine-tuning; slightly better than ImageNet weights.
why: Task-specific pretraining on related labels beats generic ImageNet init.
when: Small medical datasets with a related public labelled set
quote: These pretrained models were slightly better than pretrained models that were trained using imagenet.

what: Severity models see only asymmetric crops around predicted coordinates (e.g. 96 px left/32 right, 40 up/down for sagittal; axial crops chosen per condition and side) on 5 stacked slices, instead of the whole image.
why: Inferred: removes irrelevant anatomy and lets the CNN focus at higher effective resolution.
quote: My preprocessing strategy is cropping.

trick: Randomly pick left/right crop with jitter
what: For axial crops, randomly choose the left or right subarticular stenosis coordinate and jitter its x by +-20 px.
why: Inferred: augments crop placement and equalises sides.
quote: I picked up left or right subarticular stenosis coordinate randomly, and for adjusting cropping point, I added +-20 to ss coordinate x.

what: Randomly shift the instance_number (-2..+2) and coordinates (+-10 px) before cropping, with shift probability set from the empirical error distribution of the instance-number models.
why: Makes stage-2 robust to stage-1 prediction errors at test time.
when: Cascaded pipelines where stage 1 errors propagate
quote: Especially, random shift of instance_number was crucial for robustness of error of 1st stage.

gain: public LB 0.37 -> 0.35 with attention MIL; 0.35 -> 0.33 with bi-LSTM, aux losses, ensembling
what: Per-slice CNN features go through a 2-layer bi-LSTM, then attention-based multiple-instance pooling over slices to give the severity logits.
why: Learns which slices matter and lets context flow between slices.
quote: After implementing Attention-based MIL, my public LB score was improved from 0.37 -> 0.35.

what: A second attention head on the LSTM outputs, fed directly into cross entropy over slice position (the annotated instance), used as auxiliary loss.
why: Author: adds context about which slice annotators focused on into the LSTM features, helping the main attention layer.
quote: I wanted to incorporate the context of which slice the annotators were focusing on into the feature vectors output by the LSTM.

what: Found ConvNeXt-small beat base and large, CNNs beat ViTs, and short training (7 epochs ConvNeXt-s, 14 EffNetV2-s) beat longer.
why: Inferred: small noisy dataset overfits with larger models.
quote: large models (convnext-large < convnext-base < convnext-small in my experiments)

what: Replacing the bi-LSTM with Mamba or self-attention did not help; sharing weights between attention and aux-attention layers also hurt.
why: Not explained.
quote: MAMBA and Self-Attention instead of bi-LSTM

what: A 1mm isotropic coarse nnU-Net scans the full volume, DBSCAN removes scattered false positives, the largest cluster centroid defines a 140mm ROI, and high-resolution models run only inside it.
why: Faster and more memory-stable, lets the detailed models focus on the relevant region.
when: Large 3D medical volumes with small targets.
quote: A fast, low-resolution model first scans the entire volume to find a candidate region.

gain: 0.794 without pretraining vs 0.902 with (96x192x192 ablation score)
what: Used the vessel-segmentation nnU-Net as the backbone of the 3D classifier, rather than timm 2.5D/3D backbones, and removed the last decoder block.
why: Faster to train and more accurate; pretraining was the most important factor in the ablation.
when: 3D medical classification where a segmentation task is available.
quote: Pretraining the backbone on the vessel segmentation task was the most important factor.

what: Pool decoder features under each of 13 vessel-location masks (from both fine segmenters, concatenated), fuse with global encoder features, and model inter-location relations with a transformer before per-location MLP heads.
why: Gives location-specific predictions from a single backbone pass instead of 14 passes.
when: Multi-label location prediction on volumetric data.
quote: A "Vessel Region-Masked Pooling" layer uses the vessel masks to extract feature vectors corresponding to each of the 13 anatomical locations from the decoder's feature maps.

gain: 0.876 without vs 0.902 with auxiliary loss; all-weights-1.0 gave 0.884
what: Added an auxiliary head reconstructing a binary sphere (radius 5) at each annotated aneurysm location, with weight 1.0 versus 0.1/0.05 on classification losses.
why: Forces the model to learn precise aneurysm localisation; higher classification weights led to overfitting.
when: Weakly localised point labels in detection/classification.
quote: I found that higher weights on the classification losses led to overfitting, so this balance was important.

what: Auxiliary sparse-target loss combines Balanced BCE and Focal-Tversky++.
why: Works for highly sparse targets and avoids the over-confidence of Dice-like losses.
quote: This combination works well for highly sparse targets and helps prevent the over-confidence that can occur with Dice-like losses.

what: Added SkeletonRecall loss (weight 1 and 3) to the fine nnU-Net segmenters.
why: Improves connectivity of thin vessels that standard losses miss; recall matters more than Dice because the mask is used for ROI masking.
quote: The SkeletonRecall loss improves the connectivity of thin vessels, which standard losses might miss.

what: Trained a second fine segmenter with Tversky + CE and SkeletonRecall weight 3 to complement the balanced one; classifier pools masks from both.
why: Prioritising recall catches hard-to-find vessel segments.
when: Segmentation used as a mask for downstream models.
quote: To complement Model 2 by prioritizing recall, making it more sensitive to detecting hard-to-find vessel segments.

trick: No left-right flip on fine models
what: Disabled left-right mirroring augmentation for the fine segmentation models.
why: Preserves anatomical asymmetry.
quote: I disabled left–right mirroring for the fine models (2 and 3) to preserve anatomical asymmetry.

what: Added transforms that simulate low-resolution (thick slice) scans.
why: Makes models robust to scans with thick slices.
quote: I added low-resolution simulation transforms to make the models robust to scans with thick slices.

what: Removed roughly 60 series with orientation anomalies, corrupted DICOM or implausible slice spacing, and filtered slices by majority size/spacing.
why: Inferred: label/geometry noise hurts the segmentation and classifier.
quote: I excluded approximately 60 series due to data quality issues, such as orientation anomalies, corrupted DICOM files, and implausible slice spacing.

what: If segmentation/ROI extraction hits an anomaly, skip the model and output per-class mean OOF probabilities.
why: Avoids catastrophic errors on malformed test series.
when: Hidden-test pipelines that may crash or mis-segment.
quote: it fell back to a set of pre-determined probabilities. For each class, this probability was the mean of the out-of-fold predictions

what: Estimated the correct axis permutation from the relative positions of three coarse vessel groups to fix misoriented scans.
why: Fixed all orientation problems on train, but had no measurable LB effect, probably because test had none.
quote: However, it had no measurable effect on the leaderboard score, likely because the test set did not contain such orientation errors.

what: Treated each of the 14 labels as an independent binary problem with BCE.
why: Helps with severe class imbalance since each location is rare.
quote: This design helps with the severe class imbalance, as positive cases for any single location are very rare.

what: EMA of weights for inference, average of 4 of 5 CV fold models, TTA with left-right flip.
why: Standard stability tricks.
quote: I used the Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of the model weights for inference.

what: A single 3D classifier with auxiliary segmentation/localisation heads detected presence but failed on the 13 locations; the 2-channel mask-conditioned model needed 14 forward passes.
why: Led to the vessel-first two-stage design.
quote: While it could detect the presence of an aneurysm, it failed to predict the 13 specific locations accurately.

what: Find move sequences that only cyclically rotate three pieces and leave everything else unchanged (e.g. a commutator-style 8-move sequence), and solve each cluster with them.
why: Every move disturbs many pieces, so finishing a puzzle needs sequences touching only a few pieces.
when: Permutation puzzles with big, entangled moves (NxNxN cubes, globes).
quote: Remarkably, for both puzzles, there exist sequences of moves that only rotate three pieces and leave the rest unchanged, referred to as 3-rot.

what: Use symmetry to reduce to a few representative piece classes, then run bidirectional search to enumerate the shortest 3-rot for every triple; the longest is 14 moves.
why: Precomputing the optimal 3-rot library makes the final fix-up phase short.
when: Small symmetric clusters in puzzle solving.
quote: a bidirectional search was performed to enumerate all shortest 3-rot for any three elements, with the longest being 14 moves.

what: Only compute 3-rots for a few representative cluster types (diagonal parts of 4x4x4, cross parts of 5x5x5, etc.) and derive the rest by symmetry.
why: Inferred: shrinks the search space dramatically.
quote: taking symmetry into account, it suffices to consider the diagonal parts of a 4x4x4 (1,1)

what: For any three pieces on the globe, BFS finds a move sequence A that places them where the base 3-rot R applies, then the 3-rot is A.R.-A.
why: Conjugating a known 3-cycle moves it onto arbitrary pieces while the other pieces return to place.
when: Puzzles with a known basic commutator.
quote: the 3-rot can be obtained by A.R.-A.

what: Solve special pieces (corners, face and edge centres) first, then use elementary moves so each remaining cluster is an even permutation, then solve each cluster independently with 3-rots.
why: 3-rots are even permutations so they can only solve even-parity clusters.
quote: all 3-rot are even permutations, so the overall permutation must also be even.

what: Bring the puzzle near solved using elementary moves or short sequences, then use the long (8+ move) 3-rots only for the last touches.
why: 3-rots are long, so using many is costly.
when: Minimising solution length with a costly finishing primitive.
quote: it's more efficient to bring the puzzle to a somewhat solved state using elementary moves or short sequences before employing 3-rot for the final touches.

what: When concatenating sequences, cancel the end of A against the beginning of B (e.g. ri then -ri), saving moves.
why: Adjacent inverse moves vanish.
quote: canceling out the end of A with the beginning of B can shorten the overall sequence.

what: Rather than appending a 3-rot at the end, try inserting its equivalent 3-rot B' at every position t of the existing sequence and keep the best insertion.
why: The 3-rot needed at time t may be shorter or cancel more with neighbouring moves.
when: Building solutions incrementally from permutation primitives.
quote: Selecting the appropriate time t can make B' shorter than B or result in more cancellations.

what: Solve the inner 3x3x3 (corners and centres) first with an optimal solver, reusing precomputed solutions across reruns; later 3-rots can still be inserted into that sequence.
why: Gives freedom to insert 3-rots and avoids recomputing optimal solves that change if face moves come later.
when: Large cube puzzles in an iterative-improvement workflow.
quote: we reused precomputed solutions when making improvements to the program and re-running it.

what: For puzzles with allowed wildcards, terminate as soon as the remaining color mismatch is within the wildcard count.
why: Saves moves since an exact solve is not required.
quote: Simply terminated when the remaining color difference is below the specified wildcard.

what: Used simple beam search for the wreath puzzle and spent the effort on cube and globe puzzles which carried more total score.
why: Wreath solutions were already very short and had lower total score.
when: Multi-task competitions with differently weighted subproblems.
quote: it had a lower total score compared to the others, making it a lower priority.

what: Loop of kick (swap two random words or remove a segment and reinsert words at random positions, applied 3 times) followed by local search; keep the result only if the score improves.
why: Kicks escape local optima that pure greedy search gets stuck in.
when: Permutation/combinatorial optimisation with an expensive black-box score.
quote: Once no further improvement is possible, use a "kick" (perturbation) to escape from the local optimum.

what: Local search is a DFS over neighbours (a few words removed and inserted elsewhere); accepts the first improving neighbour, and also recurses into neighbours scoring below a depth-dependent threshold (about best_score*1.1 at low depth, best_score at high depth).
why: Allows temporarily worse intermediate states to find compound improvements.
when: Permutation optimisation where single moves rarely improve.
quote: get_threshold() returns a value like best_score * 1.1 when the depth is small and best_score when the depth is large.

what: A lightweight NN (about 1.3M params, a ConvNet inspired by SE-ResNet) trained online during the search, similar to RL, screens candidate neighbours so the expensive Gemma 9B score is computed for fewer than 1/10 of them.
why: Exact scoring is very costly; the NN excludes sequences that clearly worsen the score before Gemma scores them. Not a Gemma replacement. Pretraining was unnecessary.
when: Search/optimisation with an expensive objective where cheap surrogate learned online can rank candidates.
quote: we first use a lightweight NN to screen for promising neighbors. This allows us to reduce the number of sequences for which we compute the exact score (using Gemma) to below 1/10 of the total.

what: Chose an SE-ResNet-style ConvNet for the surrogate rather than a transformer.
why: Author was less experienced with transformers and felt local word arrangement mattered more than global relationships.
quote: in this competition, how nearby words are arranged seemed to be more important than their global relationships.

what: Implementation adds early termination based on node count limits and more efficient batch score calculation for Gemma.
why: Inferred: bounds search effort per local search and maximises GPU throughput.
quote: Early termination based on node count limits

what: Neighbourhood consists of taking a small number of words out and inserting them elsewhere (block rotation/insertion), a pattern shared by top solutions.
why: Small transformations explore the space without greatly altering the current state; different scores are local minima of the same basin (commenter's view).
quote: make_neighbors() generates all sequences obtained by taking a small number of words out of the sequence and inserting them elsewhere.

what: Constrained even-N solutions to 180 degree rotational symmetry, separating genotype (half the trees) from phenotype (full solution) throughout the GA.
why: Halves degrees of freedom; the GA tended to converge to symmetric solutions anyway.
quote: I constrained solutions with even number of trees to have 180° symmetry and used tesselated seeds (optimizing only the edge).

what: Seed most trees from a predetermined crystal (the perfect dimer), scatter the rest around the edge, and apply GA moves only to edge trees; inner trees move only in relaxation.
why: Dimer is the tightest packing, has a straight edge and is deformable.
quote: In this case we seed most of the trees from a predetermined crystal, and scatter the remaining trees randomly around the edge.

what: Minimise overlap^2 + outside^2 cost with LBFGS (PyTorch version adapted to batches) with CUDA gradients, relaxing 1500 candidates per island each generation.
why: Turns infeasible offspring into local minima so far more moves are accepted.
when: Optimisation with differentiable penalties plus GA.
quote: This is combined with a heavily optimized GPU-based relaxation scheme to find local minima. This allows far more moves to be accepted.

what: Use exact separation distance between tree pairs, precomputed via Minkowski geometry into a 3D (dx, dy, angle) table with trilinear interpolation, as the overlap term.
why: Exact distance is too expensive inline; approximations (convex breakdown, overlap area) did not work.
when: Pairwise collision penalties for fixed shapes.
quote: This lookup table is 3D (relative X,Y,angle), and is used with trilinear interpolation.

what: Islands on a ring; crossover mates are same-island individuals or lower-scoring champions of nearby islands (rule dropped when stalled); stuck or duplicate islands are reset.
why: Allows exchange of genetic material while preventing one solution dominating; lower-scoring only so young islands can mature.
quote: We only allow lower-scoring mates to give young islands time to develop; otherwise they'd quickly be overwritten by more mature solutions.

what: Keep 27 best-by-overlap survivors, then 84 more chosen by overlap but rejecting any too close to already selected, where distance is the minimal per-tree transformation set (Hungarian algorithm, approximated on GPU, up to mirror/90 degree rotation).
why: Maintains population diversity; tournament selection did worse.
quote: we pick the least-overlap individuals that has a genetic diversity over a given threshold to the already selected individuals.

what: Fix square size, search for zero-overlap, then shrink the square for that island when overlap falls below threshold; a final legalize relaxation ends at true zero overlap.
why: Treating size as a cost parameter with a squeeze force failed in the GA (only used in legalize).
quote: For any island of which the overlap falls under a certain threshold, we consider it as having found a valid solution for its current square boundary size.

what: Mutation set includes Twist (rotate trees near a point with angle decaying with distance) and Translate (shift all trees, wrapping at boundaries) besides move/jiggle and region crossover.
why: Twist preserves some continuity.
quote: Twist : rotate trees close to a certain point by a randomly selected angle. The further we are from the point, the less the rotation is applied (to preserve some degree of continuity).

what: Spent about 250 USD on vast.ai for 1000 hours of RTX 5090; used ChatGPT for literature and ideas and Claude models for code.
why: Inferred: heavy GPU search needed.
quote: I spent about $250 on vast.ai, which paid for 1000 hours of RTX 5090 time.

what: Other island connectivity patterns (star, tree, hypercube) did not beat the ring.
why: Not explained.
quote: Other island connectivity patterns, such as star, tree or hypercube

what: Precompute base pair probability matrices with EternaFold, process with conv blocks (optionally SE) and add to attention logits before softmax, one channel per head.
why: Injects secondary-structure prior directly into pairwise attention.
when: Biological sequence tasks with physics-based pair features
quote: Also we add these features with attention values before softmax operation in Self-Attention block.

what: Learnable relative positional bias map per head that depends on sequence length, with start/end tokens added.
why: Test sequences are longer than train; DPB extrapolates better than xPos or ALiBi.
quote: We found Dynamic Positional Bias to be of more use compared to other relative positional encoding methods we tried, such as xPos (rotary positional encoding) and ALiBi.

what: Add special start and end tokens so relative positional bias can see distance from sequence boundaries.
why: Relative bias alone cannot know distance from ends.
quote: so tokens < start > and < end > were added to fix that.

what: Encode the SN_filter flag with a learnable embedding added to sequence embeddings; set to 1 at inference.
why: Model knows data quality in training and is asked for clean predictions at test.
when: Noisy labels with a quality flag
quote: we encoded SN_filter values with a learnable embedding layer and added corresponding embeddings to sequence embeddings.

what: At inference set SN filter value to 1 for all inputs.
why: Inferred: predict as if from the clean subset.
quote: At the inference phase for all inputs we set the SN filter value to be 1 as if they come from a “clean” dataset.

what: Sample batch elements with weight 0.5*clamp_min(log(sn+1.01),0.01).
why: Emphasizes high signal-to-noise data; better than hard subsetting.
when: Noisy labels with a reliability score
quote: elements of each batch were sampled from dataset with the weight = 0.5 * torch.clamp_min(torch.log(sn + 1.01),0.01)

what: After AdamW one-cycle training, ~15 epochs of 500 batches with plain SGD.
why: Author reports it additionally improves performance.
quote: training model with a simple SGD optimizer for ~15 epochs of 500 batches each additionally improves model performance

what: One-cycle schedule pct_start=0.05, lr_max 2.5e-3, AdamW wd 0.05, batch 128, 270 epochs.
why: Standard strong schedule from public notebook.
quote: We used a one-cycle learning rate schedule (pct_start=0.05, lr_max=2.5e-3,) coupled with AdamW optimizer (wd=0.05), and batch size set to 128.

what: Train a model predicting 2A3 from DMS, sequence and BPPM; blend 27/28 averaged 2A3 with 1/28 of that prediction.
why: Inferred: adds small diversity from cross-target conditioning.
quote: (27/28) averaged_2a3 + (1/28) predicted_2a3.

what: Average 27 models: 15 SE-conv, 10 plain conv, 2 trained on length splits.
why: Small architecture and training variations diversify.
quote: We ensembled 15 models with SE-Convolutional block, 10 models with plain Convolutional block

what: Built hamming-distance DBSCAN clusters and tested sequence-identity and length-based splits, found relative ranking matched simple KFold, so used KFold.
why: Stricter splits lower scores but preserve model ranking.
quote: So, we decided to use simple KFold split than training final models

what: Trained on short sequences, validated on longest length; correlated with KFold metric.
why: Checks extrapolation to longer test sequences.
quote: The behavior of the validation metric was slightly noisier but still highly correlated with a metric for a simple KFold split.

what: About 13% of public test sequences appear in train; zeroed predictions for them in most submissions to avoid selecting memorizers.
why: Public LB would otherwise reward memorization.
quote: we zeroed out the predictions for these sequences in most of our submissions

what: Pseudolabeled test with confident ensemble predictions; single model improved but ensemble did not.
why: Added model is redundant to ensemble.
quote: adding such a model to ensemble doesn’t improve ensemble performance.

what: ContraFold, ViennaRNA, RNAstructure, RNA-FM, SQUARNA matrices and averaging BPPMs gave no gain over EternaFold.
why: EternaFold BPPM already captures structure info.
quote: Averaging BPPMs doesn’t result in better performance.

what: Joint training on organizer public datasets gave no boost.
why: No reason given.
quote: Unfortunately, this also gave no boost to the model performance.

what: Convolutional architectures underperformed tuned transformers.
why: Structure prediction needs long-range contacts.
quote: predicting RNA secondary structure requires attending to long-range contacts.

trick: Loss masking of noisy positions failed
what: Masked high-error positions or weighted sequence loss by SN instead of sampling weights; no gain or worse.
why: Sampling by SN was better.
quote: This resulted in poor performance.

what: Instead of averaging, filled the five allowed predictions per target with structurally different models (template-based, Boltz2, RNAPro, DRFold2, Protenix) so at least one lands close to the truth.
why: Scoring takes the best of 5 predictions, so diversity matters more than the average quality of each.
quote: Since scoring is best-of-5, the goal is to maximize structural diversity across the five predictions.

what: Chose how many of the 5 slots each model gets by sequence-length bucket (<250, 250-999, >=1000), tuned empirically per bucket.
why: Models have different strengths and cost by length; template search wins on long sequences, deep models on short ones.
when: Ensembles of heterogeneous models whose quality depends on an input attribute.
quote: Rather than a one-size-fits-all ensemble, we tuned how many predictions each model contributes based on empirical performance at each length range.

what: Ran models in order and let later models overwrite earlier ones' rows in the submission, so each length bucket's composition could be changed incrementally.
why: Makes per-bucket allocation easy to tune and fits the time limit.
when: Multi-model inference pipelines under a runtime cap.
quote: models are run in order and later models overwrite earlier ones

what: Set the 250 nt boundary by trading inference time against score: Boltz2 and DRFold2 only run on short sequences, TBM scales cheaply to long ones, letting five models fit in the 8h limit.
why: Slow models become impractical on long inputs; routing keeps all models inside the time limit.
when: Code competitions with strict time limits and several heavy models.
quote: The 250 nt boundary was selected by balancing inference time against score

what: For sequences >=250 nt gave multiple slots to template-based modeling (global alignment against train+validation structures) and filled the rest with other models.
why: Template modeling is very strong whenever a similar sequence exists in training data.
when: Structure/sequence tasks where near-duplicates of the test items exist in the labelled pool.
quote: allocating multiple predictions to TBM and using other models to cover the remaining predictions was consistently better than the reverse.

what: For sequences <250 nt deliberately avoided TBM as the main predictor and used sequence-only models (Boltz2, DRFold2, Protenix); RNAPro was conditioned on templates but regenerates structure.
why: Template-free diversity helps on private-set targets with no close template.
when: Held-out sets that are harder or less similar to training than the public split.
quote: we deliberately avoided TBM as the primary predictor and instead relied on Boltz2, DRFold2, and Protenix

what: Searched train+validation structures with BioPython PairwiseAligner (global) but only against templates within 30% of the query length, and kept the top 30 as the candidate pool.
why: Inferred: avoids poor alignments with very different-length templates and cuts search cost.
quote: filtering to templates whose length is within 30% of the query length

what: Prediction 1 uses the top template as is; predictions 2-5 sample from the top-12 templates with exponential weighting and a 0.1x weight for already-used templates.
why: Gives different TBM guesses for best-of-5 instead of duplicates.
when: Generating multiple distinct candidates from a ranked retrieval list.
quote: sampled from the top-12 with exponential weighting. Already-used templates receive a 0.1× weight penalty to discourage duplication.

what: Filled alignment gaps by linear interpolation between valid C1' neighbours, extended chain ends in 5.95 Angstrom steps along the extrapolated direction, and used a straight line along X when no template exists.
why: Produces complete, chemically plausible coordinates for every residue.
quote: One-sided gaps (at chain termini) are extended by 5.95 Å steps along the extrapolated direction.

what: Applied bond-length (5.95 A), i->i+2 distance (10.2 A), Laplacian smoothing and steric self-avoidance corrections to each TBM prediction, with strength scaled by (1 - template_similarity).
why: Near-identical templates are already accurate and should barely change; poor matches need more correction.
when: Post-processing template-derived predictions with known geometric priors.
quote: The correction strength scales with (1 − template_similarity) so that near-identical templates are barely modified while low-similarity matches are corrected more aggressively.

what: Ran DRFold2 cfg97 with a number of models scaled down with sequence length (20/10/5), scored each output by bond-length, angle and stacking energies normalised by median absolute deviation, and kept the top-5.
why: Cheap physical plausibility score selects the best structures from many raw predictions; fewer models on long sequences saves time.
when: Picking from many generated candidates when no ground truth is available.
quote: we compute an energy score (bond lengths, bond angles, stacking) and normalize by the median absolute deviation across predictions. The top-5 scoring structures are selected.

what: Fed RNAPro precomputed TBM templates (top-1 for the first prediction, top-2 for the second) with MSA and RibonanzaNet2 embeddings, so each output starts from a different template but is regenerated.
why: Combines template information with refinement while keeping predictions independent and diverse.
when: Template-conditioned generative models with multiple samples allowed.
quote: each conditioned on a different TBM template (top-1 and top-2).

what: Generated 10 diffusion samples per target with Boltz2 and kept the top 5 by combined pLDDT and confidence score.
why: Inferred: confidence scores let you pick the best of a larger pool of stochastic samples.
when: Diffusion/stochastic generative predictors with a confidence head.
quote: Top-5 selected by combined plddt + confidence score

trick: Fold only RNA chains in Boltz2
what: For multi-chain targets only the RNA chains were folded (use_all_chains = False) to avoid OOM with large complexes; ligand SMILES were still passed in the YAML.
why: Memory limit of the 16GB P100.
when: Large complexes on limited GPU memory.
quote: only RNA chains are folded ( use_all_chains = False ) to avoid OOM with large complexes

what: For sequences over 512 nt split into overlapping 512-nt windows (overlap 128), ran Protenix on each chunk independently, extracted C1' atoms, and stitched coordinates into one array with later chunks overwriting overlaps; freed GPU memory after each chunk.
why: Protenix has a per-inference memory limit; chunking lets it produce predictions for >=1000 nt targets where Boltz2 and RNAPro OOM.
when: Long inputs exceeding a structure/sequence model's memory capacity.
quote: sequences longer than MAX_SEQ_LEN = 512 nt are processed with a sliding-window chunking strategy

trick: Skip OOM-prone models on very long targets
what: RNAPro and Boltz2 are skipped for >=1000 nt; that tier uses 3 TBM and 2 Protenix predictions.
why: Avoid out-of-memory crashes that would zero out a submission.
when: Code competitions where one crash ruins the run.
quote: RNApro and Boltz2 skip sequences ≥ 1000 nt (OOM risk), so the ≥ 1000 nt tier uses TBM for 3 predictions and Protenix for the remaining 2.

what: Committed to template-based modeling (sequence alignment against PDB structures, copying coordinates) rather than training or fine-tuning a model, as no GPUs were available.
why: CASP results and literature show TBM dominates; RNA conserves 3D structure more than sequence.
when: Structure prediction with a rich database of related solved structures and small test set.
quote: showed that Template-Based Modeling approaches consistently dominated.

what: Analysed TM-score properties (length-normalised, robust to local errors) and prioritised getting the global fold right over atomic precision.
why: A few misplaced nucleotides do not disproportionately lower the score.
quote: it is robust to local errors - a small number of misplaced nucleotides does not disproportionately lower the score.

what: Re-parsed PDB CIF files that failed an A/U/G/C-only parser using a 93-variant modified-nucleotide mapping and extraction of the selected child of Biopython DisorderedAtom objects, enlarging the template library.
why: Standard parser misses modified residues and crashes on multi-conformation atoms.
quote: My method detects these (via hasattr(atom, 'selected_child') ) and then extracts the selected atom

what: Built template library from all CIF files in the provided PDB_RNA directory (about 18-19k sequences), and retuned aligner parameters as the library grew.
why: Template coverage is the main determinant of TBM quality; a 5k library gave much worse results per a commenter.
quote: as the dataset grew over time, the parameters needed retuning.

what: Ranked templates by composite score: 0.4 global alignment + 0.3 local alignment + 0.2 feature (dinucleotide frequency) similarity + 0.1 k-mer similarity, using Biopython aligner with RNA-tuned gap penalties.
why: Adds sequence composition awareness; using all 16 dinucleotides added noise (0.5895 vs 0.59298 with 10).
quote: composite_score = (

what: In the TBM-only notebook, clustered candidate templates and selected diverse ones to fill the five allowed predictions, treating different conformations of the same sequence as separate templates.
why: Different conformations give different structural information and diversify the five guesses.
when: Best-of-N scoring with multiple allowed submissions.
quote: The clustering step helps ensure the selected templates are diverse.

what: For alignment insertions/deletions, rebuilt backbone keeping about 5.9 Angstrom C1'-C1' spacing: linear interpolation for normal gaps, sinusoidal perpendicular perturbation for compressed gaps, extension along backbone for termini.
why: Keeps the backbone physically plausible where templates lack coordinates.
quote: For compressed gaps: extends the backbone with realistic curvature using sinusoidal perturbations perpendicular to the backbone direction

what: Refinement strength scaled with template confidence: minimal constraints for high-similarity templates, distance and clash/base-pairing constraints for low-confidence ones, with strength 0.8 x (1 - min(confidence, 0.8)).
why: Preserve good template geometry while repairing weak ones.
quote: Constraint strength scales as: 0.8 × (1 - min(confidence, 0.8))

gain: hybrid 0.57773 vs 0.58487 with DRfold2 disabled (no gain at all)
what: Rather than finetune DRfold2, replaced its selection and optimisation modules: float64 scoring, torch.cdist on GPU, pre-computed cubic spline energy coefficients, PyTorch LBFGS with autodiff, plus Boltz-1 integration.
why: Authors reported DRfold2 sometimes failed to select its best model; faster, more accurate optimisation.
when: Using pretrained structure predictors without GPU training budget.
quote: Rather than fine-tuning the model itself, I focused on enhancing its optimization and selection modules.

gain: hybrid scored lower than TBM-only version
what: Used TBM for shorter sequences and when time budget ran out, DRfold2 for the rest, falling back to TBM on DRfold2 failure; used first 14 sorted sequences for TBM rather than a hardcoded length.
why: Template confidence falls for long sequences where DL does better; runtime safety.
quote: Graceful fallback: DRfold2 failures automatically fall back to template approach.

what: Tuned aligner parameters by trial and error using only leaderboard feedback with no offline validation set.
why: Author gave no further reason.
when: Small test sets where local validation is hard.
quote: the parameter settings were determined through trial and error, using the leaderboard score as my only feedback mechanism.

what: Extract 768-d Phikon (ViT-B, iBOT-pretrained on TCGA) embeddings per tile and train only a small MIL head on the (n_patches, 768) bag.
why: Domain-specific pretrained features outperform other backbones and keep training cheap; Phikon beat CTransPath, LUNIT, DinoV2.
when: Whole-slide / large image classification with few labelled slides.
quote: we trained an ensemble of Chowder models on top of Phikon tile embeddings.

what: Use 448x448 patches for 40x TMA images and resize them to 224x224, so cell size matches 20x WSI tiles; a logistic regression on ResNet18 thumbnail features detects TMA at test time.
why: Matching magnification makes performance consistent; Phikon was pretrained at 20x.
quote: Therefore, we set the patch size to 448 x 448 px for TMA; These patches were then resized to 224 x 224 px.

what: Wrote custom C code using libpng's png_read_row to tile huge PNGs to disk without loading the whole image into RAM, compiled inside a Kaggle notebook.
why: Pillow/OpenCV were slow and RAM hungry on giant PNGs.
when: Very large non-pyramidal images under RAM/time limits.
quote: it uses the png_read_row function to limit the amount of data read and loaded into RAM.

trick: Cap patches and parallelise with Ray
what: Randomly sample at most 200 tissue patches per WSI, and process two images at a time on one P100 with Ray processes each given 0.5 GPU and 2 CPU cores.
why: WSIs have over 10,000 patches; this cut runtime from about 10 h to under 7 h; 400 patches gave no gain.
when: Time-limited code competitions with huge inputs.
quote: Ray would spawn two processes, each using 0.5 GPU and 2 CPU cores.

what: Detect tissue with Otsu thresholding on the HSV thumbnail before tiling.
why: Simple and worked well here.
quote: This thresholding was applied to the thumbnail image, in the HSV color space.

what: Chowder: tile-wise MLP (192), ExtremeLayer taking top-10 and bottom-10 tile scores, then MLP (96) with 30% dropout; hyperparameters hand-set.
why: Outperformed DeepMIL, DSMIL, MeanPool and TransMIL, and is interpretable.
when: Multiple instance learning on tile embeddings.
quote: The n_top and n_bottom values of its ExtremeLayer layer were both set to 10.

what: Stratified 5-fold repeated 3 times, each with an inner 75/25 train/val split, designed so each test fold contained at least 60% of TMA; splits at image level.
why: Few TMA in train, so most TMA used for evaluation rather than training.
when: Rare subpopulation that matters for evaluation.
quote: We designed the stratified 5-fold CV to ensure that each test set would contain at least 60% of TMA.

what: Train 50 Chowder models differing only by initialisation as a single ModelEnsemble.
why: Chowder is sensitive to initialisation; the ensemble was more stable and efficient.
when: Initialisation-sensitive small heads on frozen features.
quote: Chowder can be quite sensitive to weight initialization.

what: Average 65 Chowder models from chosen CV repetitions/folds only, calibrate with logistic regression on internal validation predictions, then keep only models that did well on their internal test set.
why: Selecting specific folds beat averaging all 3x5x50 models; calibration slightly improved public LB.
quote: we selected only a subset of the 50 Chowder models in an ensemble based on the performance of the calibrated models on their internal test set (CV).

what: Label a slide as the 'Other' class when the prediction entropy H=-sum(p log p) exceeds a threshold calibrated on the public LB since no outliers were provided.
why: Other class is worth 1/6 of balanced accuracy; high entropy signals unfamiliar data.
when: Open-set classification with an unseen outlier class.
quote: Our strategy to identify outliers raised our public leaderboard score from 0.59 to 0.64

what: Use variance of predictions across the Chowder ensemble members, together with entropy, to flag outliers.
why: Model disagreement indicates out-of-distribution input.
quote: Using the variance of predictions (across models in an ensemble of Chowder) to identify outliers.

what: Use weighted sampling for balanced batches and class weights in cross-entropy simultaneously.
why: Class imbalance.
quote: Weighted sampling to create balanced batches for training,

what: Continue iBOT pretraining of Phikon on 6.5M train-set patches with 4 added register tokens for one epoch (2.5 days on 2 P100); combine Chowders on original and adapted features.
why: Domain adaptation of the foundation model; alone it was slightly worse in CV but the mix scored 0.62/0.67.
when: Foundation model with a distinct target domain and abundant unlabelled patches.
quote: we added 4 register tokens to the ViT-Base.

what: Average Phikon features per slide on grayscale contrast-equalised patches, run UMAP and find 38 slides with about 12x instead of 20x magnification (probably bad PNG conversion).
why: Reveals hidden resolution shifts affecting about 8% of slides.
when: Hidden data-conversion artifacts in image datasets.
quote: noticed that 38 WSI could be told apart from the remaining 500 images.

what: Ray Tune on batch size, epochs, lr and hidden sizes raised local CV but lowered public LB, so they kept hand-picked hyperparameters.
why: Overfitting the train set.
quote: The hyperparameter tuning resulted in an increase of our local CV scores, but in a decrease of our submissions scores on the public LB.

what: Vahadane and Reinhard colour normalisation gave no improvement.
why: Consistent with literature that stain normalisation does not help histopathology classification.
quote: we tried several color normalization schemes (Vahadane, Reinhard) but did not observe any improvement doing so.

what: Trained a patch-level tumor classifier on binarised annotations and predicted Other when tumor-patch fraction was low; no change in score.
why: Idea was to find normal cases; no improvement on public LB.
quote: This idea did not provide any performance improvement on the public LB.

what: Overlapping sliding window (30-80%) to get more TMA patches; runtime exploded with no gain.
why: Timeouts and no score gain.
quote: Increasing the number of patches for TMA using a sliding window (with 30% to 80% overlap between two consecutive patches).

gain: ~0.045 CV, ~0.012 LB for balance features; ~0.005 CV for speed features
what: Ran the Ludii MCTS (UCB1Tuned, random playouts) for about 15 seconds on each game's start position and used its implicit utility estimate as a game-balance feature; also logged search iterations and actions per second.
why: The provided AdvantageP1 comes from random play and does not reflect balance under strong play; a short tree search approximates real play about 250x faster than simulating matches.
when: Simulation-based tasks where a cheap approximate simulator of the label process can run inside inference.
quote: running a tree search for a few seconds on the starting position of each game to compute additional features describing how balanced it is and how quickly the search can be executed

what: Compared MCTS selection/playout settings for the balance feature and picked UCB1Tuned with random playouts, since NST playouts worked worse on leaderboard data than on training data.
why: Only selection and playout strategy mattered; exploration constant and score bounds did not.
when: Choosing which cheap simulator configuration to use for features.
quote: That being said, NST seemed to work worse on the leaderboard data than the training data the competition organizer provided

what: Created 484 new rulesets (391 via his own GAVEL implementation, 93 via few-shot Llama 3.1 70B and Qwen 2.5 32B), annotated with only 4 matches per ordered agent pair, giving 14,365 extra rows.
why: More distinct games help generalisation to unseen games; cheap labels are noisy but still add signal.
when: Small number of distinct entities in train, with a runnable label generator.
quote: I generated a total of 14,365 extra training rows with 484 extra unique rulesets.

what: Down-weighted self-generated noisy rows relative to organiser data, tuning the weight separately per model on CV (CatBoost 0.25, LightGBM 1.0, TabM 0.5).
why: Extra labels were noisier; models differ in sensitivity to the noise. Returns diminished as extra data scaled up.
when: Mixing clean and cheaply generated noisy data.
quote: I mitigated the label noise by weighting the extra training samples less heavily than the ones provided by the competition organizer.

trick: Sample noisy features from repeated runs
what: Computed all tree-search features 10 times per training row and, in each training row, randomly picked from the 9 runs not held out for CV so models saw the feature noise instead of a single duplicated error.
why: Exposes the model to the same noise level it will face at test time.
when: Features produced by a stochastic procedure that is also run at test time.
quote: All of the tree search related features for the training examples were computed 10 times.

what: Recomputed the nondeterministic features in the competition data 5 times to get a less noisy estimate and sampled training values uniformly between that estimate and the provided value.
why: Provided columns such as MovesPerSecond contain random noise.
when: Provided features measured with noise that you can re-measure.
quote: All of the nondeterministic features in the data provided by the competition were recomputed 5 times

trick: Drop features that fail to reproduce
what: Dropped 43 features whose values were deterministic on the author's machine but differed from the organiser-provided values (suspected Ludii version mismatch), all at once.
why: Train-test feature mismatch from different simulator versions; importance filtering did not identify them, and they only helped when dropped together.
when: Features generated by external software you can re-run and compare.
quote: there were 43 features whose values were perfectly consistent from one run to the next when I generated them on my machines, but different from the values provided by the competition organizer.

what: Fit isotonic regression models taking OOF predictions as input as a post-processing step on each GBDT/NN model, replacing the public scale-and-clip trick.
why: Learns a monotone calibration that shrinks extreme predictions inwards (behaves like tanh); tuned scale+clip hurt the leaderboard.
when: Bounded regression targets such as win rate in [-1, 1].
quote: fitting isotonic regression models which use OOF predictions as features and running them as a postprocessing step improved both my CV & LB scores by around 0.002.

gain: difference in the 4th decimal CV; a commenter saw ~0.0005 over linear wx+b
what: Used centered isotonic regression instead of scikit-learn's isotonic regression for most stacks (not CatBoost, due to out-of-bounds crashes).
why: Strict monotonicity probably makes it less prone to overfitting.
when: Calibration or post-processing of regression predictions.
quote: For most base + isotonic model stacks, I used centered isotonic regression , which seemed to score slightly better in cross validation

gain: ~0.001 LB when added to the previous best ensemble
what: Used the new TabM tabular DL model with piecewise linear embeddings for numeric features, wide layers, small batch size and low learning rate (outside the paper's search range); it was the best single model in CV.
why: Embeddings likely explain why it beat a plain MLP; TabM is an efficient implicit ensemble of MLPs.
when: Tabular data with continuous numeric features, to add a diverse NN to a GBDT ensemble.
quote: TabM's piecewise linear embeddings for continuous numerical features seemed to help tremendously.
