what: Switched LightGBM to boosting=dart with tuned dart parameters (drop_rate, max_drop, skip_drop) and n_estimators around 26k, with no early stopping.
why: Not explained; it improved both CV and LB at a 5-10x training cost.
when: Small or noisy tabular data where training time is acceptable.
quote: Setting LightGBM's boosting parameter to dart was critical to getting it working well enough to be useful.

what: Ran Optuna repeatedly per model, widened search ranges whenever the best config sat on a boundary, then re-checked top configs with 10-fold CV and 3 seeds; CV grouped by ruleset name.
why: Lets the data decide the ranges and guards against single-seed luck.
when: Hyperparameter tuning when CV is noisy.
quote: I picked ranges that I thought were reasonable, ran optuna, adjusted my search ranges if the best config optuna found was on the edge of what I specified

what: Each model block is the average of 20 models from 10-fold CV repeated with 2 seeds, instead of refitting on all data, because CatBoost and TabM need early stopping. Ensemble weights tuned on CV with Nelder-Mead.
why: Early-stopped models cannot be trained on all data; averaging fold models uses all the data.
when: Early-stopped models, with inference memory limits.
quote: each of the model blocks show above is actually an ensemble of 20 models, the models trained during 10-fold cross validation repeated for 2 random seeds.

gain: Private 0.4178 vs 0.4190 for the LB-tuned ensemble
what: Ran two final strategies in parallel: ensemble tuned to the public LB versus hyperparameters, augmentation, feature selection and weights tuned to CV; the CV-tuned one won on both public and private LB.
why: CV was more reliable despite weak correlation with the public LB.
when: Code competitions with a small public LB and risk of shakeup.
quote: I really did not expect that in light of how much the public LB seemed to hate ensembles with weights tuned to my CV

what: Swap the two agents and invert the target and balance-related features. The author overlooked it and says other top teams used it, estimating a hybrid could reach ~0.407 private.
why: Doubles data with symmetric pairs; the author had dismissed it because many games are imbalanced and did not think of inverting balance features.
quote: I completely overlooked the flip/inversion data augmentation trick that was used by pretty much all other top teams!

what: Tried the public-notebook trick of multiplying predictions by a constant and clipping to a narrower range, with parameters tuned on CV; it hurt the leaderboard.
why: Parameters tuned on CV did not transfer; isotonic regression did better.
quote: using the scale + clip trick with parameters tuned to my CV did more harm than good on the leaderboard

what: Tried the public-notebook stacking (OOF predictions as features) and many others (TF-IDF/LSA, OpenFE, forward/backward selection, LM balance prediction); none helped.
why: Not explained.
when: Tabular tasks with few distinct entities.
quote: The model stacking approach I saw people using in public notebooks (OOF predictions as features)

what: Packaged tree-search code as a separate jar linking against the Ludii player and ran it inside the inference notebook, splitting 30 GB RAM as 18 for searches and 10 for models.
why: Keeps Ludii unmodified (licence) and fits time and memory limits; the host confirmed a 15-second search is acceptable.
when: Code competitions where external tools can run in the submission.
quote: of the 30 GB RAM, 18 are used for tree searches and 10 are used for the models

what: Treated the final Boolean query as a set of precomputed candidate AND-subqueries joined by OR, and searched the subset with simulated annealing: 50% chance to add an unused subquery, 50% to remove a used one; score is number of targets retrieved.
why: Combinatorial subset selection with a cheap exact objective suits local search.
when: Combinatorial set-cover style optimisation with a verifiable score.
quote: 50% chance to add one unused subquery

what: Built candidate subqueries by adding words (sorted by set size) until the matched patents were only targets; subqueries still matching non-targets were discarded, so the score reduces to counting targets.
why: Guarantees purity so the objective needs only the target count.
when: Query/rule generation where false positives are penalised.
quote: If there are non-targets after combining all the words, that subquery is not a candidate

what: Exploited query syntax so words joined by - omit the AND token, with cpc terms placed last, reducing query length cost.
why: Shorter query per term lets more terms fit under the length limit.
when: Competitions with query-length or token constraints.
quote: By connecting words with -, the AND token can be omitted

what: Kept only one subquery per distinct set of matched targets.
why: Duplicates add search space without new coverage.
quote: subqueries with the same target set do not need multiple candidates

what: Computed set intersections of sorted id arrays with cp.intersect1d on GPU, and processed words in ascending set size.
why: 2-3x faster than Python set intersection, allowing all cpc/title/abstract words on the final day.
quote: On the final day, speeding up with this allowed using all cpc, title, abstract, and the rank improved from 3rd to 1st

trick: Keep only test patents in memory
what: Loaded only the 2500*50 patents in test.csv and their words into memory.
why: Reduces memory enough to use all words.
when: Large corpora where only a subset is relevant.
quote: Reduce memory usage by placing only patents appearing in test.csv (2500*50) and the words those patents possess in memory

what: Deleted words with frequency 100,000 or more for claim and description fields.
why: Inferred: such words rarely help isolate targets and slow computation.
when: Boolean search over large text fields.
quote: Delete words with high frequency (100,000 or more) for claim, description

what: Trained nnU-Net for 4000 epochs with batch size 2 and patch size 128 on all data; authors say long epochs + small batch beats fewer epochs + large batch.
why: Training curve showed an up-surge at the end of long runs, so they kept increasing epochs.
when: 3D segmentation with nnU-Net where compute allows.
quote: long epochs + small batch size performs better than less epochs + large batch size.

what: Fine-tuned the converged 128-patch model with patch sizes 192 and 256 for only 250 epochs each, matching from-scratch 4000-epoch 192-patch models (0.614 vs 0.613 private).
why: Inferred: larger context is acquired cheaply by continuing from converged weights rather than retraining.
quote: We then fine-tuned Model 1 with larger patch sizes of 192 and 256, training for 250 epochs each.

trick: Weighted probability fusion of mixed-patch models
what: 4-model ensemble of models with different patch sizes and training histories, fusing post-softmax probabilities with hand-set weights (0.12/0.28/0.18/0.42).
why: Inferred: diversity via patch size and fine-tune vs from-scratch.
quote: we fused the post-softmax probabilities using the assigned model weights and applied different thresholds and post processing methods

what: Delete connected components of the predicted mask with fewer than 20K voxels.
why: Inferred: removes spurious fragments that hurt the topology-based metrics.
quote: We removed mask components that have less than 20K voxels.

what: For each sheet voxel look at its 2x2x2 neighbourhood and add voxels via a 256-entry lookup table so the neighbourhood is 6-connected watertight, plugging 1-voxel holes (inspired by skimage euler_number).
why: Ordinary dilation plugs holes but adds too many voxels, degrading Dice.
when: Segmentation masks where holes/cavities are penalised.
quote: (Ordinary dilation will also plug holes, but it tends to add too many voxels, which can degrade the dice score.)

what: Represent each sheet as a height map along the axis with largest projected area, linearly interpolate across gaps in x and y separately and average weighted by distance to gap edge; discard the patch if it increases hole count.
why: Repairs large holes that closing cannot; the check avoids introducing holes in strongly curved sheets.
quote: we represented each sheet as a height map, and filled any gaps in the height map by linear interpolation across the gap.

what: Apply scipy binary_closing with spherical radius-3 footprint per sheet, then binary_fill_holes on the whole mask.
why: Closes small holes and cavities which the metric penalises.
quote: Applied scipy.ndimage.binary_closing(), with a spherical footprint of radius 3. This closes holes and cavities of radius 3 or less.

what: With no validation set, varied the binarisation threshold (0.20 and 0.26 for final sets) mainly to use up submission quota; later found larger thresholds (0.35-0.4) were better on local search and private LB.
why: Public LB misled them; they overfit the threshold to public.
when: Small public LB with no local validation.
quote: larger threshold (Like 0.35-0.4 is the best searched value on our model on training set) performs better on private LB

what: Averaging logits generalised better on private LB than the post-softmax probability fusion they trusted from public LB.
why: Inferred: author gives no reason.
quote: logits fusion performs better on private LB, but we trusted (overfitted) on probability fusion

what: Chose nnU-Net over MONAI and public JAX pipelines because it performed better at equal training time.
why: Better under the same training time budget.
quote: other frameworks like MONAI, and public code shared JAX pipelines perform worse than nnUNet under same training time, therefore we focus on nnUNet

what: Instead of resizing the (5,1000,70) seismic input, reshaped it to a single-channel 350x350 image so channels and time form a spatial layout.
why: The task is not segmentation; velocity pixels do not line up with seismic pixels, so a square layout suited to a ViT worked better.
when: Physics or signal inputs whose axes do not align with the output grid.
quote: I reshape the input to (1, 350, 350), basically forcing the channels into a spatial layout.

gain: EVA02-small got close to CV 30 in 40 epochs
what: Used a vision transformer with only a linear head as an image-to-image regressor, skipping UNet-style skip connections.
why: Input and output pixels are not spatially aligned, so skip connections to early layers make little sense.
when: Dense regression where input and target are not spatially aligned.
quote: Vision transformers are secretly segmentation-like regression models:

gain: MAE under 26 on the same training
what: Ablated why EVA02 beat the plain ViT and found rotary positional embeddings were the key factor, then picked vit_small_patch14_reg4_dinov2 with RoPE and better pretrained weights.
why: RoPE explained most of the gain, and the chosen backbone was faster than EVA.
when: Choosing pretrained ViT backbones for non-natural-image regression.
quote: On the same training, ViT+RoPE got me under 26 MAE.

what: Stacked the ViT architecture twice as an encoder plus a decoder (a second ViT as decoder).
why: Scored better than scaling the single model; base/large variants of the repeated setup overfit.
quote: what was scoring even more was repeating the architecture as an encoder+decoder setup:

what: Applied a sigmoid to the logits and scaled to (1500, 4500), the physical velocity range, with an MAE loss.
why: Inferred: bounds predictions to the valid range. Author said not using it was worse in preliminary tests.
quote: I apply sigmoid on my logits and scale them in range of (1500, 4500)

what: Trained the model underfit, then repeatedly increased the input size and restarted training (350 to 476 to 588 to 700, final 896), for about 300 epochs.
why: The model was severely underfitting; gradual growth was more time efficient and stable than jumping directly.
when: Long ViT training on resizable inputs.
quote: It is much more time efficient and stable to gradually increase the image size this way

trick: Augment velocity models by affine crops
what: Used FiveCrop plus five RandomAffine augmentations (rotation 15, translation, shear, reflection padding, nearest) on existing velocity models to create new models, then forward-modeled them, yielding 10x more data (4.7 million samples) used for pretraining.
why: Heuristic and diffusion generation of new velocity models failed; transforming real ones worked as a way to scale simulated data.
when: Simulation-based tasks where a forward model is available.
quote: I went ahead with using FiveCrop and 5xRandomAffine augmentations

what: Before an exact forward model was available, ran an approximate forward-modeling function and trained a denoiser (same architecture) to predict the noise remaining in the simulated seismic data.
why: Makes simulated inputs resemble the real data distribution.
when: Synthetic data with a sim-to-real gap.
quote: I used forward-modeling + denoiser model setup where denoiser model was the architecture above designed to predict the noise still left in the forward-modeled data

what: Accelerated the public forward-modeling notebook with torch.compile on a 5090, from about 10 to over 5000 images per minute per GPU.
why: Made large-scale data generation and per-epoch regeneration feasible.
when: Using a physics simulator inside a training loop.
quote: using pytorch compile and a 5090, I sped it up to >5000 images per minute per gpu

what: After each epoch, predict velocity models for validation and test seismic data (about 95k), forward-model those predictions into synthetic seismic inputs, and train the next epoch on them.
why: Adds test-distribution-like data with physically consistent input/target pairs; author says the payout is worth the extra time.
when: Inverse problems with a known forward model and unlabeled test inputs.
quote: I take the predicted velocity models and forward-model them to generate what should be the input for them and use this input in training the next epoch.

what: Noticed most gains came from 4 of 10 data families (CurveFault_B, CurveVel_B, Style_A, Style_B), so continued training only on those, and at inference replaced predictions for those families with the specialist model.
why: Removes over half the data, speeds training and focuses capacity.
when: Heterogeneous data where a few subgroups drive most error.
quote: Then for inference, I would replace the predictions that were from these 4 methods with the predictions from the model below

what: Trained a Top4 specialist at 896x896 and ensembled it with the existing Top4 model.
why: Higher resolution improved the score further.
quote: Training this with larger image size at the end, with 896x896 and ensembling that Top4 model to the existing Top4 model yields my best submission

what: Standard recipe for all runs: AdamW, LR 1e-4 cosine to 1e-5, MAE loss, horizontal-flip augmentation and TTA, and EMA of weights.
why: Inferred: stable training and cheap test-time smoothing.
quote: HFlip and TTA

what: Tried UNet decoder, UperNet, Mask2Former, ViT-Adapter, fusion heads and heads more complicated than a linear layer.
why: Listed as not working; the author reasoned spatial misalignment makes decoders with skip connections unhelpful.
quote: Unet decoder, UperNet, Mask2Former, ViT-Adapter, Fusion heads, more complicated heads than a linear layer

trick: Large teacher to small student distillation
what: Trained 5 fold teachers (Qwen2.5-72B) on human-preference data, soft-labelled held-out folds and extra datasets, then distilled into Qwen2.5-14B with CE, KL and cosine losses.
why: Soft labels from a larger model transfer more than hard labels and extend to unlabeled data.
when: Fitting big-model quality in a small inference budget
quote: Distillation was done using three weighted losses (CE against the original label if present, otherwise a hard label, KL and Cosine loss on soft labels).

what: Soft-labelled the training data with the teacher that did not see each fold, and manually reviewed samples with highest disagreement with human labels to fix mislabels.
why: Clean labels and no teacher leakage.
quote: manually review samples which had the highest disagreement with human annotations in order to correct mislabelled pairs

what: Teacher input format added model names before each response.
why: Inferred: model identity is a strong signal for preference; teachers only used to label so it is allowed.
when: Preference data where responder identity is known
quote: we change the input format by adding model names before each response

trick: Synthetic data by difficulty and language
what: Generated 50k pairs from lmsys-chat-1m prompts filtered by Arena-hard complexity score >=3, matching 50% non-English and MT-Bench category distribution, with responses sampled from four large LLMs.
why: Mirrors test distribution.
quote: taking prompts which have ≥ 3 complexity score, while preserving language distribution (50% non-English)

what: Both student and teacher first fully finetuned on ORPO-DPO-mix and UltraFeedback-chinese before task training.
why: Inferred: warms the classifier head and preference sense.
quote: We pretrain both Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct (student) and Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct (teacher)

trick: Both response orders per gradient step
what: Training included both orderings of each pair in one gradient step.
why: Inferred: removes position bias.
quote: For training we include both response orders in a single gradient step.

what: Truncate prompt and both responses proportionally from the middle when over max length.
why: Inferred: keeps beginning and end of each part.
when: Long text inputs for LLM classifiers
quote: proportionally truncating from the middle each in case the formatted sample exceeds the maximum length

what: Increased gradient clipping threshold to 64.0 for fine-tuning.
why: Taken from earlier winners; Inferred: classifier-head gradients are large and default clipping throttles them.
quote: We increase gradient clipping threshold to 64.0 for both

trick: Linear merge of full and partial-data models
what: Final model is a linear weight merge of a model trained on all data and one excluding the last two (synthetic) datasets.
why: Inferred: merges diverse data mixes without extra inference cost.
quote: The final model is a linear merge of two models

what: Second pass with swapped response order run only on the 33% most uncertain samples, using the unmerged model.
why: Spends limited compute where predictions are uncertain.
quote: only on 33% of samples with the most uncertain predictions

what: Concatenated (unpadded) sequences at inference using code from earlier second-place solution.
why: Removes padding waste to fit 14B model in time.
quote: we use sequence concatenation (unpadding)

what: Trained critique model producing 20k GPT-4o critiques for CoT; soft labels with critiques were repeatedly worse.
why: No reason given.
quote: Yet training on soft labels made using critiques was repeatedly worse than without them.

what: Qwen2.5-72B with AWQ and vLLM only covered 5% of samples with TTA and looked much worse on LB.
why: Higher inference cost.
quote: only 5% of samples could be processed with TTA, which ended up looking significantly worse on LB

what: Pruning layers by activation similarity of gemma-2-27b or Qwen-14B was no better than gemma-2-9b.
why: No reason given.
quote: layer pruning gemma-2-27b or Qwen2.5-14B came out the same or worse than just using gemma-2-9b

what: Added PPE-Human-Preference eval set to training despite suspecting it was close to the LB.
why: Feared others would use it.
quote: we still included it into training mix fearing others would
